ARG.title: Milei pledges to abolish Argentina’s central bank and dollarize the economy
summaries: Javier Milei won Argentina’s presidential election with nearly 56% of the vote after pledging to close the central bank, abolish the peso and adopt the US dollar. Following his victory, he said he would implement radical solutions immediately rather than pursue a gradual transition.

BANREP.title: Petro pide al Banco de la República reducir las tasas de interés
summaries: Tras conocerse que el PIB colombiano creció apenas 0,3% en el segundo trimestre, el presidente Gustavo Petro pidió en una publicación en X que la Junta Directiva del Banco de la República comenzara a reducir las tasas de interés. Atribuyó el retroceso de la economía real a las tasas elevadas y afirmó que la inflación había sido controlada.

BANREP.title: Petro government opposes BANREP rate hikes and announces withdrawal from its board
summaries: Finance Minister Germán Ávila abruptly left the board meeting at which BANREP raised its policy rate by one percentage point to 11.25%. Before the bank's announcement, he said the government would not endorse the decision, argued that it restrained economic growth, called for a public debate on monetary policy, and accused the bank of favoring investors over ordinary Colombians. He had also called January's rate increase irresponsible, claiming it would generate inflationary pressure. Before the latest meeting, President Gustavo Petro called another 100-basis-point increase suicidal; afterward, he announced the government's withdrawal from BANREP's board following repeated defeats in monetary-policy votes.

Finance Minister Germán Ávila said he would no longer attend monetary-policy meetings; the next is scheduled for April 30. According to the story, the bank's statutes prevent the board from meeting without him. BANREP governor Leonardo Villar warned that the minister's absence from the next rate-setting meeting would compromise the bank's autonomy, while expressing hope that good sense would prevail.

Villar said he had had no communication with Finance Minister Germán Ávila since Ávila left the March 31 monetary-policy meeting, but remained open to talks despite the minister's attacks on him and his colleagues. He warned that using the minister's absence to force government-preferred decisions would undermine BANREP's independence, and that persistent government attacks erode confidence in both the bank and Colombia, particularly while the government needs financing.

BANXICO.title: AMLO calls on Banxico to lower interest rates and consider growth
summaries: President Andrés Manuel López Obrador told Bloomberg that Banxico should consider economic growth alongside controlling inflation and that lowering its key interest rate, held at 8.25 percent, was important to encourage growth. He said he would leave the decision to the central bank.

BANXICO.title: México propone a Esquivel para dirigir el BID
summaries: El gobierno de México decidió proponer al subgobernador de Banxico Gerardo Esquivel para dirigir el BID, sustituyendo la candidatura de Alicia Bárcena. El periodo de Esquivel en Banxico termina el 31 de diciembre y López Obrador no lo ha propuesto para un nuevo periodo.

BANXICO.title: López Obrador exige usar los DEG para pagar deuda y critica a Esquivel
summaries: El año anterior, López Obrador sugirió que Banxico entregara los derechos especiales de giro para pagar deuda. Gerardo Esquivel explicó en Twitter que, por ley, son activos de reserva que corresponde mantener al banco central. Tras esa explicación, el presidente lo calificó de «ultratecnócrata» y «cuadrado».

BANXICO.title: López Obrador critica las alzas de tasas y pide a Banxico impulsar el crecimiento
summaries: En su conferencia matutina del martes, López Obrador afirmó que aumentar las tasas de interés para combatir la inflación, como hace México, no es la estrategia idónea porque frena el crecimiento. Desde el inicio de su gobierno ha sugerido que Banxico impulse también el crecimiento, aunque su mandato único es controlar la inflación.

BANXICO.title: López Obrador critica a Esquivel como ultratecnócrata
summaries: En 2021, el presidente López Obrador calificó de «ultratecnócrata» al subgobernador de Banco de México Gerardo Esquivel, quien había sido cercano a él.

BANXICO.title: Gobierno propone a Omar Mejía para sustituir a Esquivel
summaries: López Obrador no propuso renovar el mandato de Gerardo Esquivel, que terminó el 31 de diciembre de 2022. El gobierno presentó hasta el 5 de enero la candidatura de Omar Mejía Castelazo para sustituirlo, dejando temporalmente incompleta la Junta de Gobierno. Hacienda destacó su trabajo como asesor de la Junta desde 2019. Carlos Capistrán, de Bank of America, cuestionó su falta de experiencia en política monetaria y banca, aunque expresó confianza en que se mantendría la autonomía del banco.

BANXICO.title: López Obrador pide que Banxico también vigile el crecimiento
summaries: El presidente Andrés Manuel López Obrador sugirió desde Palacio Nacional que Banco de México también debería vigilar el crecimiento económico. La subgobernadora Irene Espinosa respondió que no se necesita un mandato explícito de crecimiento, porque la estabilidad de precios fomenta la inversión y el crecimiento, mientras que tolerar la inflación los perjudicaría.

BANXICO.title: Xóchitl Gálvez pide bajar las tasas de interés de Banxico
summaries: En entrevista con Bloomberg News, Xóchitl Gálvez, coordinadora del Frente Amplio por México y aspirante presidencial opositora, pidió comenzar a bajar las tasas de interés para impulsar las inversiones productivas. También sostuvo que la fortaleza del peso perjudica a la industria exportadora y que la moneda debe reflejar la situación económica.

BANXICO.title: Sheinbaum pide mayor coordinación con Banco de México
summaries: En la celebración del centenario de Banco de México del 25 de agosto de 2025, Claudia Sheinbaum expresó interés en una mayor cercanía con el banco central y afirmó que su autonomía no significa que gobierno, banco central y banca privada deban estar descoordinados.

BANXICO.title: Sheinbaum plantea el mandato dual de Banco de México
summaries: Claudia Sheinbaum abordó semanas antes la posibilidad de un mandato dual para Banco de México y dijo haber hablado del tema con banqueros. La historia señala que no se vislumbra una propuesta concreta.

BANXICO.title: López Obrador pide que Banco de México también atienda el crecimiento
summaries: En una entrevista con Bloomberg en 2019, el entonces presidente Andrés Manuel López Obrador expresó que le gustaría que Banco de México no se ocupara únicamente de la inflación, sino también del crecimiento económico.

BCB.title: Lula questions BCB independence
summaries: Brazilian President Lula questioned the usefulness and limits of BCB independence in a speech the previous day, asking how someone he appointed could diverge from his policies. The story characterized his remarks as also threatening the central bank.
Lula called the bank's autonomy law nonsense. BCB President Roberto Campos defended autonomy, saying it disconnects monetary policy from political cycles and makes policy more effective.
Lula said he would maintain the central bank's independence despite considering it nonsense.

BCB.title: Lula demands Campos explain high interest rates to Congress
summaries: Lula said BCB President Roberto Campos owes Congress an explanation for keeping interest rates high and harming economic recovery. He argued that rates of 13.75% make it impossible to promote growth.
In a Monday-night interview on TV Cultura's Roda Viva, Campos Neto explained the central bank's actions and said he hoped to build closer ties with Lula's government.

Lula renewed his criticism of current monetary policy during a visit to Portugal on Monday. Campos Neto appeared before Congress on Tuesday for the first time since the dispute with Lula began and said monetary policymakers would not start easing until inflation risks were under control.
Lula's pressure for lower interest rates continues as Brazilian inflation has fallen to around 4%; the story links his push to a desire to accelerate the economy after the change in government.

At a Labor Day event with trade union federations, Lula said the current Selic rate was partly responsible for unemployment in Brazil. Amid his criticism, the central bank kept Selic at 13.75% on Wednesday and signaled that further increases or a prolonged period of high rates could be necessary.
The discussion noted that Lula's call for lower interest rates the previous week prompted no market reaction, and that BCB did not cut rates despite his demand.
Lula again criticized the central bank on Thursday, one day after the monetary policy committee maintained Selic at 13.75% and said high rates would remain for as long as necessary.

Analysts consulted by Bloomberg News said Lula had adopted a more moderate tone on monetary policy in recent weeks, while Finance Minister Haddad had taken a technical approach, reducing tensions between the government and the central bank.

Lula's pressure for rate cuts has intensified ahead of the June 21 Copom decision. Two government officials said his economic team increasingly fears that BCB will keep the door closed to an August cut after an expected hold at 13.75%. Finance Minister Haddad viewed Renato Dias Gomes's warning against premature easing as a message from Campos Neto.

Despite Lula's continuing pressure for monetary easing, BCB held its benchmark rate at 13.75% for the seventh consecutive time on June 21. The story says Finance Minister Fernando Haddad's concerns center on higher debt costs and an economic slowdown.

BCB cut interest rates by half a percentage point last week, partly in response to concerns about economic damage from high rates amid pressure from Lula's government. Some economists questioned whether the cut came too soon given remaining inflation pressures.

Lula and Campos Neto held their first meeting after months of tension over interest-rate policy, with Finance Minister Fernando Haddad participating. Lula repeated his criticism of high interest rates and expensive credit, affirmed respect for the central bank's constitutional autonomy, and said he had a record of fiscal responsibility. They agreed to maintain periodic dialogue. Campos Neto had requested the meeting in a letter earlier in September and told Congress before the meeting that the central bank was not opposed to the government and was ready to speak with Lula whenever called. BCB has now implemented two half-percentage-point rate cuts and promised at least two more of the same size by year-end.

BCB.title: Lula calls for a higher inflation target
summaries: Lula said Brazil should have a higher inflation target. The current targets are 3.25% for 2023 and 3% for the following two years, while annual inflation stands at 5.87%.
Campos Neto opposed changes to inflation targets during his Roda Viva interview.

BCB.title: Haddad urges interest-rate cuts following SVB collapse
summaries: Finance Minister Fernando Haddad criticized Brazil's high interest rates on Monday, saying Brazil had room to reduce them and there was little room for further increases globally. He said he had spent the weekend discussing SVB's effects on Brazil with monetary authorities, including BCB President Roberto Campos Neto.

BCB.title: Haddad advocates a longer inflation-target horizon
summaries: Finance Minister Fernando Haddad argued that Brazil was among the few countries pursuing an inflation target over 12 months and advocated extending that horizon, an issue the Lula government had been discussing for several weeks.

BCB.title: Cid Gomes criticizes Selic and demands Campos Neto's resignation
summaries: During Tuesday's Senate hearing, Senator Cid Gomes of PDT criticized the Selic rate using a chalkboard, gave Campos Neto a Santander Brasil cap and asked him to leave the central bank presidency.

BCB.title: Lula nominates Gabriel Galípulo to BCB monetary policy directorship
summaries: Lula nominated Gabriel Galípulo to the BCB monetary policy directorship amid his criticism of high interest rates. Investors feared Galípulo would advance the government's criticism within the bank; the dollar rose 1.2% following Monday's announcement. Haddad denied seeking to form a government bloc within BCB, saying the aim was greater coordination between fiscal and monetary policy, and said Campos Neto had first suggested Galípulo. The nomination requires Senate approval.

BCB.title: Lula advocates raising inflation target to enable interest-rate cuts
summaries: Lula has advocated raising the inflation target to 4.5% to allow interest-rate cuts. Investors still fear an increase at the National Monetary Council's late-June meeting, although analysts see growing chances of retaining the 3% target from next year. Eurasia executive Christopher Garman said the economic team wants to maintain the target, but Lula's agreement remains uncertain.

BCB.title: Senators press BCB for interest-rate cuts
summaries: Senators, described as the final guarantors of BCB's autonomy, are exerting growing pressure for interest-rate cuts ahead of the June 21 Copom decision.
BCB maintained its benchmark rate at 13.75% on June 21 despite senators' continuing calls for cuts, asking for patience and calm because some indicators remained above target.

BCB.title: Business leaders threaten Campos's mandate over rate-cut demands
summaries: Some business leaders told members of the government's economic team that Roberto Campos could be stripped of his mandate if BCB did not cut rates or clearly signal monetary easing at its June 21 meeting. BCB instead kept rates unchanged.

BCB.title: Senators warn of possible motion to shorten Campos's mandate
summaries: Some senators warned that persistent dissatisfaction after BCB's June 21 decision could grow into a motion to shorten Roberto Campos's mandate as central bank president, a step the story says Brazilian law permits.

BCB.title: Lula critica Campos Neto por manter juros elevados
summaries: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva criticou repetidamente o presidente do Banco Central, Roberto Campos Neto, por manter os juros elevados.

BCB.title: Lula presiona al BCB para reducir las tasas de interés
summaries: En una entrevista radial el 18 de junio, Lula afirmó que las tasas de interés no se ajustan a la realidad económica de Brasil y que no se puede continuar con tasas prohibitivas porque la inflación está totalmente controlada. Presionó al BCB para que dé mayor prioridad al crecimiento económico.

El Copom mantuvo por unanimidad la tasa Selic en 10,5%, pausando el ciclo de recortes iniciado en agosto. Tanto Roberto Campos Neto, señalado como blanco de las críticas de Lula, como los directores nombrados por el presidente votaron por mantener la tasa.

BCB.title: Lula promete nombrar un sucesor distinto de Campos Neto
summaries: En la entrevista del 18 de junio, Lula acusó a Roberto Campos Neto de actuar sin autonomía y prometió proponer un sucesor completamente diferente cuando termine su mandato en 2024. Dijo que elegiría a alguien comprometido con el desarrollo y el control de la inflación, sin centrarse exclusivamente en esta última, e inmune a las presiones de los mercados financieros.

BCB.title: Lula criticizes BCB's control of interest rates
summaries: The story reports increased political tensions between President Lula and BCB because Lula was irritated by monetary policymakers' control of interest rates.

BCB.title: Government austerity cuts constrain BCB resources
summaries: BCB has been affected by federal austerity as Lula seeks budget space to prioritize social assistance. Its inflation-adjusted 2023 budget was about 17% below its level eight years earlier, while its 2024 investment budget was just over one-fifth of the amount planned for 2023. Budget and staffing constraints have delayed Pix updates and raised concerns about financial supervision.

BCB.title: Haddad urges BCB to signal interest-rate cuts
summaries: At Bloomberg Green in São Paulo, Finance Minister Fernando Haddad criticized the BCB’s 15% policy rate as an excessive dose of medicine and said it was time to signal cuts. He argued that high interest payments drive public-debt growth and questioned how much longer inflation would take to reach the 3% target if rates were 12% instead of 15%. Haddad characterized his exchanges with the central bank as healthy dialogue.

BCB.title: Lula critica corte insuficiente da Selic
summaries: O presidente Lula criticou como insuficiente o corte de 0,25 ponto percentual da Selic realizado pelo Banco Central em março, que levou a taxa a 14,75%.

BCB.title: Durigan atribui aumento da dívida à política monetária
summaries: Em Washington, durante reuniões do FMI e do Banco Mundial, o ministro da Fazenda, Dário Durigan, atribuiu o aumento da dívida pública à política monetária, e não aos gastos, defendendo que o governo fez sua parte no campo fiscal e que a situação fiscal melhorou ano após ano.

BCCH.title: Government urges BCCH to clarify foreign-exchange intervention stance
summaries: Chile’s finance minister said BCCH had to state its position on foreign-exchange intervention, while the government spokesperson said it should intervene or clarify its stance. BCCH initially said there were no grounds to intervene, but subsequently announced a US$25 billion intervention program running daily through September amid continued peso depreciation.

BCRA.title: Javier Millet threatens to burn down Argentina’s central bank
summaries: Right-wing libertarian presidential candidate Javier Millet, who finished first in Argentina’s presidential primary, has threatened to “burn down the central bank” and wants to align the peso to the US dollar.
The story reports that following Milei’s strong primary-election performance, the peso depreciated by approximately 14–15% and BCRA raised interest rates from around 90% to 108%.

The story explicitly describes Javier Milley’s proposal to eliminate BCRA and dollarize Argentina’s economy. On August 14, the official dollar exchange rate rose 22% to 350 pesos per dollar, and BCRA raised its nominal annual LELIQ rate by 21 percentage points to 118%, with an effective annual rate of 209%.

Milei said that, if elected, he would put economist Emilio Ocampo, his informal dollarization adviser, in charge of BCRA to close it. He described BCRA as having no reason to exist. He said dollarization would be among his first measures: people would initially choose currencies voluntarily, with full dollarization once two-thirds of the monetary base had been converted. He also said he would call referendums if he could not secure legislative consensus for his measures.

BCRA.title: Javier Milei calls for closing BCRA and dollarizing Argentina
summaries: Newly elected president Javier Milei wants to close BCRA and replace the Argentine peso with the US dollar, blaming inflation on state deficits financed through money printing. He previously said on talk shows that he would blow up the central bank if elected, but has since moderated his language to calling for its closure.

BCRA.title: Milei defende novos cortes de juros para remover controles cambiais
summaries: Em entrevista a uma rádio na quarta-feira, o presidente Javier Milei afirmou que espera suspender os controles cambiais ainda este ano e que reduzir os juros para limpar o balanço do BCRA é parte essencial desse processo. Acrescentou que imaginava outro corte de juros.
Desde o início do mandato de Milei, os juros foram cortados seis vezes, passando de 136% para 40% na semana anterior à publicação.

BCRA.title: Milei reafirma dolarização e fim da emissão de pesos pelo BCRA
summaries: Em evento empresarial em Buenos Aires na terça-feira, Javier Milei reafirmou seu plano de dolarização. Após sanear o balanço do BCRA mediante pagamento de passivos locais e reformar o sistema financeiro, pretende permitir a livre concorrência entre peso e dólar, com câmbio flexível para o peso. O BCRA deixaria de emitir pesos, permitindo sua substituição pelo dólar. Milei afirmou que os pesos serão uma peça de museu; o objetivo final é fechar o banco central.

BCRA.title: Milei proposes banning BCRA financing of public spending
summaries: President Javier Milei presented a bill to prohibit BCRA from financing public spending, reinforce its currency-stability mandate, and require two-thirds approval in both congressional chambers to remove its president. In a nationally televised address, he accused BCRA of enabling political theft and said the reform would end it.

BCRA.title: Milei pledges to close BCRA
summaries: During his 2023 presidential campaign, Javier Milei pledged to dollarize the economy and close BCRA, calling it the worst garbage on earth. After one year in office, he reiterated a commitment to close it within four years. His announcement of the new reform last week did not mention that closure plan.

BCRA.title: Kirchner government expands BCRA mandate
summaries: In 2012, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner's government expanded BCRA's mandate to include employment and economic development with social equity, giving the bank greater flexibility to print money to finance public spending.

BID.title: México cambia su candidato a la presidencia del BID
summaries: México propondrá a Gerardo Esquivel para dirigir el BID en lugar de Alicia Bárcena. Según personas familiarizadas con la decisión, el cambio respondió en parte a la preocupación de Estados Unidos por la postura política de Bárcena. Bárcena confirmó el retiro de su candidatura y agradeció al presidente López Obrador su comprensión.

BID.title: Salazar pide bloquear la candidatura de Bárcena al BID
summaries: La congresista republicana María Elvira Salazar envió una carta a Janet Yellen solicitando que Estados Unidos votara contra Alicia Bárcena para dirigir el BID, acusándola de simpatizar con el comunismo y de haber elogiado a Fidel Castro y Hugo Chávez. Tras conocerse la propuesta de Esquivel, Salazar reiteró que no quería al frente del BID a funcionarios que facilitaran préstamos a regímenes opresores.

BOE.title: Martin Malone urges BOE to align policy with UK growth agenda
summaries: AlphaBook chief economic adviser Martin Malone called for the Bank of England to align monetary policy with the new government's economic agenda after Mark Carney steps aside in February. He said the BOE had made mistakes by raising interest rates and should proactively support growth, including playing its part if UK economic stagnation persists.

BOE.title: Rafa Mayoral attacks Bank of Spain governor over minimum-wage study
summaries: Podemos MP Rafa Mayoral attacked Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernández de Cos from the Congress podium after the bank published a study estimating that the 2019 minimum-wage increase reduced employment by up to 174,000 jobs, including jobs not created. Mayoral said the governor should be chased away with blows and accused the bank of attacking vulnerable people's interests.

BOE.title: Governments pressure central banks to tackle inflation
summaries: The story describes strong pressure from governments on central banks, including in its discussion of the Bank of England, to tackle inflation under their price-stability mandates because rising prices have become a political, social and purchasing-power concern. No individual political actor is named.

BOE.title: Liz Truss proposes reviewing BOE mandate
summaries: Conservative leadership candidate Liz Truss said she would look at the Bank of Japan's model when considering changes to the Bank of England's mandate, while saying she would not touch its independence.
Liz Truss, the front runner to become the next prime minister, is highly critical of the Bank of England's inflation-fighting record.
Truss ally Suella Braverman said the mandate review would examine the Bank of England's independence over interest rates, bringing that independence under scrutiny.
Conservative Party members selected Truss as party leader and next prime minister, bringing her campaign proposal to review the Bank of England's mandate into the context of her incoming government.

Carl Weinberg said the Truss government had backed away from its campaign position on intervening in Bank of England independence. He warned that conflict between Bank rate hikes and the government's deficit-financed stimulus could nevertheless prompt government interference, potentially sending sterling into a tailspin.

BOE.title: Kemi Badenoch criticizes parliamentary scrutiny of BOE
summaries: Conservative leadership candidate Kemi Badenoch said MPs had not been marking the Bank of England's homework well enough.

BOE.title: Tom Tugendhat criticizes quantitative easing
summaries: The story reports that Conservative leadership candidate Tom Tugendhat had previously blamed the Bank of England's quantitative easing.

BOE.title: UK government seeks powers to override financial regulation
summaries: The government wants call-in powers to veto independently set financial services regulations, bolstering its post-Brexit powers. It is deferring these powers from the Financial Services and Markets Bill until a new prime minister and chancellor are in place. Former Chancellor Rishi Sunak is said to favor the powers.

BOE.title: Liz Truss raises possibility of merging regulators
summaries: During her leadership campaign, Liz Truss discussed the possibility of merging regulators, causing concern at the Bank of England. Whether she will pursue the proposal remains uncertain.

BOE.title: House of Lords inquiry into BOE quantitative easing
summaries: The story cites a House of Lords inquiry into quantitative easing as a source of increased political pressure on Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey.

BOE.title: Kwasi Kwateng blames BOE for potential market turmoil
summaries: UK Chancellor Kwasi Kwateng said the Bank of England would be to blame if markets tank after its bond-buying program ends.

Speaking to Sky News on the sidelines of the IMF annual meeting, Kwateng called any turmoil after the Bank withdraws support on Friday "a matter for the governor," adding pressure on the Bank to continue its emergency bond-buying support.

BOE.title: Alleged UK government and BOE pressure to lower Libor
summaries: Andy Verity's book alleges top-down intervention during the 2008 crisis, citing a recorded Barclays manager saying the UK government and Bank of England were pressuring the bank to lower Libor rates so state interventions would appear to be working. The Bank of England told the Times the claims were completely unsubstantiated.

BOE.title: Lords committee calls for regular BOE reviews and narrower remit
summaries: The House of Lords Economic Affairs Committee called for lawmakers to assess the Bank of England every five years following errors that allowed inflation to surge. In a report marking 25 years of BOE independence, committee members, including former governor Mervyn King, also pushed to trim the bank's remit and criticised its decision-making.

BOE.title: Hunt raises prospect of interest rate cuts in 2024
summaries: UK Chancellor Jeremy Hunt raised the prospect of cutting interest rates in 2024 and told the Financial Times that the country needs to throw off its economic pessimism next year. A Bank of England governor said uncertainty over the UK labour market meant the bank needed to wait before cutting rates.

BOE.title: Sánchez to appoint minister Escrivá as Bank of Spain governor
summaries: Pedro Sánchez has decided to appoint Digital Transformation Minister José Luis Escrivá as governor of the Bank of Spain, having proposed him in negotiations with the PP. The government defends his technical qualifications; Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo will explain the choice to parliamentary groups.

Escrivá will serve a six-year term. Sánchez imposed his choice without the customary consensus with the main opposition party. The story states that the appointment will give the PSOE its greatest power within the Bank of Spain in 30 years and places Escrivá in a position to assess government decisions in which he participated.

Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo defended the appointment, saying the Bank of Spain is neither a government watchdog nor a counterweight to it, but is legally tasked with advising the government autonomously and independently.

BOE.title: PP opposes Escrivá appointment and refuses deputy-governor nomination
summaries: The PP denounces José Luis Escrivá’s appointment as an invasion and colonization of the Bank of Spain, arguing that appointing a serving minister will damage its credibility. In protest, the party refuses to propose a candidate for deputy governor.
PP politician Jaime de Olano attacked Cuerpo over the appointment, calling Sánchez’s government dangerous to institutional independence and democracy.

BOE.title: Government to choose deputy governor after PP withdraws
summaries: Following the PP’s refusal to nominate a deputy governor, Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said the government would fill the vacancy itself and appoint a woman to maintain gender balance in the Bank of Spain’s leadership.

BOE.title: Pat McFadden criticizes Carney's mixed interest-rate signals
summaries: At a British parliamentary committee hearing in June 2014, Labour MP Pat McFadden compared the Bank of England to an 'unreliable boyfriend,' criticizing Governor Mark Carney for mixed messages about future interest rates and seeking greater certainty about the bank's plans.

BOE.title: UK lawmakers challenge need for digital pound
summaries: Lawmakers in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords have attacked the Bank of England's digital pound project, questioning whether it is needed.

BOE.title: Reeves pushes for Revolut banking approval
summaries: Chancellor Rachel Reeves arranged a meeting between financial watchdogs and Revolut to advance its goal of becoming a fully fledged bank, seeking approval as soon as possible. Governor Andrew Bailey stopped the meeting, according to people familiar with the matter.

BOE.title: Reeves pushes financial deregulation
summaries: Chancellor Rachel Reeves is pushing financial deregulation. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has publicly expressed frustration with her push and distanced himself from the effort.

BOE.title: Truss calls for Bank of England accountability to politicians
summaries: Former Prime Minister Liz Truss said the Bank of England needs to be accountable to politicians and that the current system does not work. In a Bloomberg interview, she expressed sympathy with Donald Trump's approach to the Federal Reserve and stressed the importance of monetary policy.

BOE.title: Reform attacks Bank of England over quantitative tightening losses
summaries: Reform, which is leading in the polls, has criticized the Bank of England's handling of quantitative tightening, accusing it of racking up large taxpayer losses as it unwinds its balance sheet.

BOE.title: Farage threatens to replace Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey
summaries: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in a Bloomberg interview that his party might replace Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey if it came to office, saying Bailey had 'had a good run.'

BOE.title: Reeves signals pressure on Bank of England to cut interest rates
summaries: In a pre-budget speech, Chancellor Rachel Reeves said her budget choices would focus on lowering inflation and creating conditions for interest rate cuts to support growth and improve living costs. Bloomberg commentator Marcus Ashworth characterized the remarks as pressure on the Bank of England to cut rates in response to her planned fiscal restraint.

Reeves criticized the BOE in her Tuesday speech for holding rates at 4%, saying this was constraining business borrowing. Bloomberg correspondent Lizzie Burden said the BOE was the speech's real target audience and noted that cuts to 3% could save Reeves around £10 billion in borrowing costs at next year's budget compared with the OBR's March forecast.

BOF.title: Macron appoints close aide Emmanuel Moulin as Banque de France governor
summaries: President Emmanuel Macron proposed his former Élysée secretary-general Emmanuel Moulin to succeed François Villeroy de Galhau, whose departure comes a year before his term ends. Opponents accused Macron of locking in control of institutions beyond the 2027 presidential election. Parliamentary committees approved the nomination despite 58 votes against and 52 in favor, because opposition fell below the three-fifths rejection threshold. The Council of Ministers confirmed the appointment on May 27; Moulin begins a six-year term on June 2.

BOF.title: Left-wing opposition challenges Moulin’s independence
summaries: Left-wing opponents acknowledged Emmanuel Moulin’s competence but opposed his nomination as Banque de France governor because of his political proximity to the executive and rapid transition from the Élysée to an independent institution. LFI deputy Éric Coquerel, chair of the National Assembly finance committee, voted against him. Moulin defended himself by saying he had advised politicians without exercising political functions and citing previous governors’ senior government roles.

BOF.title: RN and UDR oppose Moulin’s appointment
summaries: The RN and its ally UDR opposed Emmanuel Moulin’s nomination as Banque de France governor, accusing him of embodying the deep state and being closely beholden to Emmanuel Macron. His appointment nevertheless cleared parliamentary scrutiny and was confirmed by the Council of Ministers.

BOF.title: Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposes cancelling French debt held by Banque de France
summaries: In the presidential campaign, LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposes cancelling the French debt held by the Banque de France on behalf of the ECB, approximately 18% of total French debt or €600 billion. He said the debt could simply be taken from the Banque de France and thrown into the fire.

ECB President Christine Lagarde rejected Mélenchon's proposal to cancel government bonds held by the Banque de France and ECB, saying it makes no legal, technical or financial sense and that transferring debt between pockets does not cancel it.

BOI.title: Fazzolari attacks Bank of Italy over budget criticism
summaries: Undersecretary Giovan Battista Fazzolari challenged the Bank of Italy's criticism of the Meloni government's budget, saying it represents banks' views and interests in receiving commissions. He said opposition from the bank, Confindustria and unions indicated the government was not doing badly and would not change direction. Government sources subsequently described the bank's position as legitimate and said its autonomy had never been questioned.

BOI.title: Israeli government challenges BOI governor over judicial reform criticism
summaries: The Israeli government challenged BOI Governor Amir Yaron in recent weeks for criticizing Benjamin Netanyahu’s proposed judicial reform. Although he had been due to leave his post at year-end, he will remain in office to help the economy confront the war with Hamas.

BOI.title: Fratelli d’Italia pushes amendment asserting state ownership of Bank of Italy gold
summaries: Fratelli d’Italia circulated a confidential dossier defending a budget amendment asserting state ownership of the Bank of Italy’s gold reserves, ahead of talks between Economy Minister Giorgetti and ECB President Lagarde. The dossier argues that private shareholders, including some controlled by foreign groups, must not be allowed to claim rights over the reserves. The ECB and opposition parties fear pressure on the Bank of Italy’s independence and a potentially dangerous precedent.

BOJ.title: Finance Minister Suzuki warns over yen moves as intervention looms
summaries: Japanese Finance Minister Suzuki said he was very concerned about market moves and was closely watching them as the dollar tested 145 yen. The story also reported checks with foreign-exchange market participants, described as a potential precursor to intervention.

The story reported warnings from Japan's chief currency official as well as Suzuki, describing them as the strongest words yet. Nikkei reported that the BOJ conducted a rate check, and the yen strengthened away from 145 per dollar amid expectations of possible foreign-exchange intervention.
The finance minister indicated that the ministry would collaborate with the Bank of Japan as it monitored yen moves.

Finance Minister Suzuki and Japan's top currency official renewed verbal intervention warnings, including at the G20, as the yen touched a 32-year low with 150 per dollar in sight. The story reported no indication of actual market intervention so far that day.

BOJ.title: Suzuki warns of intervention against excessive yen moves
summaries: Finance Minister Suzuki said Japan could intervene if necessary to curb excessive yen movements as the dollar-yen exchange rate approached 150. A meeting with the prime minister was also arranged to discuss economic conditions. The story linked further yen depreciation amid rising inflation to increased pressure on the BOJ.

BOJ.title: Abe government sought a weaker yen under Abenomics
summaries: The story recalled that a weaker yen was a desired outcome during Shinzo Abe's premiership under Abenomics, contrasting that preference with current concerns about depreciation amid rising inflation.

BOJ.title: Japanese politicians pressure BOJ over weak yen
summaries: Several prominent Japanese politicians had drawn attention to the weak yen in recent weeks. The story reports a view that political pressure influenced the BOJ's decision to raise interest rates, potentially straining government–BOJ relations and affecting Prime Minister Fumio Kishida's bid for reelection as ruling-party leader.

LDP leadership contender Taro Kono has publicly expressed views on what the BOJ should do. LDP Secretary General Toshimitsu Motegi, another expected contender, has advocated normalization of BOJ policy.

BOJ.title: Sanae Takaichi backs continued easy BOJ policy
summaries: Cabinet member and potential LDP leadership candidate Sanae Takaichi has backed keeping BOJ policy settings easy.

BOJ.title: Nakasone promises lower Japanese interest rates
summaries: In May 1987, Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone promised US President Ronald Reagan that Japan would lower interest rates to help stabilize the dollar.

BOJ.title: Abe appoints BOJ governor aligned with Abenomics
summaries: Shinzo Abe brought in a BOJ governor who would pursue the central-bank policies he wanted under Abenomics. According to the governor's memoirs as described in the story, Abe did not directly issue instructions, but his preferences were clear and policy followed them.

BOJ.title: Shigeru Ishiba criticizes BOJ low-rate policy
summaries: New Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba has criticized the BOJ's low-interest-rate policy and favored higher rates. His previously signaled monetary-policy stance caused market concern following his leadership victory.

BOJ.title: Ishiba says Japan is not ready for another BOJ rate hike
summaries: Japan's new Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba met with the BOJ governor and said Japan was not ready for another interest-rate increase.

BOJ.title: US Treasury Secretary Bessant criticizes BOJ as behind the curve
summaries: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant said in a Bloomberg interview that the BOJ was behind the curve, putting pressure on it to accelerate rate hikes. The yen strengthened and Japanese government bonds weakened following his comments.
Bessant said the BOJ should raise interest rates because of inflation risk.

BOJ.title: Potential Ishiba successor opposes BOJ policy normalization
summaries: Following Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba's resignation, one unnamed leading contender to replace him opposes continued BOJ policy normalization and favors a more accommodative monetary stance, alongside fiscal loosening.
The contender is identified as Sanae Takaichi, who favors stimulus measures and would likely prefer the BOJ to take a more cautious approach to rate hikes.

Sanae Takaichi won the LDP leadership race and is expected to become prime minister. The story reports that she called the prospect of BOJ rate hikes "stupid" last year, although she has since moderated her rhetoric. Her victory prompted traders to reassess the likelihood of a BOJ rate hike at its meeting later in October.

The story describes Takaichi's policy stance as opposing further BOJ rate hikes and favoring rates staying unchanged or potentially falling. Expectations of this stance, alongside targeted fiscal stimulus, contributed to a roughly 4% rally in Japanese equities and a weaker yen.
Takaichi has said the BOJ should maintain an easing policy because Japan is not fully out of deflation, despite a cost-of-living crisis, and cautioned against tightening monetary policy too much.

Now prime minister, Sanae Takaichi continues to call for the BOJ to slow interest-rate hikes. This week, she said the central bank should focus on wage-driven inflation rather than rising living costs.

The story explains that Takaichi wants the BOJ to slow rate hikes because she prioritizes economic growth over measures that could constrain it, even though higher rates could strengthen the yen and ease imported inflation.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met with the BOJ governor this week amid debate over the bank's December policy decision.

Lecturer Fumigato said government representatives sit at the table during BOJ policy decisions, making it difficult for the legally independent bank to go directly against government wishes. The lecturer suggested Takaichi's preference for lower interest rates could therefore influence BOJ decisions.

BOJ.title: Finance Minister Katayama warns over yen weakness
summaries: As the dollar approached 155 yen, Japan's new Finance Minister Katayama said authorities were on alert. The story describes her as disliking an excessively weak currency and reports that markets appeared to take the warning lightly.

Katayama sharpened her warnings over yen weakness, saying authorities could take a bolder step and that their hands were free. Markets took the warning more seriously than earlier remarks, with the yen strengthening from around 157.3 per dollar the previous day to below 156. The story notes that a September agreement with the United States permits currency intervention in cases of excessive volatility.

BOJ.title: Japan's finance minister warns of coordinated yen intervention
summaries: Finance Minister Katayama emphasized decisive action and said coordinated action with the United States was possible as the dollar approached 160 yen. Japanese officials have repeatedly issued verbal warnings, and Katayama had spoken with U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent earlier in the week.

BOJ.title: Bessent urges BOJ to accelerate interest-rate increases
summaries: During a visit to Tokyo, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the BOJ risked falling behind the curve and repeatedly emphasized Japan's strong economic fundamentals in meetings with officials, signaling pressure for the bank to proceed with interest-rate increases.

BOJ.title: Takaichi administration constrains faster BOJ rate hikes
summaries: Economists surveyed by Bloomberg viewed Prime Minister Takaichi's administration as an obstacle to faster BOJ rate increases. The government's annual economic policy guidelines were approved only in the past week after repeated revisions, particularly to language concerning expectations for the BOJ and its cooperation with the government in achieving policy goals.
Recent reports indicate that the Takaichi administration has given the BOJ a green light to turn more hawkish or at least signal the prospect of more frequent rate hikes.

BOJ.title: US pressure for BOJ rate increases to support yen intervention
summaries: The story says Americans insist that the BOJ must raise interest rates for yen intervention to succeed.

NHK reported, citing an interview with a US Treasury official, that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant told Japan's finance minister and central bank governor that Japan should raise interest rates and communicate its path toward more sustainable finances.

Speaking at an event in Texas, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant challenged traders to bet against his efforts to boost the yen, claiming asymmetric information and insight into what the BOJ and Japanese policymakers would do when intervening in the yen.

The story describes overt US pressure on the BOJ to accelerate normalization and adopt a more aggressive schedule of interest rate increases. Markets expect a rate increase next week, with speculation about a further increase in October.

Katayama indirectly criticized Bessant's public remarks, calling his phrase 'I am the house' somewhat frightening after Japanese media translated it as an illegal casino. The story says Japan's ruling party is privately unhappy with Bessant's pressure on exchange rates and interest rates, which constrains the Takaichi administration's room to pursue growth-oriented policies and fiscal expansion.

The BOJ raised its benchmark interest rate to 1.25%, its highest level in thirty years, a move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant had wanted it to take. The story reports that Bessant assisted Tokyo in supporting the yen over the summer.

BOT.title: Political pressure on BOT to cut interest rates
summaries: The Bank of Thailand faces political pressure to cut interest rates. Markets are betting that the central bank will yield to that pressure.

CBI.title: US sanctions Iran’s central bank after Saudi oil attacks
summaries: The US announced new sanctions on Iran’s central bank on Friday after President Trump threatened sanctions following attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities. Treasury Secretary Stephen Mnuchin said the sanctions cut off the country’s last remaining source of funds. The Trump administration attributed the attacks to Iran, which denied responsibility.

CBI.title: Rouhani dismisses central bank chief Hemati over presidential candidacy
summaries: Central bank chief Abdulazna Hemati was dismissed after it became clear he would run in Iran’s June 18 presidential election. Outgoing President Hassan Rouhani told him that his candidacy affected monetary policy.

CBI.title: Trump administration sanctions Iran's central bank
summaries: The story describes President Trump's 2018 withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal and renewed sanctions aimed at curbing Iran's nuclear program. Iran's central bank was placed under sanctions, restricting the country's access to the international financial system.

CBI.title: Iranian politicians demand Ayande Bank's closure
summaries: Iranian politicians criticized the central bank for printing too much money to support Ayande Bank amid soaring inflation and demanded the lender's closure as the currency crisis worsened. In October 2025, the central bank announced that Ayande would be shut down.

CBN.title: Opposition presidential candidate pledges new CBN governor and floating naira
summaries: Nigeria's main opposition presidential candidate, Mr Abu Bakr, said he would appoint a new central bank governor when the incumbent's term expires and float the naira if elected. He criticized the governor for pursuing the wrong central bank policy. The presidential election is scheduled for February 16.

CBR.title: UK, US and EU sanctions target Russia's central bank
summaries: The UK announced restrictions prohibiting UK persons from dealing with the Central Bank of Russia, acting in concert with the US and EU following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The UK measures join actions announced over the weekend and raise questions about how much of the central bank's approximately $600 billion in reserves it can access.

Senior U.S. officials announced coordinated sanctions intended to prevent Russia's central bank from using emergency reserve currencies. Amid the sanctions, the ruble reached a record low of 119 to the dollar, and the central bank more than doubled its benchmark interest rate to 20 percent and said stock trading would remain suspended on Tuesday.

CBR.title: TsMAKP warns against CBR's high-interest-rate policy
summaries: Russian think tank TsMAKP, headed by Dmitry Belousov, brother of Defence Minister Andrei Belousov, publicly warned that the central bank's actions were pushing Russia's economy toward a dangerous scenario.

CBR.title: Rostec chief criticizes CBR's high interest rates
summaries: The head of Russian defence conglomerate Rostec raised the alarm over the central bank's high interest rates amid growing criticism of their effects on businesses.

CBR.title: Oleg Deripaska criticizes CBR's high interest rates
summaries: Aluminium magnate and influential oligarch Oleg Deripaska criticized the central bank amid mounting business opposition to its high-interest-rate policy.

CBR.title: Business union seeks presidential power to lower CBR rates
summaries: The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs publicly advocated giving Vladimir Putin the authority to lower interest rates himself, challenging the central bank's independence.

CBR.title: Putin urges compromise to restrain CBR interest rates
summaries: In a speech at a congress in Moscow, Vladimir Putin suggested finding a middle ground between businesses and the central bank and said interest rates should not become too high. Governor Elvira Nabiullina subsequently said a further rate increase was not set in stone and would need to be considered.

CBR.title: Putin signals support for lower interest rates
summaries: Russian President Vladimir Putin hinted earlier in the week that he would support a lower central bank interest rate to revive economic growth, as high rates raised borrowing costs for businesses.

CBR.title: Putin calls for a cut in the central bank’s key interest rate
summaries: Putin recently advocated lowering the Central Bank of Russia’s key interest rate ahead of its leadership meeting. The story frames the meeting as a test of the bank’s independence, noting that a cut could stimulate the weakening economy but also further destabilize it.

Putin signaled several times before the July policy decision that he wanted lower interest rates. The bank subsequently cut its base rate by 25 basis points to 14%, using explanations it had not previously relied on; many analysts viewed the move as yielding to pressure despite inflation and growth data. Source reporting indicates Governor Elvira Nabiullina may have accepted arguments for greater inflation flexibility and rate cuts to help companies survive wartime stagnation. The bank also raised its year-end inflation forecast from 4.5–5.5% to 6–7%.

CBRT.title: Erdogan undermines CBRT independence
summaries: The story reports that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has brought the previously independent central bank under his control, amid a sharp fall in the lira.

CBRT.title: Erdogan pressures CBRT to block interest-rate increases
summaries: President Erdogan is exerting increasing influence over CBRT and preventing it from raising interest rates to counter inflation. The story states that he pressured the central bank to keep rates from rising amid Turkey's currency crisis.

CBRT.title: Turkey's central bank governor fired
summaries: Turkey's central bank governor was fired, raising concerns about credibility and who controls monetary policy. The lira fell nearly 3% at the market open before recovering some losses.
President Erdogan removed the central bank governor just weeks before a policy decision.

Erdogan dismissed Governor Murat Cetinkaya on Saturday ahead of the July 25 policy decision, and a replacement is now in place. Erdogan reportedly urged lawmakers to support the government's economic policies, including his belief that higher interest rates cause inflation. Nick Wall of Marian Global Investors said Cetinkaya had been unwilling to cut rates as much as Erdogan wanted and that the dismissal left the central bank effectively under Erdogan's control.

Commerzbank FX strategist Esther Reichelt said the governor's removal meant emergency rate hikes could no longer be expected, warning that lira depreciation could fuel inflation and further depreciation expectations.
Following the governor's removal, the Turkish lira one-year currency swap rate rose as much as 76 basis points to 20.3%, while the lira was down 2.66%.

Societe Generale, Credit Agricole and RBC reversed their calls for gains in the lira following the governor's removal. The story reports expectations of a rate cut on July 25 amid renewed concerns about central bank independence.
The presenter described CBRT as no longer independent and under Erdogan, saying it had cut interest rates by roughly eight and a quarter percent even as the lira continued strengthening.

CBRT.title: Erdogan calls for single-digit interest rates in 2020
summaries: President Erdogan said interest rates would move to single digits in 2020, signaling pressure on CBRT to continue lowering rates. He maintains that lower borrowing costs bring down inflation.

CBRT.title: Erdogan pressures CBRT to cut rates to single digits
summaries: President Erdogan has been pressuring Turkey's central bank to reduce interest rates to single digits in 2020. Ahead of its February 19 decision, the policy rate stood at 11.25%, with inflation accelerating and the lira depreciating after seven months of easing.

CBRT.title: Erdogan pressures CBRT to keep interest rates low
summaries: President Erdogan and his allies favor cheap credit to pursue growth. Ahead of CBRT's September 24 meeting, the bank is described as under Erdogan's close control and reluctant to raise its benchmark rate because he opposes higher interest rates, limiting its freedom to address inflation and lira weakness.

Erdogan remained silent after September's interest-rate increase, despite previously expressing displeasure with central bankers' decisions. At October's policy meeting, CBRT left rates unchanged despite expectations of another increase, followed by repeated record lows in the lira.

CBRT.title: Erdogan fires CBRT governor over rate-cut dispute
summaries: Erdogan fired the central bank governor in 2019 following a disagreement over the pace and depth of interest-rate cuts.

CBRT.title: CBRT governor fired amid Turkish economic leadership shake-up
summaries: Turkey's central bank governor was fired a day before President Erdogan's son-in-law, the finance minister, unexpectedly resigned citing unspecified health reasons. The departures could signal a dramatic shift in economic policy.

Erdogan fired the governor after briefings about the worsening economic situation and appointed Naji Abal, a bureaucrat turned politician known not to get along with his son-in-law. On Wednesday, Erdogan said he would swallow a bitter pill if necessary to restore the economy. The new governor's first policy meeting next week will test his political room to deliver an expected substantial rate increase.

CBRT.title: Turkish president fires central bank governor after rate increase
summaries: Turkey's president fired the central bank governor three months into his tenure after he raised interest rates to tame inflation, replacing him with an academic who had lobbied for lower interest rates.

Erdogan's dismissal followed a 200-basis-point interest-rate hike the previous week and was enacted by an overnight decree. Turkey now has its fourth central bank governor in less than two years. The lira plunged as much as 15% against the dollar following the replacement.

The replacement governor, described as an Erdogan party loyalist, has expressed the view that higher interest rates raise inflation. Following the dismissal, the lira initially fell about 16% and stocks fell 9% on Monday.

CBRT.title: Erdogan pushes lower interest rates despite soaring inflation
summaries: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describes himself as an enemy of interest rates and says lowering rates will slow price rises, with inflation nearly 20 percent in August. His government favors credit-driven economic stimulus as voter support declines. The CBRT cut its base rate by one percentage point despite soaring inflation.

Driven by President Erdogan's unorthodox monetary ideas, the CBRT delivered a larger-than-expected rate cut on October 21, citing transitory inflation and saying it had limited room for further reductions this year. The lira subsequently fell to a record low.

Erdogan continues to demand lower interest rates ahead of the November 18 CBRT decision. Economists generally expect a 100-basis-point cut to meet his demands, despite annual inflation above 19%. The lira has fallen for eight consecutive days, losing nearly 11%.

Under enormous pressure from President Erdogan to keep rates as low as possible, the CBRT cut interest rates by another percentage point to 15%, its third consecutive cut, and indicated another cut would follow before long. With inflation around 20%, the lira fell 4% in response, reaching about 11 to the dollar.

Erdogan intensified his campaign for lower interest rates and had a meeting or call with the central bank governor. In a speech earlier this week, he highlighted growth and employment. As the lira reached the 12–13 range against the dollar, markets remained skeptical that the CBRT could resist his pressure; an analyst said resistance could raise concerns about another replacement of the governor and other CBRT members.

Erdogan said high interest rates would not curtail inflation and would only dampen economic growth. The lira dropped as much as 18 percent on Tuesday following his remarks. Interest rates have fallen four percentage points since August.

Erdogan says lower interest rates and a weaker lira will make Turkish exports more attractive. He remains committed to this policy despite the currency crisis, describing it as a war of independence and blaming unspecified foreign meddling for economic turbulence.

The CBRT is expected to cut rates by another 100 basis points to 14% amid Erdogan's continuing pressure for lower rates. Annual inflation is now almost 22%, a three-year high, while the lira has lost almost half its value this year and breached 15 per dollar despite central bank foreign-exchange interventions with muted results.

On Sunday, Erdogan pledged further interest-rate cuts and tied his policy to Islamic teachings, contradicting the CBRT's statement after its latest cut that there was limited room for further reductions. The lira weakened to a new record low, trading at 17.4 per dollar.

Erdogan announced measures to bolster the lira, including a Treasury pledge to compensate retail lira depositors if foreign-exchange losses exceed their interest earnings. Despite these measures, Erdogan continues to signal further central bank rate cuts, with no change in his interest-rate policy.
The lira surged on Tuesday morning after Erdogan announced a deposit guarantee intended to encourage people to keep their money in lira.
Erdogan blamed foreign currency traders and previously accused an international interest-rate lobby of trying to destroy Turkey.
Economist Edin Mujagic interprets Erdogan’s low-rate policy as an effort to transform Turkey from an import-dependent economy into a major exporter before the 2023 elections.

Under Erdogan's pressure, the CBRT has cut rates by a total of 500 basis points since September. Annual inflation is expected to exceed 27% in December, up from 21% in November, marking a seventh consecutive monthly acceleration and a nineteen-year high. The lira lost 44% of its value in 2021, its worst performance in two decades.

Erdogan remains ideologically opposed to any interest-rate increase. December inflation reached 36%, its highest level since September 2002. Investors viewed the central bank as having lost its independence and acting on Erdogan's orders.
Following the government's guarantee for lira investments, the lira briefly rose almost 50% but has begun losing value again. Erdogan continues to reject interest-rate increases.

Independent researchers estimate annual inflation at about 80%, compared with the official 36%. The story reports that the CBRT has been spending billions of dollars to support the lira and that its reserves are running down while Erdogan persists in his low-rate policy.

Erdogan has eased political pressure on the CBRT to cut rates quickly, with his current language favoring a gradual pace of reductions. All economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the bank to hold its benchmark rate at 14% at its January 20 meeting, its first pause since easing began in September.

CBRT.title: Erdogan fires three CBRT rate-setting committee members
summaries: President Erdogan fired three members of the CBRT's rate-setting committee in a midnight decree. Bloomberg reported that the changes removed members who disagreed with his call to continue cutting interest rates despite high inflation.

CBRT.title: Erdogan replaces CBRT head with ally favoring lower rates
summaries: Earlier this year, President Erdogan replaced the central bank head with a political ally more amenable to lowering interest rates.

The replacement occurred in March, a couple of days after the previous governor raised interest rates to control inflation. Erdogan fired him in the middle of the night and appointed an official from his own party who supported his economic policies.
The story reports that Erdogan has dismissed three central bank governors since 2019 over disagreements about interest rates.

CBRT.title: Tusiad calls for an end to experimental monetary policy
summaries: Prominent business group Tusiad called on Erdogan's government to stop the experimental monetary policy he advocates. Erdogan rejected the criticism on Sunday, saying the group wanted him out of power.

CBRT.title: Erdogan fires other central bank officials opposing lower rates
summaries: Erdogan fired other senior central bank officials this year who stood in the way of his policy of lowering interest rates.

CBRT.title: Turkish banking supervisor files complaints against former central bank governors and critics
summaries: The Turkish banking supervisor filed a complaint against more than 20 people, including former central bank governors, journalists and an economist, notably over their social-media publications. Authorities threatened legal proceedings against people accusing them of manipulating the currency.

CBRT.title: Erdogan pressures CBRT to cut interest rates
summaries: President Erdogan exerted substantial pressure on CBRT to cut interest rates despite a weak lira and already uncontrolled inflation.

The story reports that CBRT cut interest rates by 500 basis points last year with Erdogan's encouragement and continues to refrain from raising rates despite rising inflation. Erdogan favors low rates to turn Turkey into an industrial powerhouse and believes high interest rates cause inflation.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan pressures CBRT not to raise interest rates
summaries: President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's pressure has kept the CBRT from raising interest rates despite annual inflation reaching 79.6% in July. Erdoğan believes higher interest rates cause faster inflation.

CBRT.title: Erdogan demands continued interest rate cuts despite soaring inflation
summaries: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said this month that interest rates would continue falling for as long as he remained president and rejected advice on the subject. He favors lower borrowing costs to encourage growth and investment and believes high rates cause inflation. CBRT cut rates by 1.5 percentage points, its third consecutive cut since August, despite official inflation of 83 percent.

CBRT.title: Erdogan fires central bank governors, weakening independence
summaries: The story describes Erdogan's repeated firing of central bank governors as creating a revolving door of leadership and diminishing CBRT independence, leaving him effectively directing the bank.

CBRT.title: Opposition challenges depletion of CBRT foreign-exchange reserves
summaries: The opposition launched a campaign asking where $120–128 billion in reserves had gone after reserves were spent, turning reserve management into a political issue. The story links subsequent efforts to increase reported reserves to that campaign.

CBRT.title: Erdogan announces target to raise foreign-exchange reserves
summaries: President Erdogan recently said reserves stood at around $120 billion and would be raised to $130 billion by the end of the month. The commentator interpreted this as a gross-reserves target, noting that a discussed $5 billion deposit would increase gross reserves but not net reserves because it also creates a liability.

CBRT.title: Exporters seek exchange-rate increase and relief from foreign-exchange conversion rules
summaries: Ahead of a scheduled meeting between TİM President Mustafa Gültepe and CBRT Governor Şahap Kavcıoğlu on a support package, exporters reportedly demanded an exchange-rate increase of at least 5–10%, citing declining profitability. They also asked CBRT for a mechanism preventing losses when repurchasing foreign currency sold under the requirement to convert 40% of export earnings, and for faster, more effective access to rediscount credits.

CBRT.title: President’s earlier remarks reinforce expectations of CBRT rate cuts
summaries: The story cites the President’s earlier statements as a factor supporting expectations that CBRT will cut interest rates following the earthquake. A survey of 16 institutions had a median expectation of a 100-basis-point cut, and foreign institutions also expected a reduction.

The story specifies that President Erdoğan said in early February that interest rates, then at 9%, would be lowered further. His statement is cited as one of the two main reasons for expectations of a rate cut at CBRT’s February 23 meeting.

The commentator cites messages from President Erdoğan that rate cuts will continue as grounds for expecting no easy return to higher rates or policy normalization if the incumbent government remains in power after the election.
The story cites President Erdoğan’s statement that he will keep interest rates low in discussing post-election economic policy.
After winning Sunday's presidential runoff, Erdoğan reiterated that he would keep interest rates low despite inflation above 40%.

CBRT.title: Commentators criticize CBRT inflation forecasts and urge tighter policy
summaries: Commentators criticize CBRT’s 22.5% food-inflation forecast against actual food inflation near 70%, calling for more accurate forecasts and appropriate policy responses. They argue that monetary policy is not restrictive and that the existing policy mix is insufficient to reduce inflation, urging tightening through monetary policy, fiscal policy, regulations, or a combination.

CBRT.title: Commentator challenges CBRT’s coercive banking regulations
summaries: A commentator criticizes CBRT regulations compelling banks to convert deposits into lira and hold securities, arguing that they sustain low interest rates at the expense of inflation and increase financial instability risks. The commentator calls for banks to determine deposit and lending rates through their own risk assessments rather than being forced to compensate for monetary policy failures.

CBRT.title: Millet Alliance pledges gradual monetary policy normalization
summaries: The story reports that the Millet Alliance has announced gradual policy normalization in its published platform, contrasting this position with the incumbent president’s messages supporting continued interest-rate cuts.

CBRT.title: Commentator urges CBRT to explain reported Grand Bazaar FX purchases
summaries: A commentator calls on CBRT to explain reports that it collected foreign currency from the Grand Bazaar, noting that the bank had not denied them and describing the reports as concerning.

CBRT.title: Commentator urges post-election return to conventional policies and merit-based institutions
summaries: A commentator argues that simultaneously suppressing interest rates and the exchange rate is unsustainable and urges a post-election return to internationally accepted economic policies and a merit-based institutional structure led by qualified experts. The commentator cites depleted reserves, substantial short-term foreign debt and the risks accumulated under existing policies.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan signals policy shift with appointments
summaries: Erdoğan appointed Mehmet Şimşek as finance minister. Şimşek announced a return to rational economic and financial policies, prioritizing fiscal discipline and price stability. The story also reports an impending replacement of the central bank governor as a possible further sign of Erdoğan seeking a policy shift.
Şimşek said fiscal policy and structural reforms would support the central bank’s fight against inflation, and pledged transparency and consistency alongside rational policies.

Following Erdoğan’s appointments, CBRT raised interest rates by 6.5 percentage points to 15%. The story questions whether Erdoğan will allow the policy shift to continue ahead of next year’s local elections.

CBRT raised interest rates by 7.5 percentage points, its third large increase in three months. Investors remain concerned Erdoğan could reverse tightening in favor of stimulus and low rates if slower growth threatens prospects in the March local elections, particularly in Istanbul and Ankara. This concern has contributed to cautious investor re-entry and a lack of large inflows into Turkey's markets.

A commentator argued that Erdoğan’s limited tolerance for high interest rates prevents the new CBRT team from raising rates as far as it otherwise would. The commentator interpreted Mehmet Şimşek’s discussion of quantitative tightening in an interview the previous day as suggesting restrictions on money supply and credit without substantially changing interest rates.

The discussion says Erdoğan reiterated after the election that his view of the relationship between interest rates and inflation had not changed. Despite his statements prioritizing fighting inflation and Şimşek's assurances of presidential support, concern persists that Erdoğan could dismiss the CBRT team and reverse tightening. The commentator attributes uncertainty about future rate increases primarily to Erdoğan's reaction rather than CBRT's intentions.

CBRT.title: Commentator demands accountability for failed economic model and lasting monetary normalization
summaries: A commentator urged the new economic leadership to explicitly abandon and account for the previous economic model, citing Governor Şahap Kavcıoğlu’s unfulfilled claims that it would lower inflation, interest rates, dollarization and the current-account deficit while increasing reserves. The commentator called for restoring central bank independence, raising the policy rate sufficiently to reduce inflation, and clearly committing to lasting conventional policies rather than a temporary reversal.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan fires central bank chief after rate increases in 2021
summaries: In 2021, Erdoğan fired a central bank chief just months into the job after the chief began raising interest rates. The story attributes the dismissal to Erdoğan’s opposition to high interest rates.

CBRT.title: Commentator urges CBRT to raise credit-card interest rates
summaries: A commentator called on CBRT to raise credit-card interest rates to realistic levels, arguing that an annual borrowing cost of about 30%, against expected inflation around 60%, encourages spending and stockpiling, fuels inflation and brings imports forward. The commentator said tightening was clearly necessary and that allowing such consumption incentives was no longer justified after the elections.

CBRT.title: Commentator urges CBRT to use policy rates boldly
summaries: A commentator urged CBRT to use its policy rate boldly and without hesitation, arguing that stronger rate increases are needed to enable deposit rates that protect savers against inflation. The commentator said differentiated deposit rates and quantitative tightening would not prevent dollarization without positive real deposit returns.

CBRT.title: Selva urges further CBRT tightening and clearer communication
summaries: A commentator addressed as Selva urged another five-percentage-point rate increase following CBRT's latest increase, arguing that a 35% policy rate would provide a positive real rate against its 33% inflation forecast for 2024. She called for sustained high rates, more reliable inflation forecasts and clearer forward guidance, and urged CBRT to explain to markets and small businesses complaining to Erdoğan about expensive credit why tightening is necessary.

CBRT.title: Naci Ağbal’s removal as CBRT governor
summaries: The commentator recalled that Turkey’s risk premium declined when Naci Ağbal became CBRT governor and rose sharply when he was removed, citing governor changes as a source of abrupt movements in sovereign risk.

CBRT.title: Political directives erode CBRT’s institutional capacity
summaries: The commentator said CBRT had in recent years shifted from decisions guided by reason and science toward implementing political instructions, weakening its institutional framework. Valuable staff, including research personnel, left or were forced to leave. The revival of its research blog was welcomed as a signal of renewed science-based policymaking rather than reliance solely on political directives.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan intervenes in CBRT controversy to signal continuity
summaries: President Erdoğan indirectly addressed controversy at CBRT, describing it as a storm in a teacup and affirming determination to preserve hard-won economic confidence. Commentators interpreted his remarks as signaling no change in the economic management team and calling for an end to the controversy.

CBRT.title: Pre-election pressure to keep credit-card interest rates unchanged
summaries: Commentators suggested that political considerations ahead of local elections were preventing CBRT rate increases from being passed through to credit-card borrowers, to avoid curbing spending or upsetting consumers. Monthly credit-card interest had remained at 3.66% since November 1, 2023, despite a cumulative 1,000-basis-point policy-rate increase. They expected this pressure to continue until the elections.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan appoints Karahan after Erkan’s abrupt resignation
summaries: President Erdoğan appointed deputy governor Fatih Karahan as CBRT governor hours after Hafize Gaye Erkan resigned on Friday night. Her departure followed nearly a month of unverified press allegations that she had given her father an unofficial central-bank role and had difficulties with senior staff. The correspondent assessed that she had been pushed out, while emphasizing that the circumstances remained unclear.

CBRT.title: Pre-election pressure to restrict foreign-exchange demand
summaries: Commentators said election-related concerns had obliged CBRT to introduce restrictions it was not eager to impose, including renewed limits on foreign-exchange transaction hours and measures blocking liquidity channels that could feed foreign-exchange demand. They discussed whether these restrictions could ease after the election once election concerns subsided and confidence in policy continuity was established.

CBRT.title: Turkish president pressures CBRT to keep interest rates very low
summaries: The story recalls that Turkey’s president influenced CBRT to keep interest rates very low, causing an inflation crisis.

CBRT.title: Concern over year-end political pressure for CBRT rate cuts
summaries: A commentator warned that persistent inflation could make CBRT reluctant to cut interest rates, potentially prompting political authorities to demand cuts and creating friction by year-end.

CBRT.title: Industrialists press CBRT for interest-rate cuts
summaries: Industrialists are explicitly demanding interest-rate cuts as tight monetary policy strains the real economy. The discussion warns that industrialists conveying their difficulties to politicians could increase political pressure on CBRT to ease policy, despite its continued commitment to monetary tightening.

CBRT.title: Commentator urges CBRT easing to relieve real-sector distress
summaries: An unnamed commentator urged CBRT to move toward an interest-rate-cutting cycle, gradually relax monthly credit-growth limits of 1.5–2%, and allow some exchange-rate adjustment. The commentator warned that tight monetary policy, weak profitability and high financing costs were contributing to debt restructuring, payment difficulties and reduced bank lending, arguing that lowering inflation by halting real-sector activity would not constitute success.

CBRT.title: Commentator urges CBRT to avoid premature interest-rate cuts
summaries: An unnamed commentator argued that CBRT should not signal November or December rate cuts and should maintain, or even increase, monetary tightening if committed to its 17.5% inflation target. The commentator said cuts motivated by concern over growth would prolong inflation and suggested that any such easing would be better delayed until near the end of the following year's first quarter.

CBRT.title: İSO president urges CBRT to ease exporter financing and foreign-exchange requirements
summaries: At İSO’s November meeting, President Erdal Bahçıvan urged CBRT to lower its 35% rediscount credit interest rate and reopen foreign-currency rediscount lending. He proposed distributing rediscount loans directly through Eximbank and removing guarantee-letter requirements or capping related bank fees. He also requested easing foreign-currency holding restrictions on commercial lira borrowers, abolishing or gradually reducing exporters’ 30% foreign-exchange surrender requirement, and increasing the 2% conversion support for export proceeds sold to CBRT.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan signals interest-rate cuts in 2025
summaries: President Erdoğan declared that interest rates would definitely begin to fall and that 2025 would mark this shift, arguing that rates must fall for inflation to fall. He also said reducing inflation remained the economic programme’s priority.

CBRT.title: Call for CBRT to preserve corporate credit liquidity
summaries: An unidentified speaker urged CBRT not to restrict liquidity even if it raises interest rates, and to avoid excessively tightening foreign-currency credit access. The speaker warned that companies facing declining profitability need affordable funding and could be forced to close foreign-currency positions if they cannot roll over their loans.

CBRT.title: Call for CBRT to update credit-growth assessments to reflect corporate funding needs
summaries: An unidentified speaker serving on several company boards urged CBRT to align its credit-growth indicators with current conditions rather than historical comparisons. The speaker argued that slower inventory turnover and delayed collections have increased working-capital needs, warned of rising concordats and loan-restructuring requests, and said restrictive policies risk irreversible damage to production, growth and employment.

CBRT.title: Nihat Zeybekçi criticizes high interest rates as obstructing production and investment
summaries: Former minister and current AK Party economic policymaker Nihat Zeybekçi publicly argued that businesses cannot produce or invest at prevailing interest rates, invoking his own experience as a businessman. This week, he also acknowledged the negative effects of the March 19 events.
