CBRT.title: Political leadership expects a larger CBRT rate cut
summaries: A commentator stated that the political leadership expects a larger interest-rate cut at CBRT's meeting next Thursday than the 2–2.5 percentage-point reduction anticipated by markets, while noting that the economic administration currently has a stronger hand.

CBRT.title: Concerns over political support for CBRT tightening ahead of elections
summaries: Commentators questioned whether the ruling government would continue supporting tight monetary policy as elections approach and economic strains on companies and consumers grow. They raised concerns about potential policy reversals and constraints on CBRT’s freedom to act, without reporting a specific government demand or intervention.

CBRT.title: Erdoğan replaces central bank chiefs to enforce his interest-rate policy
summaries: President Erdoğan demanded that Turkey’s central bank follow his views on interest-rate policy and repeatedly replaced its leadership when appointees did not comply sufficiently. The story describes three successive appointees, followed by a collapse in the lira and inflation reaching 85%. Erdoğan subsequently backed down and appointed a somewhat more independent central bank chief.

CBRT.title: İTO president urges rapid lending-rate cuts following CBRT normalization
summaries: The İTO president said he expected banks to reflect CBRT’s normalization in lending rates rapidly, calling for a three-percentage-point reduction within the week.

CBT.title: Erdogan uses interest-rate cuts to boost growth
summaries: President Erdogan used interest-rate cuts as a political tool to boost growth while other central banks were raising rates. After surviving a tight election, he brought in more orthodox policymakers, including a new finance minister and a Princeton-trained former Wall Street executive to head the central bank. Turkey subsequently raised its policy rate from 8.5% to 15%, reversing the previous cuts.

DNB.title: Finance minister proposes shortening DNB presidents’ terms
summaries: Caretaker Finance Minister Ilko Heijnen proposes reducing DNB presidents’ terms from seven to five years to encourage organizational renewal. Outgoing president Klaas Knot criticized the proposal, warning that shorter tenure could prevent Dutch central bankers from securing influential international positions. The story also reports concerns that shorter terms could increase political pressure on appointments and indirectly on monetary policy.

ECB.title: Trump criticizes Draghi's proposed monetary easing
summaries: Donald Trump angrily criticized ECB President Mario Draghi's signal at a central bank meeting in Sintra that the ECB could return to very loose monetary policy through additional stimulus, further interest-rate cuts and relief for banks. Trump objected that this would weaken the euro and strengthen European exports.
Trump contrasted Draghi and the EU's monetary stance with that of the Federal Reserve, saying he wanted a level playing field and had not been given one.
Trump portrayed Draghi's proposed easing as an attack on the United States after the euro fell about half a percent, returning to its level roughly 24 hours earlier.
Trump tweeted that the EU was manipulating its currency by pumping money into its system and said the United States should match it.

ECB.title: German CDU leader urges Lagarde to align ECB policy with its mandate
summaries: The head of Germany's ruling Christian Democratic Party said incoming ECB chief Christine Lagarde should shift monetary policy to make it comply with the bank's mandate.

ECB.title: European leaders select Lagarde for ECB in Franco-German leadership bargain
summaries: European leaders selected Christine Lagarde to head the ECB as part of negotiations over EU leadership posts. Her selection depended on a German taking the Commission presidency, and leaders' desire to appoint women to key positions also influenced the choice. Emmanuel Macron worked with Angela Merkel to reach the compromise.

ECB.title: Italian leaders demand greater ECB support and Italian appointments
summaries: Italian political leaders expressed dissatisfaction with the ECB and demanded a more responsive bank that would do more for Italy, including extensive purchases of government debt. They also sought to place Italians within the ECB to advance that aim.

ECB.title: Olli Rehn urges significant ECB stimulus exceeding expectations
summaries: Finnish central banker Olli Rehn called for an impactful and significant ECB stimulus package, telling the Wall Street Journal that it was better to overshoot market expectations for support measures ahead of the September 12 policy meeting.

ECB.title: Andreas Jung criticizes prolonged low ECB interest rates
summaries: Andreas Jung, deputy leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group, criticized prolonged low ECB interest rates, saying ECB must not stand for an eternal brake on interest rates, as the bank considered further monetary easing.

ECB.title: Trump accuses ECB of weakening euro through stimulus
summaries: President Trump accused the ECB of cutting interest rates and introducing stimulus to weaken the euro against the dollar. ECB President Mario Draghi denied targeting the exchange rate and cited a pledge among major economies not to devalue currencies for competitive advantage.

ECB.title: Johan Van Overtveldt challenges Draghi over low rates and mortgage warnings
summaries: At a European Parliament hearing on Monday, N-VA MEP and former Belgian finance minister Johan Van Overtveldt challenged Mario Draghi over an apparent contradiction between stimulating borrowing through low interest rates and warning against loose mortgage lending. Draghi rejected the contradiction, saying monetary stimulus and targeted prudential supervision were complementary.

ECB.title: Robert Holzmann criticizes Draghi's liquidity stimulus and leadership
summaries: Austrian central bank governor Robert Holzmann told the nation's public broadcaster that Mario Draghi's attempt to inject more liquidity could be counterproductive. He also criticized the outgoing ECB president as not inclined to consider divergent views, amid a continuing split over restarting quantitative easing.

In an interview, Holzmann criticized both negative interest rates and the ECB's continued bond purchases as dangerous distortions. He challenged the dominant neo-Keynesian approach of using expansionary monetary policy to close demand gaps.

ECB.title: German parliamentarians challenge ECB bond purchases in court
summaries: German parliamentarians challenged the validity of ECB sovereign-debt purchases under OMT and subsequently its asset purchase programme before the Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe. The story reports that the court sided with the ECB, but opposition to these measures persists.

ECB.title: ECB dissenters pressure incoming Lagarde to reverse monetary policy
summaries: Opposition within the ECB Governing Council intensified following the September policy package. The story describes public dissent as pressure on Christine Lagarde to reverse the direction of monetary policy when she succeeds Mario Draghi on November 1.
The story reports that nearly a third of ECB decision-makers voted against the September decision to buy more government bonds, and several publicly distanced themselves from it the following day.

ECB.title: Jens Weidmann opposes Draghi's monetary policy
summaries: The story identifies Bundesbank chief and ECB council member Jens Weidmann as the best-known German critic of Draghi's monetary policy, amid opposition to large-scale bond purchases and negative interest rates over their effects on savers.

ECB.title: Dutch parliament challenges Draghi over pension losses
summaries: At a 2017 hearing in the Dutch House of Representatives, Draghi faced criticism that his monetary policy had depleted Dutch pension savings. He responded that his job was to fulfill his price-stability mandate, not to be a hero.

ECB.title: German criticism of the ECB
summaries: Incoming ECB executive board member Isabel Schnabel warned Germany against unjustified criticism of the institution.

ECB.title: Macron urges stronger ECB response to coronavirus crisis
summaries: Emmanuel Macron said the ECB would have to try harder to combat the coronavirus outbreak after its newly announced stimulus measures failed to calm markets.
Macron said Europe should do whatever it costs to fight the coronavirus.

ECB.title: Conte criticizes ECB crisis response
summaries: Italy's Giuseppe Conte criticized the ECB for making matters worse through its decisions and attitude in responding to the coronavirus crisis.
Conte said Christine Lagarde has a responsibility to maintain stability in the European Union, potentially including addressing fragmentation in bond spreads.
Conte said the central bank's task is not to hinder but to facilitate, responding to Lagarde's statement that she was not there to close Italian bond spreads.

ECB.title: Mattarella calls for ECB solidarity with Italy
summaries: Italian President Sergio Mattarella said Italy expected at least solidarity, amid criticism of Christine Lagarde's statement that narrowing bond spreads was not her job.

ECB.title: Conte and southern European nations call for joint coronavirus bonds
summaries: Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte joined other southern European nations in calling for issuance of as much as €1.5 trillion in joint bonds to aid economies crippled by the coronavirus, setting the stage for a clash at the European summit.

ECB.title: German court gives ECB three months to justify bond purchases
summaries: The German court issued a ruling giving the ECB three months to explain its bond-buying program and how support was allocated. It questioned purchases favoring Italy exceeding 30% despite Italy's 15.6% share of ECB capital, and said sharing financial risk among European countries requires transparent political decisions through democratic procedures.

Four ECB council members told the FT they opposed answering the German court directly, arguing that doing so would threaten ECB independence and expose it to pressure from other national courts. Several council members suggested that the German central bank could instead provide the proportionality assessment. The ruling stems from a 2015 case brought by nearly 2,000 people alleging that ECB sovereign bond purchases constituted monetary financing prohibited by the EU treaty.

ECB.title: Schäuble blames Draghi’s monetary policy for AfD’s rise
summaries: Wolfgang Schäuble accused former ECB president Mario Draghi of being responsible, through the effects of his monetary policy, for 50 percent of the AfD’s rise.

ECB.title: Italian prime minister's aide calls for ECB to cancel pandemic debt
summaries: A top aide to Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte called on the ECB to cancel government debt incurred during the pandemic or hold the bonds forever. The demand reflects Italy's fiscal difficulties and already high pre-pandemic debt.

The Italian government fears that market tensions could make highly indebted countries such as Italy targets for financial markets. Christine Lagarde had rejected the debt-cancellation idea the previous week, saying the ECB lacked the authority to do so.

ECB.title: Dutch and Austrian policymakers call for reduced ECB crisis support
summaries: ECB Governing Council member Klaus Knott said the euro area's inflation outlook could allow an immediate slowdown in monetary policy support. Dutch and Austrian policymakers, concerned about inflation and seeing the economy on a firmer footing, called for discussion of reduced support at the September 9 meeting.

ECB.title: Five EU countries press for phaseout of €500 banknotes
summaries: Italy, Belgium, France, the Netherlands and Spain submitted a paper to the European Commission during the summer urging it to engage with the ECB on further measures concerning €500 banknotes, including a gradual phaseout allowing the public to convert them into smaller denominations. The demand aims to combat money laundering and tax evasion.

ECB.title: World Bank president urges ECB to act more decisively against inflation
summaries: World Bank President David Malpass called on central banks, including the ECB, to act more decisively against inflation. He argued that rising prices hit the poor hardest because they are less able to protect themselves, and that stronger action would help small firms and developing countries.

ECB.title: Governments pressure ECB to tackle inflation
summaries: The story describes strong pressure from governments on central banks, including the ECB, to tackle inflation because of its political, social and purchasing-power implications, invoking their price-stability mandate. It says central banks are increasingly responding to politicians' concerns, while their policy actions remain relatively moderate.

ECB.title: European politicians warn ECB against excessive rate increases
summaries: Some European politicians have warned the ECB not to raise interest rates too high ahead of its next policy meeting in mid-December.

ECB.title: Commentary criticizes Lagarde’s pessimistic crisis messaging
summaries: The commentary criticizes ECB President Christine Lagarde for portraying crises as permanent and offering no clear way out beyond technical messaging. It urges her to inspire confidence and hope rather than resignation, citing financial markets’ sensitivity to communication.

ECB.title: Spanish government bars banks from passing on tax despite ECB objections
summaries: The Spanish government’s extraordinary bank tax requires the sector to pay €1.5 billion annually in 2023 and 2024 to help fund anti-inflation measures. The law prohibits banks from passing the cost on to customers, despite an ECB opinion saying some pass-through should be allowed to avoid harming credit provision.

ECB.title: Political criticism of ECB interest-rate increases
summaries: The story reports criticism from unspecified political actors who say the ECB is making a mistake with its repeated interest-rate increases, particularly the speed of the increases.

ECB.title: Anti-European political attacks on the ECB
summaries: The story describes the ECB as a frequent target of Italian and other anti-European actors, without identifying specific actors or demands.

ECB.title: Trade unions urge ECB to pause interest-rate increases
summaries: Trade unions have called for a pause in ECB interest-rate increases as inflation conditions have changed. A survey also indicates that many companies in Germany oppose further rate increases.

ECB.title: Salvini attacks ECB rate increases as harmful to families and businesses
summaries: Lega leader Matteo Salvini accused the ECB of knowingly harming families and businesses after it raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point and Christine Lagarde indicated another increase was very likely in July.

ECB.title: Criticism of ECB rate increases and advance announcements
summaries: An unidentified speaker criticized continued ECB interest-rate increases as harmful to growth and opposed announcing increases far in advance. The speaker expressed disappointment at Christine Lagarde’s announcement of a July increase, arguing that European inflation stems from raw-material costs and the nearby war rather than domestic factors.

ECB.title: Belgian politicians criticize central bank advice on savings rates
summaries: Belgian politicians accused the National Bank of Belgium of siding too closely with banks after it advised Finance Minister Vincent van Peteghem against abrupt intervention in savings rates and recommended gradual increases. Vooruit, Groen and PS sought government measures forcing banks to raise savings rates, but compulsory increases were not adopted.

ECB.title: Government leaders press ECB to ease restrictive monetary policy
summaries: Unspecified government leaders are pressuring central banks, including the ECB, to ease restrictive monetary policy to avert economic slowdown or recession.
At the beginning of the summer, the Italian, Portuguese and Spanish governments expressed concern about the ECB's persistence in raising interest rates.

ECB.title: EU Commission advances Russian reserve profits plan despite ECB warnings
summaries: The European Commission plans to propose using interest profits from frozen Russian central bank reserves for Ukraine despite ECB warnings that doing so could damage the euro area's reputation as a safe haven. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wants the funds also used for weapons purchases. Germany, France and Italy support the plan, which requires unanimous approval by all 27 EU member states.

ECB.title: Commentator urges earlier ECB rate cuts to counter structural stagnation
summaries: An unnamed economic commentator urged the ECB not to wait for the Federal Reserve before cutting interest rates, arguing that Europe's structural stagnation risk calls for earlier cuts and support for structural policies beyond interest rates.

ECB.title: Tajani urges bolder ECB rate cuts
summaries: After the ECB cut interest rates by 25 basis points, Antonio Tajani said more courage was needed, urging a bolder approach to rate cuts.

ECB.title: Trump criticism prompts Lagarde to defend central bankers
summaries: Lagarde defended monetary policymakers after Donald Trump said Jay Powell had the easiest job, likening it to a monthly coin flip. She invited Trump to visit the ECB, emphasized its staff's hard work and stressed the importance of defending central bank independence from politics.

ECB.title: Trump threatens punitive tariffs on the EU
summaries: President Donald Trump recently threatened tariffs on the EU, saying it treats the United States badly. The threats create uncertainty for ECB policymaking over their effects on eurozone growth and inflation. ECB President Christine Lagarde said policymakers would continue their gradual, data-dependent approach irrespective of US economic policy.

ECB.title: French prime minister urges ECB interest rate cuts
summaries: French Prime Minister Francois Beirut called for ECB interest rate cuts in the near future as France faces high debt and weak growth. He said France faces challenges similar to those of the US but lacks the strong dollar that, he argued, allows the Federal Reserve to create money to support economic optimism.

ECB.title: Italian governing coalition seeks state ownership of gold reserves
summaries: Italy’s centre-right governing coalition proposed a budget amendment, introduced by Lucio Malan, declaring that gold reserves belong to the Italian state. The ECB and EU opposed the wording because it threatened central-bank independence and conflicted with European treaties; the ECB had not been consulted. After a revision declaring ownership by the Italian people also raised objections, the government planned to resubmit wording stating that the reserves belong to the Italian people and are managed independently by the Bank of Italy.

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti reached an agreement with the ECB on the gold-reserves amendment in the 2026 budget law. The amendment specifies that the reserves belong to the Italian people, while ownership and custody remain with the Bank of Italy, leaving their practical management unchanged.

ECB.title: Macron urges ECB to consider growth and employment targets
summaries: French President Emmanuel Macron argued that the ECB cannot focus solely on inflation while China and the Trump administration pursue weaker currencies. He urged the ECB to discuss also targeting growth and employment.

ECB.title: Italian ministers criticize ECB for neglecting Italian interests
summaries: In 2023, ministers in Giorgia Meloni’s Italian government, including Matteo Salvini, criticized the ECB for not sufficiently considering Italian interests. The story says these statements were quickly criticized as undermining central-bank independence.

ECB.title: Banking lobby presses ECB to limit digital euro
summaries: The commercial banking lobby is pressuring politicians and the ECB to keep the digital euro small and prevent it from becoming an important alternative to bank deposits. Banks oppose losing deposits to the central bank because this would make their funding more expensive; the proposed holding limit is €3,000.

ECB.title: Privacy First criticizes digital euro privacy safeguards
summaries: Stichting Privacy First criticized the digital euro plans, saying they do not rule out every payment becoming fully traceable and therefore fail to guarantee privacy and anonymity.

ECB.title: Ons Geld calls for a more ambitious digital euro
summaries: Stichting Ons Geld criticized the proposed restrictions on digital euro holdings as too limiting. It argued that citizens and businesses should be able to choose to store their money safely, rather than receive a weak alternative to commercial bank deposits.

ECB.title: Tridico-led MEP group presses for full digital euro rollout
summaries: A cross-party group of 47 European Parliament members, led by Pasquale Tridico, submitted two amendments to the ECB annual report supporting accelerated introduction of both online and offline digital euro versions. They argue that both versions are essential for monetary sovereignty, reduced dependence on non-European payment infrastructure and universal access to payments. Debate is scheduled for Monday in Strasbourg with the ECB president present, followed by a Tuesday vote.

ECB.title: Navarrete pushes offline-first digital euro legislation
summaries: European Parliament rapporteur Fernando Navarrete of the European People's Party is pushing to split the digital euro legislation and prioritize only the offline version, which he calls 'euro e cash,' rather than the Commission and ECB's combined online and offline project. At the latest rapporteurs' meeting, he was effectively supported only by the Patriots group. Critics say his approach risks narrowing the project and delaying approval.

ECB.title: Mélenchon proposes cancelling French debt held on behalf of the ECB
summaries: During the presidential campaign, LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposed cancelling the French debt held by the Banque de France on behalf of the ECB, representing approximately 18% of total French debt, or €600 billion. He said this debt could simply be taken and burned.

ECB President Christine Lagarde rejected Mélenchon's proposal to cancel government bonds held by the Bank of France and ECB, saying it made no legal, technical or financial sense and that moving debt from one pocket to another does not cancel it.

FCA.title: Jeremy Hunt urges FCA to reconsider naming firms under investigation
summaries: Chancellor Jeremy Hunt publicly criticised the FCA's plans to name companies it is investigating and said he hoped it would reconsider following an industry backlash. The FCA said the plans remained at the consultation stage and argued that firms and consumers would benefit from knowing which issues it is examining.

FDIC.title: Republican FDIC board members demand recusals from workplace investigation
summaries: Two Republican FDIC board members called for Chair Martin Gruenberg and the general counsel to recuse themselves from an investigation into the agency's workplace culture and for the board to take control of the investigation.

FDIC.title: Congressional pressure on Gruenberg over workplace misconduct testimony
summaries: Gruenberg faced pressure on Capitol Hill after testifying that, as a general matter, he did not know of allegations of harassment, discrimination or a toxic workplace. Subsequent reporting described misconduct issues involving him in which he did not take a hard line against those accused.

FED.title: Trump blames Fed for stock market plunge
summaries: Following a sharp decline in US stocks, Trump blamed the Federal Reserve and said it had gone crazy.

In a Tuesday interview with Fox Business Network, Trump called the Fed his biggest threat, said it was raising rates too fast, and expressed dissatisfaction with Chairman Jay Powell. Despite the criticism, September meeting minutes released Wednesday indicated policymakers remained prepared for further rate increases, including a possible fourth rise before year-end and potentially restrictive borrowing costs to prevent inflation.

On Monday, Trump criticized Jerome Powell, saying he was not even a little happy with his choice of Fed chair. The following day, Powell indicated in New York that interest rates could rise more slowly.

Trump urged the Fed not to raise interest rates at its meeting that evening, despite widespread expectations of an increase. He warned central bankers against making further mistakes and urged them to feel the market rather than rely solely on meaningless numbers.
Despite Trump's warnings, the Fed raised interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to a range of 2.25–2.5 percent. Powell said political considerations played no role in the decision.

On December 24, after a Bloomberg report that he had discussed firing Powell, Trump tweeted that the Fed was the economy's only problem, saying it lacked a feel for markets and did not understand necessary trade wars, strong dollars or shutdowns over borders.
Trump tweeted that the previous administration had zero interest rates and suggested he could achieve more if he had the same rates.
Stephen Bell said Trump's heavy criticism of the Fed had raised the stakes by effectively blaming it in advance for an expected slowdown in the US economy.

Trump criticized Powell as someone who likes raising rates and said the U.S. economy was doing well despite the central bank's actions. He reiterated that the dollar was too strong, saying excessive strength hindered dealings with other nations and competition for their business.

An interview participant suggested that Trump was directly or indirectly pressuring the Fed to keep interest rates lower than warranted. The participant cited the Fed's shift from four annual rate increases to potentially none despite sharply rising wage growth, suggesting political influence and concern about keeping one's job.
Trump said interest rates should be lowered.
Fed watchers looked for signs that the Fed had responded to Trump's recent calls for rate cuts, but the commentary found no such indications.
Trump said the stock market would be 5,000 to 10,000 points higher were it not for the Federal Reserve's actions.
Trump added in a tweet that the Fed should have loosened monetary policy instead of tightening.
Trump said the US economy would be growing at 4 percent were it not for the Fed's actions.
Mario Draghi expressed concern about the Federal Reserve's independence as Trump again attacked the central bank over stock market performance.

In a series of tweets, Trump called for a steep one-point interest-rate cut, saying it would help the US economy take off like a rocket. He criticized the Fed for raising rates despite low inflation and praised China for adding stimulus.

Fed Chairman Jay Powell pushed back against Trump's call for interest-rate cuts, saying inflation would rebound and the economy would remain healthy without fresh central-bank support. He said the current policy stance was appropriate and there was no strong case for moving rates in either direction.
Trump called for the Federal Reserve to match some of China's stimulus moves to help him win the trade dispute.
Trump tweeted that it would be “game over” if the Fed matched Chinese central bank moves to offset the trade war's impact.
Trump lamented his lack of China-style control over Federal Reserve policy.

Trump criticized the Fed chair a few days earlier, saying he was not doing his job properly. Commentators suggested that Trump's aggressive criticism could act as indirect pressure for a rate cut. The discussion suggested that a sharp fall in the Empire State index could provide an economic justification for cutting rates rather than appearing to comply with Trump's demands.

Trump contrasted the Fed's stance with Mario Draghi's and the EU's, saying European action had helped that part of the world. Ahead of the Fed's policy announcement, he demanded a level playing field and said he had not been given one.
Trump said Powell had made multiple mistakes by raising interest rates after Trump became president. He said the Fed should have cut rates in December and afterward.

Commentators said Trump wanted higher stock prices and would continue pressuring the Fed during the election campaign. They argued that rate cuts should come when the economy needs them, not because Trump keeps demanding them, and saw no current economic justification for a cut.

On Monday, Trump again attacked the Fed on Twitter for raising rates too quickly last year. On Tuesday, Powell defended the Fed's independence, saying it was insulated from short-term political pressures.
Following the weekend US-China trade truce, Trump said the Fed had hindered the US position in the trade war, declaring that it had been no help and that the US was not playing on a fair field.
Trump tweeted that China and the EU were manipulating their currencies and pumping money into their systems, and said the US should match them.

Commerzbank FX strategist Tulan Lyon said Trump's increasing attacks on the Fed and complaints about dollar strength were raising clients' concerns about US currency intervention. She argued that political pressure could amplify the negative effect of Fed rate cuts on the dollar and leave the Fed reluctant to cut for fear of appearing to yield to Trump, despite a deteriorating economic outlook.
Despite strong June jobs data, Trump renewed pressure for lower interest rates over the weekend, telling reporters that if the Fed knew what it was doing, it would cut rates.

Pimco's Joachim Fels said repeated attacks on Powell and his colleagues and calls by Trump and other administration members for rate cuts and quantitative easing left the Fed in a no-win situation. Esther Reichelt warned that a rate cut prompted by global conditions could be interpreted as yielding to political pressure, potentially damaging confidence in the Fed and the US dollar over the long run.
The story identified Trump's jawboning as one of three factors driving the dollar, alongside rate cuts and Powell's upcoming remarks.

Michael O'Sullivan cited Trump's insults directed at the Fed as an example of reckless political behavior enabled by central banks' expanding role in the political economy after years of quantitative easing.
Peter Dixon said Trump's desire for a weaker dollar created a political risk of US currency intervention that investors should flag, although he did not expect the Fed to engage in such intervention.

Ahead of Powell's congressional testimony, senators interviewed from both parties declined to endorse Trump's criticism of Powell and affirmed the Fed's independence to set policy, including Republicans supportive of Trump's other initiatives.
During Powell's House testimony, Democrats and Republicans praised his performance. Democrats explicitly pledged support, with Representative David Scott telling Powell, "We've got your back."

Powell's testimony to Congress signaled that the Fed intended to cut rates at its late-July meeting, consistent with Trump's longstanding demand for lower rates. Powell cited global economic weakness, unresolved government policy issues and persistent weak inflation; he said the strong jobs report did not meaningfully change his outlook.

Goldman Sachs warned that Trump's repeated complaints about other currencies had renewed attention on US currency policy. Analysts were considering possible US intervention to forcibly weaken the dollar, a step the US had not taken since 2000.

Goldman Sachs described direct US intervention to weaken the dollar as a low but rising risk. Janet Mui said the US had few levers to depress the dollar, questioned how much further Fed rate cuts could help, and suggested restarting quantitative easing might be necessary. She warned that active currency manipulation could damage investor confidence and market sentiment.
Trump tweeted that the country was doing great economically despite the Fed's "antiquated policy of rates and tightening."

An ING analyst said the probability of US government currency intervention had increased and suggested the administration could justify expanding euro and yen holdings by citing the size of US foreign-exchange reserves. He warned that the administration could become frustrated if Fed easing failed to weaken the dollar because the ECB was also easing.

Embark Group CIO Peter Toogood argued that Powell had fallen into line with Trump's pressure and that the Fed's shift toward cutting rates lacked a fundamental economic justification, given the absence of an economic collapse or crisis.
Ahead of the Fed's expected Wednesday rate cut, Trump tweeted that a small cut was not enough and that the Fed had made all the wrong moves.
Wall Street Journal reporter Nick Timoros said the Fed maintains that Trump's pressure has no effect on its decisions and that evidence of such an effect is hard to find.

The story traces Trump's public criticism to July 2018, when he told CNBC he was unhappy with Fed rate increases, followed by criticism at the UN in September. Powell told associates that the priority was getting policy right, even if decisions sometimes appeared to yield to Trump or defy him.

After the Fed cut interest rates by a quarter point to 2.0–2.25 percent, its first cut in ten years, Powell rejected a long series of cuts and cited economic risks from Trump's trade policy. Trump criticized Powell for letting the US down and argued that further cuts were needed to keep pace with Europe and China.

Trump announced 10% tariffs on a further $300 billion of Chinese imports, effective September 1. CCLA CIO James Bevan interpreted the escalation as another shot across the Fed's bow intended to secure further rate cuts after its quarter-point cut and cautious guidance on additional easing. Bloomberg Opinion's Robert Burgess said the tariff announcement all but guaranteed more rate cuts.

Janet Mui said Trump had pressured the Fed for a 50-basis-point cut and, after not receiving it, announced additional China tariffs within 24 hours in the expectation that escalating trade tensions would prompt further Fed support.

Former Fed chiefs Janet Yellen, Ben Bernanke, Alan Greenspan and Paul Volcker jointly responded to Trump's recent attacks in a Wall Street Journal op-ed, urging that the Fed and its chair be free to act independently without threats of removal or demotion for political reasons.

Hassium Asset Management CEO Yogi Dewan suggested Powell's current dovish stance might reflect pressure from Trump, but expected Powell's rhetoric to become more hawkish in the first or second quarter of 2020.

Trump called for a rate cut of at least 100 basis points, saying it would greatly and quickly enhance the global economy. He said the strong dollar was hurting other parts of the world and described Powell and the Fed as showing a horrendous lack of vision. Boston Fed President Eric Rosengren pushed back against further easing, saying US unemployment and inflation did not justify it and that Fed policy should focus on domestic conditions rather than the exchange rate or global economy.

Trump also called for quantitative easing. A commentator interpreted his demands as pressure on the Fed to weaken the dollar, arguing that dollar strength transmits tighter monetary conditions globally and contributes to slower global growth.

Commentators interpreted Trump's demand for a one-percentage-point rate cut as an effort to boost the economy, employment and earnings ahead of the election in just over a year. They suggested his pressure could lead the Fed to cut by 50 basis points rather than an intended 25 basis points.
Trump dismissed recession concerns and said that if the Fed would do its job, the US would have a tremendous spurt of growth.
Trump issued a new tweet attacking Fed Chair Jerome Powell, comparing him to a poor golfer who cannot get the ball into the hole even when standing close to it.

Trump reacted to market moves by asking, "Where is the Fed?" Ahead of Powell's Jackson Hole speech, Marcus Morris Eaton said Powell faced growing pressure from Trump to abandon the mid-cycle adjustment rhetoric and adopt more pronounced monetary easing, despite US economic data not appearing to justify the scale of cuts Trump sought.

The story noted that market interest-rate expectations dipped sharply in August after Trump tweeted his demand for a 100-basis-point cut, but subsequently moved closer to the current federal funds rate as expectations for deep cuts lessened.

Ahead of Powell's Jackson Hole speech, a commentator said most observers expected him to partly yield to Trump's pressure and signal further US interest-rate cuts, potentially lifting the stock market as Trump wanted.

Trump questioned whether Fed Chair Powell or Chinese President Xi was the bigger enemy. Portfolio manager Said Abukhaz suggested further escalation against China could force the Fed to act again in September, while noting that Fed officials at Jackson Hole emphasized responding to economic data rather than preemptively reacting to Trump's actions.
ABN Amro strategist Georgette Bowles said Trump's comments about the Fed and his suggestion that he may act on the dollar were dampening the dollar's upside.
Trump said the Federal Reserve "cannot mentally keep up with the competition."

Trump blamed the Fed rather than China for US economic problems following the inversion of the Treasury yield curve. In a tweet, he said the Fed had raised rates too much and too quickly and was now too slow to cut them, accused it of holding back US gains, and criticized Powell as clueless. Economist Bruno Cavalier argued that uncertainty created by Trump's trade policy was forcing the Fed to adapt by easing financing conditions.

A commentator argued that Trump has an incentive to delay a trade deal because prolonged tensions make Fed rate cuts more likely, boosting equities and potentially allowing a deal combined with lower rates to stimulate the economy ahead of the 2020 election. He said Trump was portraying the Fed as responsible for economic health and obliged to cut rates, making it harder for the central bank to remain apolitical and independent.

On Friday morning, Trump mocked Powell on Twitter, asking, "Where did I find this Jerome guy anyway?" Asked in Zurich about the mockery, Powell declined to make the dispute personal and said the Fed would do its job.

An interview participant argued that Trump had brought the Fed on board with extending the economic expansion, noting that it was cutting rates and expected to cut further despite unemployment being at its lowest level in 50 years. The participant said Trump's tariffs had weakened growth and indirectly induced the Fed to change its rate-setting stance.

Trump said on September 11 that the Fed should take interest rates below zero. JPMorgan Asset Management strategist Hugh Gimbert described the Fed as the administration's lever for pursuing a strong stock market, a strong economy and a strong stance on China, but said reaching zero rates would require significant economic deterioration.
A commentator warned that Trump's demand for the Fed to use its remaining policy firepower immediately could leave it unable to respond if inflation rises over the next 12 to 24 months.

Trump criticized the latest FOMC decision on Twitter after the Fed lowered rates to a range of 1.75–2 percent and indicated no further cuts were forthcoming, continuing his push for more aggressive rate cuts.

Trump called Powell a “bonehead” and accused him of lacking “guts” after the Fed cut rates by only 0.25 percentage points to 1.75–2.0 percent. The story described Trump's desired zero or negative rates as a means to weaken the dollar, support US exports and sustain a boom ahead of his reelection bid.

Dudley said Trump's attacks had politicized perceptions of the Fed, leaving people unsure whether easing reflected appropriate policy or presidential pressure. He cited findings that Trump's tweets caused market participants to lower their federal funds rate expectations.

A commentator said Trump had demanded another interest-rate cut and threatened to fire the Fed chair if it did not happen, citing expectations of a further cut as a driver of US stock-market optimism.

The Fed cut its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage points to a range of 1.5–1.75 percent. The story portrayed the move as bringing the Fed closer to the ECB's easy-money policy under Trump's persistent pressure, and Powell as seeking to meet expectations stirred by Trump for further monetary easing.

Speaking at the Economic Club of New York, Trump renewed his criticism of the Fed, saying it was harming the US economy and putting the country at a competitive disadvantage by failing to follow other central banks into negative interest rates.
Commerzbank's Peter Dixon said that, despite the Fed's high bar for further rate cuts and the economy's solid footing, pressure from the White House remained a concern.

Trump and Powell held their second face-to-face meeting of the year at the White House, discussing interest rates, low inflation and dollar strength, including negative interest rates. Trump described the meeting as cordial but subsequently said he had protested that Fed rates were too high relative to competitor countries. The Fed said Powell did not discuss monetary-policy expectations except to stress that policy would depend entirely on incoming information relevant to the economic outlook.

The dollar weakened after investors learned that Trump and Powell had discussed negative interest rates and dollar policy. An interview participant said potential presidential pressure on Powell in the 2020 election year would inhibit dollar strength.

Seema Shah expressed skepticism that the US would adopt negative interest rates, noting that the Fed had repeatedly said they would be inappropriate for the US. She conjectured that Powell pushed back against Trump's mention of negative rates during their conversation.

Trump linked renewed criticism of the Fed to his reinstatement of tariffs on Brazilian and Argentine steel and aluminium, accusing those countries of devaluing their currencies to the detriment of US farmers. The story described this as his first explicit linkage of tariffs, Fed action and currencies.
Powell has extensively sought advice from former Fed chairs and officials to gain perspective on the challenges he faces amid Trump's frequent attacks on the Fed.

Trump has intimated that he could appoint people who would vote against Powell. Powell has responded to questions about Trump's pressure by saying the Fed will never allow politics to interfere with doing the right thing.

FED.title: Toomey challenges potential Fed inflation overshooting
summaries: Republican Senator Pat Toomey questioned Powell about a potential shift to average inflation targeting, expressing concern that deliberately allowing inflation above 2 percent would be risky because inflation has historically been harder to control.

FED.title: Crapo raises concerns over Fed balance sheet
summaries: Republican Senator Mike Crapo expressed concern about the Fed's quantitative easing programs and balance sheet size during Powell's Senate testimony. Powell indicated that the balance sheet reduction program would retain sufficient excess reserves plus a buffer to avoid disruptive money-market movements.

FED.title: Trump seeks Fed appointments for Stephen Moore and Herman Cain
summaries: Trump is seeking to bring the Federal Reserve under his control by appointing loyalists. He has proposed Stephen Moore, a journalist who left the Wall Street Journal over demonstrated bias, as a Fed governor, and Herman Cain, who withdrew his presidential candidacy following sexual harassment allegations that he denied.
Several Republicans indicated that Herman Cain may not be able to win Senate confirmation.

The White House is interviewing candidates to potentially replace Herman Cain and Stephen Moore as Trump's Fed picks as Republican support for both has dwindled. Larry Kudlow said Cain should decide for himself whether to withdraw.
More senators have expressed doubts about Stephen Moore, making his prospects for confirmation to the Fed board increasingly uncertain.

FED.title: Trump calls for QE4
summaries: Trump made comments in the preceding week calling for a fourth round of quantitative easing. Fed watchers looked for signs that the Fed had taken up those comments, but found none.
Trump called in a series of tweets for the Fed to resume bond purchases.

FED.title: Kudlow calls for half-point Fed rate cut
summaries: Trump's economic adviser Larry Kudlow is calling for a half-percentage-point interest-rate reduction by the Federal Reserve.

FED.title: Judy Shelton urges Fed not to restrain growth during China trade war
summaries: Judy Shelton, a potential nominee to the Federal Reserve board, said the Fed should avoid restraining US growth during the trade war with China and should not be a burden to the US. She criticized the Fed as too interventionist, saying attempts to artificially move interest rates can create problematic distortions.

FED.title: Wilbur Ross criticizes Fed for overly aggressive rate increases
summaries: Wilbur Ross said Federal Reserve economists were wrong to believe falling unemployment would inherently cause inflation, arguing that this mistaken view led the Fed to raise interest rates more aggressively than the facts warranted.
Speaking to Bloomberg Television, Wilbur Ross urged the Federal Reserve to reconsider its December policy action.
Wilbur Ross said the Fed's December interest-rate increase was at best premature.

FED.title: White House explores demoting Fed Chairman Powell
summaries: White House legal officials explored in February whether Jerome Powell could be removed as Fed chairman while remaining a governor, after Trump mused about firing him. The administration concluded that firing him without cause would be questionable. Asked whether he still wanted Powell demoted, Trump said, "Let's see what he does," pointing to the Fed's upcoming announcement.

The White House denied the suggestion that Trump could demote Powell. Asked how he would respond if Trump demanded his demotion, Powell said he intended to serve his full four-year term. He reaffirmed the Fed's independence and said decisions should be based on incoming data rather than political considerations.

At Wednesday's House Financial Services Committee hearing, Chairwoman Maxine Waters asked Powell whether he would leave if Trump told him he was fired. Powell said no and reiterated that he intended to serve his full four-year term.
Just before Christmas in December, Trump asked advisers whether he could replace Powell. His advisers told him he could not fire Powell.

FED.title: Trump nominates Shelton and Waller to Federal Reserve Board
summaries: Trump announced Tuesday night that he would nominate Judy Shelton and Christopher Waller to the Federal Reserve Board, subject to Senate confirmation. Shelton, an adviser to Trump's 2016 campaign, has attacked the Fed for wielding undemocratic, Soviet-style power over markets and suggested it should not set interest rates. Trump's previous proposed nominees, Stephen Moore and Herman Caine, withdrew from consideration.

FED.title: Elizabeth Warren criticizes dollar strength
summaries: Elizabeth Warren was identified as complaining about the strength of the US dollar. The story did not specify a policy demand.

FED.title: Nixon administration pressures Fed to keep rates low
summaries: The story recalls pressure by the Nixon administration in the 1970s for the Fed to keep interest rates low.

FED.title: Johnson pressures Fed chair and explores removal
summaries: President Johnson opposed higher borrowing costs during the Vietnam War, confronted the Fed chair at his Texas ranch, and sought a legal opinion on replacing him. The Justice Department told Johnson he could not replace the chair.

FED.title: George H. W. Bush criticizes insufficient Fed rate cuts
summaries: In 1991, George H. W. Bush was unhappy that the Fed was not cutting interest rates more, amid concerns about his 1992 reelection.

FED.title: Navarro calls Fed biggest obstacle to US growth
summaries: President Trump's top trade adviser Peter Navarro called the Federal Reserve the single biggest obstacle to strong economic growth in America.

FED.title: Warren and lawmakers urge Fed to offer instant payments network
summaries: Elizabeth Warren and other lawmakers proposed that the Federal Reserve offer an instant payments network so people would not have to wait for paychecks to clear, arguing that payments should be a government utility. Banks objected that they already offer an instant payments system.

FED.title: Dudley urges Fed to consider Trump's reelection in policy decisions
summaries: Former New York Fed president Bill Dudley wrote a column suggesting the Fed consider allowing Trump's trade escalation to hurt his reelection next year. Asked about the proposal in Zurich on Friday, Powell firmly rejected it, saying the Fed serves all Americans and is committed to nonpolitical decision-making.
Dudley clarified that, in a second opinion piece, he said the Fed should not consider Trump's reelection in setting policy because doing so would politicize the institution and risk its independence.

FED.title: Other politicians press Fed for more aggressive easing
summaries: An interview participant said politicians other than the president were pressuring the Fed for a more aggressive policy response, in line with the ECB's actions in Europe. The politicians were not identified.

FED.title: Judy Shelton questions Fed independence
summaries: Judy Shelton, one of Trump's picks for the Fed, privately questioned whether the central bank should operate free of political influence in comments to a UBS executive last month. She also described Trump's public criticism of the Fed as healthy.

FED.title: Politicians oppose Volcker's aggressive inflation tightening
summaries: During the inflation crisis of 1979–80, politicians opposed radical Fed action that could crush the recovery. Fed Chair Paul Volcker faced criticism but sharply raised interest rates to bring inflation down.

Volcker feared that Congress would remove the Federal Reserve's independence if his tightening policy failed to produce results amid severe economic distress. The story also describes continuing criticism from the political left that his tightening inflicted excessive, lasting harm on American workers.

FED.title: Johnson pressures Fed against interest-rate increases
summaries: President Lyndon Johnson pressured the Fed chairman not to raise interest rates, fearing a recession that would hurt his reelection chances. The story says such political pressure helped allow high inflation to take root.

FED.title: Nixon pressures Fed against interest-rate increases
summaries: President Richard Nixon pressured the Fed chairman not to raise interest rates, fearing a recession that would hurt his reelection chances. In October 1979, former Fed Chairman Arthur Burns attributed inflation's rise to politicians preventing the Fed from taking necessary action.

FED.title: Trump pushes Fed for emergency rate cut amid coronavirus fallout
summaries: The Trump administration pushed for an emergency Federal Reserve rate cut to contain the economic and market fallout from coronavirus. Trump tweeted Monday that Fed Chair Jerome Powell had been slow to act, despite the Fed's willingness to cut rates.

After the Fed cut rates by 50 basis points between scheduled meetings, Trump said on Twitter that the cut was too small, that the central bank was lagging rather than acting ahead of developments, and that it should cut rates further.

Trump urged Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin on Monday to push Fed Chair Jerome Powell toward more radical monetary easing. During the meeting, Trump said Powell should never have been appointed and was harming the country and his presidency.

After the Fed cut its policy rate by one percentage point to zero and announced a $700 billion asset purchase programme and other support measures on Sunday, Trump said he was delighted and surprised.

FED.title: Lawmakers press Fed to intervene in municipal bond market
summaries: Some lawmakers expressed concern that the Fed was too hesitant to enter the municipal bond market despite having the powers to do so.
On April 27, the Fed announced it would broaden its municipal lending program after lawmakers pressured it to expand the program.

FED.title: Lobbying groups urge swift Fed action on municipal bonds
summaries: Lobbying groups urged the Fed to act quickly in the municipal bond market, while the central bank had not yet announced details of its intervention.

FED.title: Trump urges Fed to adopt negative rates
summaries: President Donald Trump suggested that the Federal Reserve adopt negative interest rates. Fed Chair Jerome Powell pushed back against the suggestion.

FED.title: Kudlow criticizes Powell's economic outlook as overly negative
summaries: White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow criticized Fed Chair Jerome Powell's economic assessment last week as overly negative, ahead of Powell's expected testimony to lawmakers.

FED.title: Bernstein and Jones urge Fed to target Black unemployment
summaries: Jared Bernstein, former economic adviser to Vice President Joe Biden, and Janelle Jones of the Groundwork Collaborative are urging the Fed to target Black unemployment in monetary policy. They propose amending the Federal Reserve Act to require attention to addressing racial employment gaps. Jones said senators recently questioned Chair Jerome Powell about Black unemployment and racial discrimination, and Powell indicated he had read about and was considering the issue.

FED.title: Democratic lawmakers push Fed to eliminate bank dividends
summaries: Some Democratic lawmakers are pushing the Fed for tighter restrictions on bank capital distributions, including a total elimination of dividends, as the Fed extends its dividend and share-buyback restrictions for the biggest U.S. banks through the end of 2020.

FED.title: Trump criticizes Fed Chair Jerome Powell
summaries: President Trump has been critical of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell. Powell remains relatively popular among Republican and Democratic members of Congress, and markets columnist Mike Bird said he did not think Powell's job was at risk.

FED.title: Trump pushes Judy Shelton's nomination to Fed Board
summaries: The Senate blocked Judy Shelton's nomination to the Fed Board, a setback to President Trump's drive to shake up the central bank before leaving office. Republican supporters lacked votes because one senator had COVID-19 and another was quarantining. Mitch McConnell voted no as a procedural tactic allowing reconsideration. The confirmation window could narrow when Democrat Mark Kelly joins the Senate following certification of his Arizona election victory.

FED.title: Mnuchin seeks return of Fed emergency funds and ends lending facilities
summaries: Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin wrote to Fed Chair Jay Powell saying Treasury would not extend several emergency lending facilities expiring in late December and sought the return of $455 billion in unused funds for Congress to spend elsewhere. The affected facilities include corporate debt purchases, state and local government lending, and support for asset-backed securities. The Fed said it preferred retaining the full suite of facilities as an economic backstop. Mnuchin also requested 90-day extensions for four facilities supporting short-term funding markets, including commercial paper and money market mutual funds.

The story identifies the Main Street lending program as among the programs slated to end at year-end. Raphael Bostic supported keeping the facilities available, citing economic uncertainty and the need for borrowers to draw on them if stress arises.

Mnuchin said the programs had worked so well that markets no longer needed them and that he did not believe he had legal authority to extend them. The Fed disagreed, saying they could be extended beyond December 31.

In opening remarks ahead of congressional testimony, Mnuchin urged Congress to pass a new, more targeted relief package using funds earmarked for the Fed emergency lending facilities he had asked to unwind.

FED.title: Mick Mulvaney challenges Yellen's discussion of inequality
summaries: At a congressional hearing in 2015, Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney criticized Fed Chair Janet Yellen for discussing inequality, suggesting she was being political and addressing matters outside her jurisdiction. Yellen responded that her predecessors had also discussed major economic trends and problems affecting the country.

FED.title: Trump declines to renominate Yellen as Fed chair
summaries: President Trump did not nominate Janet Yellen for a second term as Fed chair despite economic expansion during her tenure. Sources told the Journal that Trump suggested one concern was that Yellen was too short. The White House declined to comment.

FED.title: Democratic lawmakers to press Powell to support Biden stimulus plan
summaries: Democratic lawmakers are expected to press Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell during his congressional testimony on February 23 and 24 to support President Joe Biden's $1.9 trillion stimulus plan.

FED.title: Warren and Brown urge Fed not to extend bank capital relief
summaries: Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Sherrod Brown warned the Federal Reserve and other US regulators in a letter against extending looser bank capital requirements introduced at the beginning of the pandemic. They said the relief had created new economic risks and extending it would be a grave error.

FED.title: Yellen suggests interest rates may need to rise
summaries: Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said at an Atlantic conference that interest rates may have to rise to prevent the economy from overheating amid Biden administration stimulus, contrary to Fed Chair Jay Powell's indication that rates would not rise before 2023. Her remarks unsettled markets. Later that day, at a Wall Street Journal event, she clarified that she was not predicting or recommending a rate increase.

FED.title: Congressional scrutiny of Powell over accelerating inflation
summaries: U.S. lawmakers are expected to question Fed Chair Jay Powell about the Fed's support for the economy and whether inflation is temporary after June consumer prices rose at the fastest pace since August 2008. Republicans have argued that inflation is getting out of control and harming consumers; questions are also expected about the inflationary impact of the Biden administration's proposed spending programs.

Republican and Democratic lawmakers questioned Powell on Wednesday over inflation and criticized the Fed as too complacent. Powell reiterated that price increases were temporary and would eventually subside, and said the Fed was ready to act if needed to bring inflation down.

FED.title: Progressive Democrats seek replacement of Powell as Fed chair
summaries: Some progressive Democrats want Biden to replace Powell, citing a desire for greater diversity, dissatisfaction with his approach to bank regulation, and demands for a stronger Fed role on climate change. Sitting Fed governor Lael Brainard is described as the leading potential replacement.

Powell's term ends in February, and the administration is expected to announce its decision around Labor Day. Powell defended avoiding a more activist climate role as necessary to respect the Fed's mandate and independence. Potential replacement Lael Brainard has formally dissented against easing bank regulation, making her popular with progressives such as Elizabeth Warren.

Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen supports Powell. The story reports recent speculation about a compromise in which Powell would remain Fed chair and Lael Brainard would take responsibility for banking regulation.
Senator Elizabeth Warren called Fed Chair Jay Powell a "dangerous man" and explicitly stated that she would oppose his reappointment.

President Biden voiced confidence in Powell after Elizabeth Warren questioned his leadership, and reporting indicates Biden leans toward supporting another term. Powell has also won support from a majority of Republican senators on the Senate Banking Committee.

Speaking on the Senate floor, Elizabeth Warren accused Powell of bad judgment for failing to prevent unusual trading by top Fed officials. In a Bloomberg interview, she reiterated her opposition to his reappointment, saying replacing him would make the Fed better off and the economy safer.

Other Senate Democrats have not joined Warren in threatening to vote against Powell if Biden renominates him, and most Democrats appear to be giving him the benefit of the doubt. Biden's economic team largely favors reappointing Powell. Some people argue that the trading controversy could also raise confirmation questions for potential replacement Lael Brainard because she oversees the reserve banks through the Fed board's committees.

The Fed banned senior officials from trading individual stocks and bonds, required transactions to be reported within 30 days and 45 days' advance notice for certain trades, and prohibited trading during extreme financial stress. Bloomberg's Garfield Reynolds said Powell's swift adoption of comprehensive restrictions could improve his renomination prospects and weaken Warren's attacks, though she was unlikely to ease her campaign.

Randall Quarles announced he will leave the Fed next month, after his term as vice chair for supervision expired in October. Reporting points to a possible package deal in which Biden reappoints Powell while appointing more Democrat-friendly officials to other Fed positions, including vice chair for supervision. Democrats on Capitol Hill want tougher financial regulation, contrasting with Quarles's light-touch approach.
The story describes the Democratic caucus pushing for a leadership change at the Fed as seeking a more dovish governor, with Lael Brainard in contention.

Biden announced Powell's nomination for a second term and chose Lael Brainard as vice chair. Senator Jeff Merkley joined Elizabeth Warren in saying he would vote against Powell, citing loosened bank regulations and insufficient attention to climate change.
Biden praised Powell for providing steady leadership during an extraordinarily challenging period, citing the economic downturn and Donald Trump's attacks on Fed independence.

The story reports that Powell's perceived success managing the pandemic downturn and recovery outweighed progressive criticism of his regulatory record in Biden's renomination decision. It describes Brainard's nomination as vice chair as a signal that the administration wants to take regulatory matters more seriously.

FED.title: Trump insults directed at Powell
summaries: The story recalls that Donald Trump directed insults at Powell, who avoided engaging in a fight.

Trump attacked Powell for raising interest rates, demanding low rates to accelerate economic growth. Powell largely ignored the pressure and said the Fed would not consider politics. The Fed subsequently cut rates three times in 2019 amid trade-war uncertainty and slowing global growth, creating the appearance that Powell had yielded to Trump despite the Fed's economic reasons.

FED.title: Biden pushes for simpler inflation messaging
summaries: Joe Biden is pushing for simpler language on inflation, and Fed Chair Jay Powell may tweak his inflation messaging to align with that push.

FED.title: Trump replaces Yellen seeking softer bank regulation
summaries: Donald Trump declined to offer Janet Yellen a second term in 2017, seeking his own choice with a softer stance on bank regulation. Republicans opposed retaining Yellen, a Democrat. Trump selected Republican Jerome Powell, who had voted alongside Yellen on monetary policy, to preserve market stability and continuity.

FED.title: Warren calls for SEC investigation of Fed officials' trading
summaries: Senator Elizabeth Warren called on securities regulators to investigate whether top Fed officials' financial trades violated insider trading rules. She wants scrutiny of Richard Clarida's trades in late February 2020, a day before Powell signalled potential action to support the economy. The Fed said the trades were a preplanned portfolio rebalancing with prior approval. Two regional Fed presidents announced their resignations last week amid a probe into their trading activity.

FED.title: Biden administration directs Fed to study bank merger competition
summaries: The Biden administration signed an executive order shortly before the summer directing the Fed to study the competitive effects of bank mergers and acquisitions.

FED.title: Summers criticizes Yellen's assessment of inflation
summaries: Larry Summers took to Twitter to criticize Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen, saying she was ignoring the reality of inflation on the ground.

FED.title: Republicans criticize Powell's support for increased stimulus
summaries: Some Republicans are unhappy with Powell's support for increased stimulus, which they view as favoring Democratic priorities.

FED.title: Trump attacks Fed independence
summaries: The story recalls Donald Trump's attacks on the Federal Reserve's independence, which Biden cited when praising Powell's leadership.

Arc Capital senior executive officer Said Abrakash said Powell had reversed his earlier hawkish stance after political criticism, and described his focus following renomination as clearer and more hawkish again.

FED.title: World Bank president urges stronger action against inflation
summaries: World Bank President David Malpass urged central banks to act more decisively against inflation, arguing that rising prices hit the poor hardest and that stronger action would help small businesses and developing countries. The story links his appeal to the Fed's expected announcement of faster monetary tightening.

FED.title: Governments press central banks to tackle inflation
summaries: The story describes strong pressure from governments on central banks, including the Fed, to tackle inflation because of its political, social and purchasing-power consequences. Governments invoke central banks' responsibility for price stability. Central banks are responding to political demands but their actions remain relatively moderate, reducing liquidity injections and asset purchases rather than substantially withdrawing support.

FED.title: Senators press Powell on the Fed's inflation response
summaries: At Powell's January 11 confirmation hearing, Senate Banking Committee lawmakers questioned how Fed policy would address inflation and support the recovery. Republicans were particularly unhappy with high inflation, although neither party attacked Powell aggressively.

FED.title: Warren presses Powell to link inflation to corporate pricing power
summaries: Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed Powell to acknowledge that increased corporate concentration and higher profit margins suggested companies were raising prices beyond their increased costs. Powell resisted endorsing her argument, emphasizing strong demand as another explanation for price increases.

FED.title: Warren demands transparency over Fed trading scandal
summaries: Senator Elizabeth Warren called on Monday for more information and transparency concerning the Fed trading scandal, as Richard Clarida stepped down two weeks early.
Warren described a culture of corruption at the Fed and called for an SEC investigation after scrutiny of trades by Robert Kaplan, Eric Rosengren and Richard Clarida.

FED.title: Lawmakers rebuke Powell over Fed officials' trading
summaries: At Powell's Senate testimony the day after Kaplan and Rosengren announced their September resignations, several lawmakers criticized the trading scandal as damaging the Fed's image as an impartial, independent institution and said the Fed should serve the public rather than officials' stock portfolios.

FED.title: Ackman urges Fed to hike rates by 50 basis points
summaries: Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said the Fed needs to raise interest rates by 50 basis points to restore its credibility.

FED.title: Biden urges Fed to address inflation
summaries: President Biden said a couple of days earlier that the Fed had to do something about inflation, according to the interviewee, who linked political pressure on the central bank to declining real wages and the November midterm elections.

FED.title: Manchin presses Fed to tackle inflation
summaries: Democratic Senator Joe Manchin said over the weekend that the Fed must confront rising prices, adding political pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates.

FED.title: Summers urges emergency Fed meeting to end QE
summaries: Former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers said last week that the Fed should hold an emergency meeting to at least turn off quantitative easing.

FED.title: Trump pressed Fed and Powell to lower rates
summaries: The story recalls that during Trump's presidency, he pressured the Fed and Chairman Jerome Powell to lower interest rates.

FED.title: Senate Republicans block Fed nominees over Raskin dispute
summaries: Senate Republicans refused to attend a vote on Biden's Federal Reserve nominees, delaying confirmation of all five, including Chair Jerome Powell. Republicans questioned whether Sarah Bloom Raskin used government contacts to help Reserve Trust, a Colorado payments firm whose board she joined after leaving the Obama administration in 2017. Raskin said she followed all ethical requirements.

Republicans also expressed concerns about Raskin's past calls for the Fed to do more to address climate change. Democrats could potentially overcome the blockade through rule changes requiring a separate vote, but Senator Ben Ray Lujan's absence while recovering from a stroke leaves them without their fiftieth senator for several weeks.
Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said Biden should find a better, more mainstream nominee than Sarah Bloom Raskin.

Republicans remain united against Raskin's nomination. GOP lawmakers, especially those from energy-producing states, oppose her in part over her past criticism of federal pandemic loans to highly indebted fossil fuel companies.

FED.title: Manchin opposes Sarah Bloom Raskin's Fed nomination
summaries: Senator Joe Manchin said he would not support Sarah Bloom Raskin's nomination to the Federal Reserve Board, likely blocking confirmation because she needs every Senate Democrat's support in the evenly divided chamber.
Manchin remains opposed to Raskin. The story describes a potential deal to advance the other four Fed nominees while dropping her nomination.
The White House said Raskin withdrew from consideration a day after Manchin opposed her nomination, citing her views on climate change.

FED.title: Industry and conservative groups attack Raskin nomination
summaries: President Biden said Sarah Bloom Raskin had been subjected to baseless attacks from industry and conservative interest groups. The White House announced her withdrawal from consideration for the Fed board.

FED.title: Elizabeth Warren warns Fed against driving economy off a cliff
summaries: Senator Elizabeth Warren warned the Fed to be careful not to drive the economy off a cliff, pressuring it over the risk that its efforts to curb inflation could cause a severe slowdown.

FED.title: Pat Toomey criticizes Fed's handling of inflation
summaries: Senator Pat Toomey criticized the Fed's management of monetary policy, saying its mindset treats inflation as a psychological rather than a monetary problem and has contributed to the current dilemma. He argued that inflation poses the greater risk and could cause enormous long-term damage unless brought under control quickly, while acknowledging a significant recession risk within the next 12 months.

FED.title: Brazilian finance minister accuses Fed of waging currency war
summaries: In 2010, Brazilian finance minister Guido Montega accused the US and the Fed of deliberately weakening the dollar to gain an international trade advantage, calling it a currency war. He objected to US monetary policies that weakened the dollar and strengthened the Brazilian real, making Brazilian exports less competitive.

FED.title: Larry Summers criticizes Powell's neutral-rate claim
summaries: Former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers criticized Fed Chair Jay Powell's assertion at his press conference that the Fed's 2.5% interest rate was neutral, calling Powell's statements analytically indefensible and wishful thinking.

FED.title: Democrats predicted to dismiss Fed chief if inflation stays high
summaries: A commentator predicted that Democrats would blame and dismiss the Fed chief if US inflation did not begin falling quickly, arguing they could not face the November election with excessively high inflation that was not declining.

FED.title: Pål Ringåh criticizes Powell's handling of inflation
summaries: Investment director and author Pål Ringåh criticized Fed Chair Jerome Powell as inconsistent and difficult to read. He said Powell had made one of the biggest policy mistakes in Fed history by denying inflation despite evidence last year, leaving the Fed behind the curve.

FED.title: Politicians call for Volcker's impeachment over economic damage
summaries: Politicians called for Fed Chair Paul Volcker's impeachment, accusing him of wrecking the US economy as his anti-inflation tightening pushed interest rates above 20% and caused a deep recession in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

FED.title: UN and World Bank warn Fed tightening threatens developing countries
summaries: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development warned the Fed earlier this week that US rate increases threaten developing countries. The UN and World Bank urged the Fed and other central banks to consider strains on poorer nations dependent on dollar borrowing and global investors, as tightening draws investment back to the US and a rising dollar makes debt repayments more expensive.

FED.title: EU diplomat Borrell criticizes Fed hikes over global recession risk
summaries: EU High Representative Josep Borrell told EU ambassadors that Fed rate increases were forcing other central banks to raise rates to protect their currencies, warning that the global rush to tighten monetary policy could tip the world into recession.

FED.title: Congress pushes legislation to tie Fed policy to monetary rules
summaries: In 2014 testimony to the House Financial Services Committee, John Taylor recommended legislation requiring the Fed to report its policy rule. Congress subsequently pursued bills encouraging the Fed to follow a rule such as the Taylor rule, including one requiring an audit explanation for deviations. Fed Chair Janet Yellen opposed the proposals as infringing Fed independence. The legislation did not pass; the Fed voluntarily began publishing twice-yearly charts comparing its interest-rate decisions with the Taylor rule.

FED.title: Trump's criticism of Powell despite appointing him
summaries: The story recalls that Donald Trump subjected Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell to strong criticism despite having appointed him, citing this as part of the political backdrop Powell must navigate.

FED.title: Nixon pressured Burns to keep interest rates low
summaries: President Richard Nixon pressured Fed Chair Arthur Burns to keep interest rates low to stimulate the economy and boost Nixon's 1972 reelection prospects. At Burns' 1970 swearing-in ceremony, Nixon joked about lower interest rates and more money and said he hoped Burns would independently follow his views. Burns recorded presidential pressure in his diary, though the story disputes whether that pressure drove his rate decisions.

FED.title: Warren challenges Powell over unemployment from tightening
summaries: During Powell's Senate hearing, Elizabeth Warren questioned whether it was necessary to send two million people into unemployment. Powell responded by asking whether the Fed should do nothing.

Warren asked Powell what he would say directly to the two million workers she said he was planning to have lose their jobs over the next year, and how he would explain that outcome. Powell responded that high inflation was hurting all working people.

FED.title: Republicans seek tighter Fed policy ahead of election
summaries: The story says Republicans want Powell to tighten monetary policy as much as possible to produce an economic downturn ahead of next year's election and undermine President Biden's reelection prospects.
During Powell's Senate Banking Committee appearance, Republicans blamed President Joe Biden for overstimulating the economy and urged Powell to continue fighting inflation.

FED.title: Biden calls for stricter rules after US bank failures
summaries: President Joe Biden called for stricter rules after Signature Bank, Silicon Valley Bank and Silvergate Capital failed within days of one another.

FED.title: Brown pushes Fed for stronger bank safeguards
summaries: Senator Sherrod Brown said he is pushing the Federal Reserve to strengthen capital and liquidity standards and conduct stress tests following Silicon Valley Bank's collapse. He also plans to push Congress for these changes.

FED.title: McHenry pledges congressional probe of Fed supervision
summaries: House Financial Services Committee Chairman Patrick McHenry said his committee will investigate Silicon Valley Bank's collapse, including whether supervision failed at the Washington Fed or the San Francisco Fed and what happened among supervisors overseeing the bank.

FED.title: Warren calls for outside investigation of Fed
summaries: The story cites Elizabeth Warren's call for an outside investigator as Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michael Barr prepares to investigate the Fed's role in Silicon Valley Bank's collapse.

FED.title: Yellen calls for tighter US bank regulation
summaries: Janet Yellen expressed a clear desire to tighten US banking regulation following the banking turmoil.

FED.title: Trump calls on Fed to lower interest rates
summaries: The story recalls Donald Trump's public calls for lower interest rates during his presidency. It says these calls intensified as inflation was falling, but research found no effect on the Fed's policy reaction function.

FED.title: US opposition calls for higher Fed interest rates
summaries: The story describes public calls from US opposition politicians for higher interest rates. Research discussed in the story found that these calls did not affect the Fed's policy reaction function.

FED.title: Warren criticizes Fed tightening over job-loss risks
summaries: Senator Elizabeth Warren has been highly critical of the Fed. Ahead of Powell's congressional testimony, Michael McKee expects her, based on past performance, to criticize excessive monetary tightening because it could increase unemployment.
During Powell's congressional testimony, Senator Elizabeth Warren warned that the Fed's policies risk leaving millions of people unemployed.

FED.title: Republicans press Powell to endorse budget discipline
