summaries: Michael McKee says Republican lawmakers usually try to get Powell to endorse budget discipline and expects them to raise national debt, deficits and government spending during his upcoming congressional testimony.

FED.title: Warren expected to press Jefferson to back off rate hikes
summaries: Ahead of Philip Jefferson's vice-chair nomination hearing next Wednesday, Kate Davidson expects Senator Elizabeth Warren to push him to commit to backing off the Fed's rate-hiking campaign.

FED.title: Republicans challenge Lisa Cook's Fed appointment
summaries: Republicans opposed Lisa Cook's initial confirmation, arguing that she lacked proper experience and qualifications despite widespread support from the economic community. Ahead of her hearing for a new 14-year term, Davidson says similar criticism has not resurfaced but Cook could face tough questioning about her decisions and statements as a governor.

FED.title: Republican presidential candidates criticize Fed inflation record and mandate
summaries: Republican presidential candidates criticize the Fed for being behind the curve on inflation, arguing that its easy-money policies helped fuel inflation and forced steep interest-rate increases. They also accuse it of straying into climate risks and social equity and want it focused on inflation and stable prices.

FED.title: DeSantis pledges to replace Powell as Fed chair
summaries: On Monday, Republican presidential candidate Ron DeSantis said he would seek to replace Jay Powell as Federal Reserve chair if elected, potentially before Powell's term expires in 2026.

FED.title: Trump pressured Fed for lower interest rates
summaries: The story recalls that Donald Trump attacked Powell and, around 2019 while president, pushed for lower interest rates.

FED.title: Javier Milei criticizes Federal Reserve
summaries: Argentine presidential candidate Javier Milei described the Federal Reserve as one of the world's bad central banks in an interview.

FED.title: DeSantis criticizes Fed-controlled digital dollar
summaries: Republican presidential candidate and Florida governor Ron DeSantis criticized a Fed-controlled digital dollar, claiming it could be used to impose an ESG agenda by blocking transactions such as gas purchases deemed excessive.

FED.title: Governments press Fed to ease restrictive monetary policy
summaries: The story reports pressure from unspecified government leaders on central banks, including the Fed, to ease restrictive monetary policy to avoid economic slowdown or recession.

FED.title: Trump publicly pressures Fed and Powell to lower interest rates
summaries: The discussion recalls Donald Trump's public demands that the Fed lower interest rates and his insults directed at Jerome Powell. One speaker claims Trump induced policy changes, while another says an analysis of the Fed's reaction function found no statistically significant effect from Trump's statements.

FED.title: Republican senators challenge Fed's proposed higher bank capital requirements
summaries: Republican senators wrote a letter to the Fed questioning whether it should pursue the proposed Basel III endgame rules and higher bank capital requirements. Republicans on the Senate Banking Committee have vocally opposed the proposals ahead of an oversight hearing with major bank CEOs.

FED.title: Democratic lawmakers resist Fed's proposed bank capital rules
summaries: A broad cross-section of Democratic lawmakers has opposed the Fed's proposed higher capital requirements for large banks, adding to resistance that threatens to complicate the proposal.

FED.title: Affordable housing advocates urge Fed to ease capital rules
summaries: Affordable housing advocates are asking the Fed to ease proposed capital rules, warning that higher capital requirements for mortgages with high loan-to-property-value ratios could raise costs for lower-income and minority borrowers and widen racial homeownership gaps. Federal officials have signaled willingness to change the proposed rules.

FED.title: Trump voices preference for low interest rates and less regulation
summaries: Former President Donald Trump publicly voiced his preference for low interest rates and less regulation. The story attributes the day's gains in small-cap stocks partly to his comments.

FED.title: Election-year pressure on Fed to cut rates before August
summaries: The story describes mounting political pressure on the Fed to cut interest rates before August so cuts can take effect before the election campaign begins after Labor Day. It argues that alternative inflation measures near 1.4% imply excessively high real interest rates and reports growing pressure to measure actual inflation differently. No specific political actor is identified.

FED.title: Yellen and Treasury accused of overriding Fed through liquidity expansion
summaries: A commentator alleges that Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and the Treasury Department have overridden the Fed by expanding liquidity and pouring money into the economy. The commentator argues that this fuels price increases and limits the Fed's ability to cut interest rates.

A commentator says Janet Yellen has supplied substantial liquidity through reverse repos and that these pandemic-era funds are running out. He argues that Powell is preparing to slow quantitative tightening to continue supplying liquidity.

FED.title: Trump election victory linked to Powell losing his job
summaries: A commentator claims Powell would lose his job if Trump wins the election and portrays Powell's policy approach as motivated by retaining his position and supporting favorable market sentiment ahead of November's election.
Trump has said he would not reappoint Jerome Powell as Fed chair and has provided a list of preferred replacements whom he describes as more open.
People close to Trump say he has informally discussed possible Fed chair candidates with advisers and asked associates whether they would be interested in the job.

FED.title: Biden and Democrats urge Fed rate cuts
summaries: Biden and Democrats have called for the Fed to cut interest rates, arguing that high rates harm most of the population and hinder investment.

FED.title: Trump allies propose curbing Fed independence
summaries: A group of Donald Trump's allies has been developing proposals that would require the Fed to consult Trump as president on interest-rate decisions and subject Fed regulations to White House review. It could not be determined whether Trump knows of or has approved the effort. Several Republican lawmakers have opposed challenges to Fed independence.

Fewer than a dozen Trump allies have spent months developing a ten-page proposal. They envision a tacit agreement with a future Fed chair to consult Trump regularly on rates and have discussed Trump himself serving on the Board of Governors. They argue that informal consultation and White House regulatory review could proceed without congressional approval, citing a first-term Justice Department opinion for the latter. Some participants believe they have Trump's blessing, but his senior advisers say nothing is official unless announced by Trump or his campaign. Trump has privately questioned why the president has no input on interest rates.

FED.title: Trump pressured Fed for lower rates and a weaker dollar during his presidency
summaries: During his 2017–2021 presidency, Trump pressed the Fed for lower interest rates and a weaker dollar to compete with China and stimulate the economy. Powell resisted, saying the Fed needed to do what was right for the economy, resulting in a major political dispute.

Trump began publicly criticizing Powell when the Fed raised rates in 2018, later asking whether Powell or Chinese President Xi Jinping was the bigger enemy of the United States. Trump considered firing Powell, but senior cabinet officials convinced him he lacked the authority.
In 2019, Trump wanted substantially more monetary easing than Powell delivered, despite the Fed cutting rates a couple of times.

FED.title: Trump allies propose demoting Powell before his term ends
summaries: Trump allies' draft proposes removing Jerome Powell as chair before his term ends in 2026 while leaving him on the Fed board. Trump would then elevate another sitting governor to chair, potentially choosing someone more aligned with him.

FED.title: Arthur Burns deferred to presidents on interest rates
summaries: The story describes Fed chair Arthur Burns as deferring to presidents during the Nixon, Ford and Carter administrations and keeping interest rates low longer than many experts thought appropriate, contributing to an inflation spike.
Ahead of his 1972 reelection, Nixon successfully pressured Arthur Burns to cut interest rates when cuts were inappropriate, helping lay the groundwork for inflation in the 1970s.

FED.title: Trump portrays pre-election Fed rate cuts as pro-Biden interference
summaries: Trump has said that if Powell cuts interest rates before the election, it would be part of a deep-state operation supporting Biden.

FED.title: Trump threatens to fire Powell if reelected
summaries: The story says Trump has explicitly threatened to fire Powell if reelected, regardless of whether he has the legal authority to do so.
The story links Trump's potential replacement of Powell to whether Powell implements rapid interest-rate cuts needed for the weak-dollar policy advocated by Trump and his team.

In a Bloomberg Businessweek interview, Trump said he would allow Powell to serve out his term, with the caveat 'as long as I thought he was doing things right.' He said he did not plan to oust Powell unless Powell did something unusual.

FED.title: Senate bill seeks to bar a digital dollar
summaries: A bill to bar a US central bank digital currency was introduced in the Senate in February.

FED.title: DeSantis bans central bank digital currencies in Florida
summaries: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis banned central bank digital currencies in his state last year, opposing the prospect of a US digital dollar.

FED.title: Trump pressured the Fed to keep interest rates low during his presidency
summaries: Trump repeatedly urged the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates low while he was president, challenging its traditional independence.

FED.title: Trump advisers draft plan to eliminate Fed independence
summaries: Trump's advisers are drafting a plan to eliminate the Federal Reserve's traditional independence. The story links this effort to Trump's view that keeping interest rates low is politically popular.

The draft proposal would have the Fed chair regularly consult the president about interest rates, giving the president a voice in those decisions. The Trump campaign says the proposal is unofficial and becomes official policy only if Trump states it himself.

FED.title: Democrats urge Powell not to delay interest rate cuts
summaries: During Powell's semi-annual congressional testimony, Democrats warned him that delaying interest rate cuts risked harming the economy, citing rising unemployment, elevated housing costs and a manufacturing slowdown.

FED.title: Trump warns Fed against rate cuts before election
summaries: Trump said the Fed should not cut interest rates before the election, implying that such cuts would be a political move benefiting President Biden.
In response to Trump's demand, Powell emphasized that the Fed acts solely according to its mandate to ensure price stability and promote full employment.

The story describes Trump's opposition to pre-election rate cuts as reflecting concern that they would benefit Kamala Harris's campaign. It reports that the Fed has signaled a September cut for purely economic reasons, not electoral ones.

FED.title: Trump calls for presidential say over Fed
summaries: Trump emphasized that the U.S. president should have a say over the Federal Reserve.

At a press conference, Trump said his business experience made him more qualified to make monetary policy decisions than many Fed officials and characterized their decisions as based on little more than gut feeling.
Trump criticized the Fed for raising its policy rate 'a little too early and a little too late.'

Kamala Harris rejected Trump's proposal for presidential influence over Fed decisions, saying the Fed is independent and that she would never interfere with its decisions as president. Powell pledged not to allow political pressure to influence the central bank's decision-making.

Trump's running mate JD Vance supported greater presidential input over monetary policy, saying voters dissatisfied with interest-rate policy should be able to elect someone to change it and that such questions should not be above democratic debate.

FED.title: Senator Kennedy presses Powell on rate-cut timing
summaries: Republican Senator John Kennedy grilled Fed Chair Jerome Powell last month about when interest rates would be lowered. Powell declined to signal the timing of future actions.

FED.title: Nixon pressures Burns to loosen monetary policy
summaries: President Richard Nixon pressured Fed Chair Arthur Burns for looser monetary policy to help his reelection chances.

FED.title: Johnson pressures his Fed chair
summaries: The story recalls that President Lyndon Johnson pressured the Federal Reserve chair serving at the time, without specifying his demands.

FED.title: Trump publicly criticizes Fed and Powell
summaries: Trump began publicly criticizing the Federal Reserve during the 2016 election campaign and continued during his presidency, making public swipes against his appointed Fed chair, Jerome Powell, beginning in 2018.

FED.title: Trump opposes Fed rate cuts ahead of election
summaries: Donald Trump said the Fed should not cut interest rates, arguing that a cut would be unfair and would boost Biden and Harris.
After the Fed cut interest rates by 50 basis points, Trump responded that the decision indicated the economy was worse than expected.

FED.title: Unspecified political pressure for a Fed rate cut
summaries: A commentator attributed the Fed's 50-basis-point rate cut partly to requests or pressure from unspecified political sources, alongside public and business demands, and suggested the November election influenced the decision.

FED.title: Trump threatens to remove Powell as Fed chair
summaries: The commentator recalled that Trump threatened to dismiss Jerome Powell after their relationship deteriorated during Trump's presidency. The commentator also predicted that Republicans would not renew Powell's chairmanship if they won the election and would appoint leadership aligned with their policies.
A commentator said Trump could remove the Fed chair if he returns to office, but might choose not to do so.

A commentator recalled Trump's statement that he wanted to fire Powell because he was ineffective, and warned that repeating such a threat as president would carry greater weight. The commentator predicted that a Trump presidency would influence Fed decisions, including money-market and balance-sheet decisions, while saying Powell would not make biased decisions out of fear for his job.
A commentator said Trump has threatened to replace Powell at any time if Powell does not do as Trump says, describing Trump as a potential threat to Federal Reserve independence.
A commentator described Powell as a “dead man walking” following Trump's election victory, saying Powell knows he will lose his job and must deliver the expected 25-basis-point rate cut on Thursday.
A commentator noted that Powell's term ends in May 2026 and suggested Trump could exert influence by choosing a more political successor as Fed chair.

Asked whether he would resign if Trump pressured him to leave, Powell said he would not. He said Trump lacks legal authority to remove him and that he intends to remain until his term ends in May 2026.
Powell said the president also lacks legal authority to demote the Fed chair or remove other senior Fed officials.
Jessica Ami characterized talk of Powell potentially stepping down as market 'white noise,' saying investors are more focused on the health of the US economy and company earnings.
A commentator noted that any replacement for Powell would require Senate approval.
The story reports that some Trump advisers have suggested asking Powell to resign.
The story says Trump has stated he will not reappoint Powell. A commentator predicted that Powell's successor would favor interest-rate cuts.
The commentator said Trump had announced that he would continue with Powell.

A commentator claimed Trump had said the previous day that he would reconsider Powell's position if the Fed did not respond to circumstances that Trump believed warranted lower rates. Another commentator said he had seen no threats behind Trump's remarks and doubted Trump could override Fed independence.
After Trump fired two FTC commissioners on Tuesday, experts fear he could also remove Fed Chair Jerome Powell, breaking a major taboo.

A commentator claimed Trump had asked Chief Justice Roberts whether he could fire Jerome Powell. Amid rumors of large hedge-fund losses and a possible Fed rescue over the weekend, the commentator suggested Trump could blame Fed mismanagement as a pretext for firing Powell, and linked these fears to the rising gold price.

Commentators said the legal challenge to Trump's firing of National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox could weaken Fed officials' removal protections because her statutory protections were identical to theirs. They considered waiting until Powell's chairmanship ends the likeliest course, citing the potential bond-market backlash to firing him.

Trump posted on Truth Social that Powell's 'termination cannot come fast enough.' Later, he said Powell would leave if asked and that he could remove him 'real fast.' Greg Ip said current law permits removing Fed governors only for cause, while whether the president can demote the chair remains unclear. He predicted Powell would likely pursue legal options if fired.

National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Friday that removing Powell was being studied. Powell said he was closely following a Supreme Court case concerning dismissals at independent agencies but did not believe it applied to the Fed, reiterating that its independence is established by law and removal requires cause. French Finance Minister Eric Lombard warned that removing Powell would jeopardize the dollar's credibility and destabilize the US economy.
Finance editor Alex Frangos said Trump's threat to fire Powell was contributing to investor jitters and weighing on markets because investors worldwide value the Federal Reserve's stability.

Trump and economic adviser Kevin Hassett indirectly questioned the Fed's independence over Easter weekend. On Monday, Trump called Powell a 'big loser.' Amid the debate over Powell's future, major US stock indices fell nearly 2.5%, and the euro rose more than 1% against the dollar to above $1.15, its highest level since November 2021.
The S&P 500 fell as much as 3% after Trump's social media post about Powell.

Daniel Moss said Powell's removal was a real possibility but not necessarily probable. He said markets had reacted swiftly and punitively since Trump resumed his removal threats on Thursday, and cited ISI Evercore's warning of a severe market reaction if Powell were dismissed.

Mark Gardner said Trump's renewed threats to remove Powell were deepening concerns about authoritarian behavior and policy uncertainty. He linked the threats to Trump's desire for lower interest rates as the US faces refinancing $7 trillion in debt this year.

The story reports that, according to several sources, Trump is attempting to have Powell removed. All three major Wall Street indices fell more than 2% on Monday after Trump criticized Powell on Truth Social, while the VIX rose above 30.
Following Trump's attack, the dollar fell further and Germany's DAX opened lower. Correspondent Heike Buchter said fears that the Fed could lose its independence were adding to market uncertainty.

Federico Fubini said the prospect of Trump removing Powell before his term ends and replacing him with someone who follows presidential orders had accelerated investors' flight from US Treasury securities and the dollar into alternative safe havens, helping explain gold's rise.

Trump said on April 22 that he had no intention of firing Powell. IMF officials emphasized that a loss of central bank independence would increase instability in the global economy and financial markets, without specifically naming the Fed or the United States.
Trump said he never intended to fire Powell and blamed the press for interpreting his remarks otherwise. His reversal eased market tensions, with stocks and the dollar gaining.
Australia's ASX 200 rose 1.3% to 7,921 points, following Wall Street gains in response to Trump's statement that he would not sack Powell and his more conciliatory comments on tariffs toward China.

Commentators linked Trump's reversal on removing Powell to concerns about dollar dominance and potential market liquidation, saying statements by Treasury Secretary Bessent and Commerce Secretary Lutnick helped him recognize the risks.
According to Wall Street Journal reporting, some senior officials took Trump's statements about firing Powell seriously, and White House lawyers looked into options for removing him.
The commentators said oil and gold also rose as financial markets reacted to Trump's softer rhetoric toward Powell and on tariffs.

Candriam investment chief Nicolas Forest described interference with Fed independence as a red line for investors, warning that it could undermine US debt's safe-haven status and the dollar's reserve-currency status.
At the Michigan rally, Trump did not renew his earlier language about firing Powell. Newsdesk editor Jill Desis said the renewed criticism did not appear to escalate his earlier campaign.

The story links political pressure on the Fed under Trump to declining investor confidence and fears that compromised independence could impair inflation control. It identifies that pressure, alongside growth concerns and tariff uncertainty, as a factor in the dollar's weakening: the DXY has fallen nearly 9% since Trump returned to office.
A commentator interpreted Trump's retreat from removing Powell as a response to market backlash and a realization that he lacked the legal authority to do so.

Former Dallas Fed president Rob said removing Powell might not change policy because he did not believe there was a consensus among Fed voters to cut rates at the May meeting even without Powell. He suggested the administration may have concluded that removal would be legally problematic and institutionally unsettling, and urged that Powell's successor make no policy pre-commitments to the administration.

The Justice Department is arguing in litigation over other agency officials' dismissals that the 1935 Humphrey's Executor precedent prevents adequate presidential supervision of officials who execute laws. Chris Hughes warned that these dismissals make a similar move against Powell more credible and threaten the Fed's institutional design. The story recalls that Powell reportedly said in 2018 he would spend his last nickel fighting dismissal to preserve Fed independence.

A commentator said market concerns about Fed independence had diminished despite Trump's renewed harsh comments about Powell after the Fed held rates unchanged, and that Powell now appeared able to serve properly until his term ends.

The Supreme Court ruled that Trump can remove leaders of independent government agencies but distinguished the Federal Reserve. Although the order does not explicitly prevent him from firing Powell or other Fed members, Chelsea Delaney said it would ease lingering investor concerns about Fed independence following Trump's removal threats and subsequent retreat.

A commentator predicted Trump would scrutinize his choice of Powell's successor in 2026 more carefully and might seek a Fed chair to whom he could dictate decisions. The commentator warned that markets would test the new chair's independence and limits, potentially causing substantial volatility during candidate selection and after the chair takes office.

The story reports that in late 2018, Kevin Hassett and other advisers urged Trump not to fire Powell, warning it would be disruptive. Hassett publicly assured markets that Powell's job was safe, prompting a market rally and praise from Trump.

Bessent said Trump is not looking to remove Powell before his term ends next year. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon publicly warned that Fed independence is absolutely critical and that interfering with the Fed could have adverse consequences, becoming the first leader of a major US financial institution to publicly address the administration's attacks on Powell.

Trump denied planning to fire Powell after polling Republican lawmakers at a closed-door White House meeting the previous day. He said almost all supported firing Powell. A senior administration official said Trump then suggested he could move to fire Powell in the near future. Trump told reporters removal was highly unlikely but did not rule it out.
The dollar dropped 0.9% after reports that Trump asked Republican lawmakers whether he should fire Powell, then trimmed some losses after Trump appeared to backtrack.

Mary Nicola said the removal speculation steepened the US Treasury yield curve. Polymarket was pricing about a 20% chance of Powell leaving in 2025. Wall Street bank CEOs reiterated the importance of Fed independence and keeping fiscal and monetary policy separate.
A commentator predicted Trump would not fire Powell, arguing that vice chair Philip Jefferson would become Fed chair until May and that Trump would oppose that outcome.

FED.title: Trump proposes changing the Fed's governing law
summaries: A commentator recalled Trump's statements during his presidency and election campaigning about changing the law governing the Fed. The commentator described the proposal as undefined and said it could initially alarm markets if Trump wins.

FED.title: Trump calls for presidential say in Fed interest-rate decisions
summaries: In a Bloomberg interview, Donald Trump argued that the president should have a say in whether interest rates rise or fall. He also mocked Jerome Powell's role as the easiest government job, likening rate decisions to a monthly coin toss and saying the Fed chair is treated like a god.

ECB President Christine Lagarde responded to Trump's criticism of Powell's job as a monthly coin toss by defending central bank staff as hardworking and conscientious. She stressed that central bank independence is critical to institutional credibility and must be defended.
Jerome Powell has repeatedly emphasized that the Fed is not a political agency.

Following Trump's election, Paul Hannan said investors do not expect him to restrain the Fed directly or immediately. He noted institutional safeguards and possible congressional support for Fed independence, while warning that growing fears about independence could revive inflation strongly enough to warrant a rate hike.
The story says Lagarde invited Trump to Frankfurt to see how central banks work after his remarks mocking Powell's job as a monthly coin toss.

A commentator predicted a dispute between Trump and Powell that could become more important for markets than economic data, recalling Trump's complaint that Fed officials make decisions on matters for which he bears political responsibility and prevent him from doing what he wants.

At his confirmation hearing, incoming Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent affirmed that the Fed is independent when asked about Trump determining interest rates or controlling the Fed. A commentator nevertheless expected Trump to publicly communicate his views, warning that his interference could make markets less predictable.

Joe Matthew predicted that Trump's criticism of the Fed could be even more aggressive in his second administration, potentially through Truth Social or Twitter, and that he would be vocal about interest rates.
Jenny Leonard described Trump's stance on influencing Fed interest-rate policy as having hardened since his October interview, when he said he should weigh in but not make the decisions.
The story reports that groups of Trump's allies argue he should be consulted on interest-rate decisions.

FED.title: Trump promises lower interest rates
summaries: A commentator noted Trump's promises of lower interest rates and questioned whether they would be problematic or significant for the Fed.
The story says Trump sought to intervene in monetary policy during his first term and is interested in lower interest rates and a weaker dollar to help American exports.

The story recalls that Trump's relationship with Powell deteriorated about six months after Powell's appointment because Powell refused Trump's demands to lower interest rates further to stimulate the economy. Trump responded by calling Powell crazy and un-American.
A commentator predicted that Trump would insist on lower interest rates while continuing to spend as he wishes, putting Powell under considerable pressure.
A commentator predicted that Trump would press Powell to address interest rates by contrasting the roughly 0.5% rate during his previous presidency with the current roughly 4.5% rate.

A commentator contrasted Trump's desire for rapid growth with Powell's message that he is in no hurry to cut interest rates, saying a central bank would have to apply the brakes if a politician pushes for faster growth.

A commentator predicted that Trump would continue pressuring the Fed through daily tweets questioning why interest rates had not fallen, while pursuing expansionary policies that prioritize growth and increased spending over inflation.

The story reports that Trump said the previous day that interest rates were too high. A commentator predicted the Fed would continue cutting rates partly to avoid obstructing Trump's agenda or being blamed if conditions deteriorate, expecting a cut in March or April and total cuts of up to 75 basis points in 2025.

Speaking at the World Economic Forum, Trump said he would ask Saudi Arabia and OPEC nations to lower oil prices and would demand that interest rates fall immediately as oil prices decline. He also said interest rates should fall globally.
Jessica Ramiere predicted that Fed Chair Powell would effectively ignore Trump's demands for lower interest rates, emphasizing the Fed's inflation-control mandate.
White House correspondent Jenny Leonard predicted Trump would use every opportunity and lever available to pressure Powell over interest-rate policy, but said she did not expect Powell to bend.
The story reports that Trump claimed nobody knows more about interest rates than he does while demanding that Powell cut rates immediately.

Michael McKee predicted Trump would criticize the Fed if it remains on hold for a while because officials consider some of his policies inflationary, though Trump may not focus on this week's meeting amid his other immediate priorities.

Trump said last week that interest rates should fall rapidly and that he thought Fed officials would listen to him. A commentator linked his demand to concerns about the dollar's strength and the trade balance, particularly with Europe, and expected recurring friction between Trump and the Fed while the Fed continued following its own policy.

Experts expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged at its first policy meeting since Trump took office, despite his calls for further cuts to stimulate the economy. The story says the Fed is likely to wait to assess the economic effects of Trump's announcements, noting that his threatened tariffs could significantly fuel inflation.

The Fed held its policy rate at 4.25–4.50% on Wednesday, pausing its series of rate cuts despite Trump's demand the previous week that rates fall. Powell declined to respond to Trump's remarks, saying he had no reaction or comment and that doing so would not be appropriate.

After the Fed held rates steady, Trump posted on Truth Social that it had done very little to fight inflation, said he would solve inflation himself, and criticized the Fed's efforts in other areas as having stoked price pressures for US citizens.

After the Fed held rates steady, Trump specifically blamed its attention to gender ideology, green energy and what he called "fake climate change" for inflation, posting that inflation would never have been a problem had the Fed spent less time on those issues.

Powell said he had not been in contact with Trump. He reiterated that there was no hurry to cut rates and said the Fed needed to let Trump's policies take shape before assessing their economic implications.
Trump's Truth Social criticism also blamed the Fed's attention to diversity, equity and inclusion for distracting it from fighting inflation.
A commentator predicted Fed rate cuts, citing Trump's request for cuts alongside expectations that his tariff policies would weaken the economy and produce poor economic data.

A commentator predicted Trump would be upset if the Fed left rates unchanged at its upcoming meeting, as expected, because he wants lower rates. The commentator attributed the expected hold to uncertainty about the economic impact of tariff policy despite reasonable recent inflation figures.

Trump criticized the Fed for not moving on rates, saying it would be much better off cutting interest rates as tariffs are introduced. The Fed signaled half a percentage point of cuts this year but said it was awaiting further inflation progress and clarity on Trump's trade policies before acting.

A commentator predicted that Trump would repeatedly demand rate cuts on the grounds that inflation is falling, likening his expected persistence to children repeatedly asking for chocolate until they get it.
A commentator cited an unverified report that Trump was angry after the Fed left rates unchanged and had privately told it to lower rates.

Matthew Tan said Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent are using recession risk as a negotiating tool to force Fed rate cuts, signaling willingness to cause a slowdown unless Powell cuts rates. He described lower rates as part of their fiscal strategy to reduce Treasury interest expenses alongside tariffs, spending cuts and tax-cut negotiations.

Ahead of Powell's remarks in Virginia, Trump posted on Truth Social that he hoped the Fed would cut interest rates. Powell maintained a wait-and-see stance, saying it was too early to determine rate adjustments despite warning that larger-than-expected tariff increases would bring higher inflation and slower growth.

Over the weekend, Trump urged Powell to stop playing politics and cut interest rates. Asked whether he was deliberately driving markets down to force Fed rate cuts, Trump denied doing so, saying markets were afraid because they did not yet understand his plans and would eventually see that tariffs would enrich America.

A commentator predicted Trump would renew demands for Powell to cut rates after Thursday's US inflation release, expecting inflation around 2.5% because of weaker oil prices. He predicted Trump would argue that inflation was approaching 2% and insist Powell listen to him.

Philippe Wechter said Powell appeared reluctant to follow the White House's agenda, but argued that it would be difficult for the Fed to resist it indefinitely, noting that monetary policy had already eased through rate cuts and a slower reduction of the balance sheet.

Commentators said Trump is using improved inflation figures, with March CPI inflation falling to 2.4% from 2.8% in February, to press for rate cuts on Truth Social and other platforms. They said Fed officials are concerned that cutting rates could be seen as capitulation to Trump and insist on evidence of economic weakening and anchored inflation expectations before acting.
A commentator said Trump's recent demand that Powell stop playing politics raised concerns about whether the political authorities and the Fed could coordinate decisions in a future liquidity crisis.

Trump called Powell 'always too late and wrong' and demanded that he cut interest rates as other central banks have done. The remarks followed Powell's warning that tariffs could raise prices and weaken the economy, creating a difficult tradeoff for the Fed.

During his press conference with Giorgia Meloni, Trump accused Powell of playing politics and doing a poor job. He said the Fed must follow the ECB in cutting interest rates and expressed confidence that it would eventually do so under strong political pressure.

Heike Buchter said the tone of Trump's dispute with Powell over rate cuts had sharpened considerably in recent days. She expected participants at the IMF and World Bank spring meetings in Washington to discuss whether Powell could withstand the pressure and what would happen if he could not.
Trump again pressured Powell on social media to cut interest rates to stimulate the economy. Powell said he would not be influenced by political pressure.
Mark Gardner linked Trump's push for lower interest rates to the need to refinance $7 trillion in US debt this year.

A commentator said Trump wants Powell to cut rates preemptively and linked that demand to $8 trillion in debt needing refinancing, with investors holding short-term Treasury securities yielding 4.5–5%. The commentator argued that lower rates would push investors further out on the yield curve to finance government deficits, and that further economic deterioration could force the Fed to cut rates.

Trump claimed there was almost no inflation and warned of an economic slowdown unless Powell, whom he called 'Mr. Too Late' and a 'major loser,' lowered interest rates immediately. His post followed Powell's comments that tariff uncertainty could require rates to remain on hold. The story reports that bond yields rose, the dollar traded at a three-year low against a basket of currencies, and gold exceeded $3,450 for the first time amid Trump's attacks.
Trump said he wanted Powell to be more active in lowering interest rates, calling this the perfect time for cuts, but added that failure to cut would not be 'the end.'

A commentator interpreted Trump's repeated rate-cut demands as an effort to blame Powell for a potential tariff-driven economic slowdown. Another cited research finding that Trump's first-term pressure did not influence Fed policy beyond economic conditions or materially affect US bond yields and the dollar, contrasting that with current market turbulence.

A commentator cited rumors that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent meets Powell weekly and that they have agreed Powell will cut interest rates if the 10-year Treasury yield remains above 4.5% for two weeks. The commentator suggested this could begin a period of aggressive monetary easing amid excessive US debt.
Greg Ip said Trump was seeking help from the Fed after markets responded to his tariff plan by driving down stock prices.
A commentator suggested Trump may be trying to push the Fed to cut rates sooner rather than wait for further economic weakening, and said his remarks can disrupt the recent easing of market tensions.

Economists and former U.S. policymakers warned that Trump's demands for lower interest rates and criticism of the Fed could undermine investor confidence in Powell's successor, creating suspicion that future rate decisions reflect presidential wishes or a side deal rather than economic conditions and inflation control.
At his Michigan rally marking 100 days in office, Trump renewed criticism of Powell, saying he was not doing a good job and that Trump knew interest rates better than Powell.

A commentator predicted that two Fed rate cuts this year would result from Trump's pressure and another from economic necessity, while markets were pricing four cuts. He also predicted that a slowdown caused by Trump's trade policies and uncertainty would bring further pressure and attacks from Trump on the Fed and Powell to lower rates.
At his Michigan rally, Trump said inflation was basically down and interest rates had fallen despite Powell, whom he accused of not doing a good job.
Rob Kaplan defended the Fed's slower approach to rate cuts against Trump's criticism, saying economic uncertainty and still-sticky US inflation justify caution.

Trump renewed pressure on the Fed over the weekend to cut interest rates. A commentator said Powell would need a strong reason to cut, such as substantial economic weakening and rising unemployment, while shortages caused by trade disruption could fuel inflation and prevent near-term cuts.

A commentator warned that the alleged arrangement between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Powell to cut rates if long-term Treasury yields remain elevated would make US interest rates politically determined and harm the dollar.

On May 7, the Fed again held its policy rate at 4.25–4.5% despite Trump's repeated criticism that rates were too high and Powell was to blame. Powell said the Fed could remain patient, noting that the economy remained solid but risks to both inflation and the labor market had increased.
The story says Trump accuses Powell of delivering rate cuts only to help Democratic politicians.

Following the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged, Trump attacked Powell as not merely slow but stupid. A commentator said Trump wants lower rates to improve households' finances and encourage home and car purchases, and predicted the continuing dispute could delay US rate cuts for a long time.
Trump called Powell "a fool who doesn't have a clue" the day before publication, continuing his criticism and demands for lower interest rates to stimulate the economy.

A commentator said Trump was trying to shift the costs of the negative economic environment onto Powell as falling popularity prompted him to soften his rhetoric. The commentator noted that expectations had been revised from four Fed rate cuts to three, while the Fed would wait to assess the severity of tariffs' price effects before acting.

Following April inflation figures showing headline and core prices rising 0.2%, Trump renewed his demand for rate cuts. He claimed there was no inflation and that gasoline, energy, groceries and practically all other prices were down, urging the Fed to lower rates as Europe and China had done and asking, "What is wrong with too late Powell?"

A commentator contrasted Trump's intense pressure on the Fed to lower rates with his own fiscal policies pushing market interest rates higher through expectations of increased borrowing, inflation and risk premiums. Jamie Dimon defended the Fed's decision to hold rates, citing serious stagflation risks.

At a White House meeting on May 29, Trump told Powell he was making a mistake by not lowering interest rates. The Fed said Trump invited Powell to their first meeting of Trump's second term. Powell did not discuss specific monetary-policy expectations and stressed that policy decisions, including the path of interest rates, would depend on economic data.
The White House spokesperson said Trump reiterated his public calls for lower interest rates face-to-face with Powell. The story also reports that they exchanged views on inflation and employment.

The story says Powell explained the potential side effects of cutting rates during his meeting with Trump. A commentator predicted that Trump would blame rising unemployment and job losses in a possible recession on Powell's refusal to cut rates, rather than accept responsibility for his own policies and the uncertainty they created.

After ADP reported that employers added just 37,000 jobs in May, down from 62,000 in April and the weakest growth in more than two years, Trump posted on Truth Social that Powell should lower interest rates. The Fed reiterated last week that rate decisions rely solely on careful, objective and nonpolitical analysis.
Trump said last week that Powell should lower interest rates by one full percentage point.
Trump said that a good Fed chair would cut interest rates.

Following May CPI figures showing annual inflation of 2.4% and underlying inflation of 2.8%, Trump called the figures great and urged the Fed to cut rates by one percentage point ahead of its meeting next week.
A commentator argued that Trump's pressure would make Powell more determined to demonstrate Fed independence and could deter a rate cut even if he otherwise intended one.
A commentator predicted that Trump would continue attacking Powell for the remaining 10–11 months of his chairmanship.

Trump preemptively criticized the anticipated June 18 rate decision and called for much more dramatic cuts. The Fed held rates steady while leaving open cuts in the second half of the year. WSJ correspondent Nick Timiraos said Trump's pressure had not influenced the decision and that Trump argues the economy is strong but would be stronger with lower overnight borrowing costs.
Trump said on the morning of June 18 that he wanted the Fed to cut interest rates by at least two percentage points, rather than a quarter point.
Trump called Powell stupid ahead of the June rate decision for keeping interest rates unchanged for so long.

About three hours before Powell's June 18 press conference, Trump again attacked Powell and called for interest rates to fall to 2.5% to lower government borrowing costs. A commentator said Trump's pressure was causing greater concern about Fed independence than during his first term and interpreted rising University of Michigan household inflation expectations as evidence of damage to the Fed's credibility.

Frédéric Ducrozet warned that pressure on the Fed could eventually extend beyond rate cuts to directives on regulation and long-term debt management, normally Treasury responsibilities. He said such potentially involuntary cooperation could deepen market concerns about debt sustainability and the credibility and stability of US institutions.

Michael McKee predicted that Republican lawmakers would give Powell a hard time for not cutting rates during his upcoming congressional testimony because Trump wants cuts. He said this would be Powell's first Capitol Hill testimony since Trump's latest round of insults began.

During June 24 congressional testimony amid continued pressure from Trump to cut rates, Powell kept his options open. He leaned against a July cut without explicitly ruling it out, saying weaker-than-expected tariff inflation or a weakening labor market could justify earlier cuts, while higher inflation or continued labor-market strength could delay them.

A commentator said Trump's influence over Powell remains limited despite his pressure. Discussing Powell's remarks the previous day, the commentator said Powell maintained a wait-and-see approach, stressing that data would determine the policy path and that the Fed needed to assess tariff effects. Some other Fed officials supported his stance.
Trump said the previous day that Powell was not doing his job because he had not lowered interest rates.

A commentator interpreted Trump's attacks on Powell as a deliberate strategy to weaken the dollar and shift blame to the Fed if economic conditions deteriorate, while allowing Trump to claim credit if conditions improve. The commentator predicted Powell would eventually yield somewhat on rate cuts and expected three cuts during the remainder of the year, with inflation remaining decisive.

A commentator said Trump stated today that inflation had almost disappeared and described the pressure on the Fed to cut rates as stronger than any they remembered, independent of economic data and developments.
A commentator said Trump had insulted Powell by comparing his head to a brick, alongside criticism that he was not doing his job well.

A commentator said Trump wants interest rates at 1%, rather than merely the two cuts broadly expected this year, and warned that his demands and attacks on Fed credibility could harm US and global markets.

WSJ columnist Spencer Jacob said the stronger-than-expected June jobs report reinforced the Fed's case for waiting despite Trump's pressure to cut rates, while officials await evidence of tariffs' inflationary impact.

A commentator said Trump's requested interest-rate level had fallen to between zero and 1%, and that Trump argued low rates from the Federal Reserve would help the government service its debt. The commentator warned that such easing would increase demand, wage growth and inflation, potentially raising long-term rates; counteracting that rise through large Fed purchases of government bonds could undermine the dollar.

Trump called Powell terrible and accused him of "whining like a baby about non-existent inflation for months" and refusing to do the right thing, demanding: "Cut interest rates, Jerome, now is the time."
A commentator said Trump's demand for a 1% interest rate with inflation at 2.5% would imply a negative real interest rate, and described interest rates as becoming increasingly political.

A commentator said Trump's rhetoric against Powell had reached extreme levels, but the Fed continued pursuing policy different from the president's demands. The commentator defended its wait-and-see approach, warning that cutting rates could further stimulate demand in an already strong economy with unemployment at 4.1%, while tariff effects on inflation remained uncertain.
The story says Trump advisers have joined his attacks on the Fed, calling it idiotic for keeping interest rates high.

A commentator interpreted Trump's push to cut rates immediately to 1% as an effort to avoid waiting through a recession ahead of the November 2026 election, warning that such cuts would fuel inflation.
US inflation rose three tenths of a percentage point to 2.7% in June. The story says the increase could make it harder for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates despite Trump's demands.

Following the latest US inflation data, market expectations for the first Fed rate cut shifted to October and the second to around late January, widening the gap between expected Fed policy and Trump's wishes.
Trump renewed his call on social media for the Fed to cut rates despite the latest inflation figures. The story says tariff-driven price increases will stiffen the Fed's opposition to lowering rates.
Trump told reporters Powell was not doing a good job and described his job as easy: lowering interest rates.

A commentator predicted that Powell would feel Trump's pressure more strongly when considering a second rate cut, while saying he did not currently expect Powell to be swayed by Trump's repeated attacks. He expected a September cut as clearer tariff arrangements and relatively limited inflationary effects eased the Fed's decision.
Bessent questioned the Fed's tariff analysis, arguing that tariffs had produced little or no price pressure and that any effects would be one-time price adjustments rather than inflationary pressure.

Trump's July 24 visit to the Fed brought his pressure for lower interest rates directly to Powell's workplace. WSJ reporter Meredith McGraw described the visit as an escalation ahead of the Fed's meeting the following week, when it was expected to keep rates steady.

During his tour of the Fed renovation site, Trump again urged Powell to “do the right thing” and lower interest rates. Mark Cranfield warned that continued attacks undermining Fed independence could prompt investors to discount American assets, particularly the US dollar.

A commentator predicted that Trump would adopt calmer economic policies and reduce pressure on the Fed ahead of the midterm elections to retain voters burdened by inflation and mortgage payments, arguing that lower rates would increase their disposable income.

Trump again pressured Powell to lower interest rates on July 28, ahead of this week's Fed meeting. Most economists and analysts expect rates to remain unchanged as most rate-setting committee members await evidence of tariffs' inflation effects, though growing divisions could produce a split vote.

Trump is demanding a three-percentage-point interest-rate cut, arguing that prospective homebuyers and other borrowers should benefit. Markets expect the Fed to resist his pressure and keep rates at 4.25–4.5% at its July 30 meeting.

The Fed left rates unchanged for a fifth consecutive meeting despite Trump's desire for cuts. Two officials dissented in favor of an immediate cut. Spencer Jacob said the dissents did not add pressure on Powell to cut rates.

Trump called Powell terrible, very stupid and probably highly political. After the Fed again held rates unchanged, Powell emphasized that central-bank independence allows unpopular decisions that benefit the economy, saying he assumed Congress understood its importance without extending that assurance to the White House.

Mark Cranfield said Powell's press conference pushed back against expectations of a September rate cut, making it closer to a coin toss, with another hold possible if Powell's narrative remains unchanged.

Trump reiterated yesterday that each percentage point Powell fails to cut costs the United States $365 billion annually. The White House said keeping rates unchanged would hurt citizens' finances. The story notes that this was the first time since 1993 that more than one Fed governor voted against the policy decision.
Trump praised preliminary second-quarter US GDP growth of 3% on social media as much better than expected and reiterated his call for Powell to lower interest rates.

Christopher Waller and Michelle Bowman dissented from the July 30 decision, favoring a quarter-point rate cut. Powell said rates were appropriately positioned to manage continuing uncertainty over tariffs and inflation, adding that many uncertainties remained unresolved and the process did not appear close to its end.

Commentators said Powell's unexpectedly hawkish remarks showed continued resistance to Trump's pressure following his Fed visit. They cited Powell as saying the central bank's role is not to finance government spending or growth ambitions. Following the meeting, the estimated probability of a September rate cut fell from above 60% to 44%, and expectations increasingly favored only one cut by year-end.

Powell said the economy did not appear to be held back inappropriately by restrictive policy, a view shared by almost the whole committee. He also acknowledged downside risks to the labor market, particularly over the next couple of months.

Storebrand's Olav Tjen warned that Trump's interference with Fed independence could rapidly erode institutional trust. He stressed that the Fed had not yet become an agent following government instructions and that Powell had not expanded quantitative easing to accommodate larger budget deficits.

Market analyst David Scott linked Trump's attacks on Jerome Powell to an expected priority of lowering long-term bond interest rates. He predicted that a dramatic decline in US interest rates could substantially weaken the US dollar.

Following downward revisions of 258,000 to prior employment figures, commentators said September rate-cut expectations rose to about 85%, with markets anticipating at least three cuts by March. They contrasted expectations of roughly one percentage point of easing over the next year with Trump's demand for a three-percentage-point reduction.
Trump called Powell too angry for persistently refusing to vote to lower interest rates.
Following the weak employment report and downward revisions to earlier job figures, Trump renewed pressure on the Fed and Jerome Powell to cut interest rates promptly.
A commentator predicted that Trump would quickly criticize the Fed, particularly Powell, for having waited too long if it delivered a 50-basis-point rate cut.
A commentator said political pressure for rate cuts appeared to be accelerating, reiterating an expectation that one cut this year would reflect employment conditions and another political pressure.

Commentators said weak employment data within the ISM services index, following downward employment revisions, further undermined Powell's case for holding rates steady amid intensifying Trump pressure. Markets were debating whether the Fed would cut by 25 or 50 basis points in September. They warned that pressure on the Fed to lower rates could harm the dollar amid growing debate over its reserve-currency status.

A commentator described Trump's demand for a 300-basis-point rate reduction as opening bargaining with an extreme demand, saying neither the Fed nor markets supported such a move. The commentator expected cuts at three of the five meetings through March because of economic conditions rather than political pressure.

A commentator predicted that inflation below expectations in the August 12 release would give Trump grounds to renew pressure on Powell for rate cuts, while higher-than-expected inflation could vindicate Powell's cautious approach.

July US consumer inflation was 2.7% year-on-year, below the expected 2.8%, strengthening expectations of a Fed rate cut at its mid-September meeting, which the White House is strongly demanding to support growth. Observers warned that tariff costs may increasingly reach consumers between late summer and autumn.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the Fed should be open to a 50-basis-point rate cut at its September meeting. Markets largely expected a 25-basis-point cut, while some policymakers continued to favor waiting.

A commentator said September rate-cut expectations rose to about 90% after the latest inflation report despite continuing political pressure from Trump. He predicted Powell would resist cutting if inflation rose again the following month and suggested that refusal could result in his dismissal.

In a Fox interview, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a September Fed rate cut was essential and called for a 50-basis-point reduction. He argued that, had the Fed seen the employment data now available, it would have cut rates in both June and July, so a larger September cut would allow it to catch up.

A commentator predicted that no rate cut would satisfy Trump: a 25-basis-point cut would leave his criticism continuing, while a 50-basis-point cut would prompt him to attack Powell for not acting sooner.
Powell said he would already have lowered interest rates without Trump's tariffs, while reiterating that political factors must not influence Fed policy.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent encouraged the Fed to cut interest rates by 1.5 to 1.75 percentage points.

Commentators warned that continued pressure from Trump and Bessent could backfire by prompting the Fed to move more slowly to demonstrate independence or by raising inflation expectations and market interest rates. They said the Trump administration is increasingly using the Fed's employment mandate to press for easing, while cutting rates before an expected inflation increase could damage the Fed's credibility.

Gary Tan characterized Bessent's call for a 150-basis-point rate reduction as tactical messaging intended to shape the narrative and influence Fed thinking, noting that Bessent himself described it as "working the referee." Tan said a full 150-basis-point cut would likely require a much more pronounced deterioration in economic conditions.

A commentator said political pressure had weakened the Fed's credibility. July producer inflation of 0.9% month-on-month supported Powell's caution over tariff effects, while expectations of a September quarter-point cut fell from about 96% to about 80%. The commentator expected Powell to avoid signaling a policy change at Jackson Hole before seeing August data and anticipated further questions about how strongly Trump would pressure him.

Mark Cudmore said administration pressure for excessively easy Fed policy was worsening inflation expectations and raising long-term yields. He predicted that enough Fed committee members could yield to pressure for a September cut if early-September employment data were very weak and inflation data were not highly problematic, but considered a September cut unlikely.

FHFA head Bill Pulte has criticized the Fed for keeping interest rates high, arguing that this has raised mortgage rates. Minutes released today showed that a majority of officials at July's meeting considered higher inflation a greater risk than weaker employment.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly claimed that Fed interest rates were too high according to all calculations, without identifying any calculation. The story says nobody else has found such a calculation.
Trump wrote on Truth Social this week that Jerome Powell was hurting the housing industry very badly by refusing to cut interest rates.
Trump called Powell a numbskull and a moron for refusing to cut interest rates.
A commentator described intense political pressure ahead of Powell's Jackson Hole speech and said Trump had scheduled a speech roughly ninety minutes afterward to reclaim the news spotlight.

In his Jackson Hole speech, Powell opened the door to a September rate cut but did not signal a prolonged series of cuts. Nick Timiraos said this was unlikely to satisfy Trump's demand for much more easing, though it might temporarily ease tensions. Powell reiterated that the Fed considers only the economic outlook and risks to its employment and inflation goals, saying it would never deviate from that approach.

FT US Economics editor Claire Jones said Powell's Jackson Hole speech did not suggest capitulation to Trump's pressure: attendees viewed it positively as an economically grounded case for a rate cut. Powell received an ovation, with central bankers seeing his dispute with the White House as a fight on their behalf amid rising populism.

Commentators described Trump's efforts to expand his influence within the Fed and discredit officials who resist him as damaging to institutional credibility. They suggested he wants a weaker dollar without sacrificing its reserve-currency dominance and may expect negotiated large purchases by other countries to offset the consequences of undermining the Fed.

Commentators warned that Trump's efforts to lower rates while undermining Fed credibility could turn a one-time tariff-driven price increase into persistent, self-reinforcing inflation through expectations, particularly as services inflation is also picking up. They described this as a major risk to his economic strategy.
A commentator predicted that the dispute between Trump and the Fed would continue until Trump obtained rate cuts, and suggested that a September cut could partly serve as a political concession.

FED.title: Trump criticizes Fed's election-campaign rate cut
summaries: Trump criticized Powell for cutting interest rates by 50 basis points during the election campaign.

FED.title: Bessent floats shadow Fed chair to undermine Powell
summaries: Trump's Treasury Secretary nominee Scott Bessent floated the idea of a shadow Fed chair, which Joe Matthew said could potentially undermine current Fed chair Jerome Powell. Matthew expressed uncertainty that the proposal would be implemented.

FED.title: Trump supporters question Fed's rate-cut timing
summaries: Trump supporters questioned why the Fed cut interest rates by half a percentage point ahead of the election but did not cut rates after the election.

FED.title: Trump subjects Fed bank regulation to White House oversight
summaries: Trump signed an executive order in mid-February tightening presidential control over agency spending and regulation, including the Fed's financial-system supervision role but explicitly excluding monetary policy. A senior administration official said the Office of Management and Budget will oversee all Fed regulations unrelated to monetary policy. The story also reports that Trump criticized the Fed's banking regulation in January as a terrible job.

FED.title: Biden directs Fed to study and develop digital dollar
summaries: In 2022, Joe Biden signed an executive order urging the Federal Reserve to begin studying and developing a digital dollar, amid concerns that the United States was falling behind China's digital-currency efforts.

FED.title: Republicans oppose digital dollar project
summaries: Republicans have opposed the digital dollar project since 2022, arguing that a central bank digital currency could be used by the government as a tool of mass control.

FED.title: Trump bans development of digital dollar
summaries: Donald Trump issued a decree on January 23 prohibiting development of the digital dollar entirely.

FED.title: Trump reportedly seeks to abolish the Federal Reserve
summaries: A commentator claimed Trump wants to abolish the Federal Reserve, leaving banks to set interest rates and using their balance sheets to refinance the government, which the commentator warned would reduce credit available to businesses.

FED.title: Trump could dismiss governors resisting his future Fed chair
summaries: A commentator predicted Trump might fire other Fed governors if he believed they were not cooperating with his chosen Fed chair next year. The commentator linked this possibility to a pending legal test of removal protections and said market opposition might not deter the administration.

FED.title: Trump's Fed succession plans raise concerns about a compliant chair
summaries: The Wall Street Journal reportedly identified Scott Bessent as a favorite to succeed Jerome Powell as Fed chair. A commentator argued that Trump would not tolerate an independently minded Fed leader, dismissed Bessent's prospects on that basis, and suggested Waller could become Trump's preferred compliant candidate.

A commentator cited speculation that Trump would replace Powell with Scott Bessent, describing Bessent as potentially dovish and willing to follow the Trump administration's preference for easier monetary policy.
A commentator said Trump had named Scott Bessent as his next Fed chair candidate earlier in the week, despite Powell's term not ending until May 2026, and characterized the announcement as blackmail.

Michael McKee said Trump's potential Fed chair candidates include former Fed governor Kevin Warsh and National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett, alongside Scott Bessent. He said Trump appears to want a chair who will cut rates, but Warsh has historically been hawkish on inflation. McKee noted that Trump can fill Adriana Kugler's governor seat when her term expires in January and potentially Powell's seat if Powell resigns as governor after his chairmanship ends, leaving Trump insufficient appointments to dictate monetary policy if other Fed officials remain concerned about inflation.

Commentators said Powell could remain on the Fed's board after his chairmanship ends but would probably leave, warning that his continued presence could create conflict if Trump appoints a successor closely aligned with him.

Asked whether Trump would appoint a successor who bows to his pressure, a commentator said the prospect remained uncertain and suggested adverse financial-market reactions could restrain Trump's choice.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump has considered selecting and announcing Powell's replacement by September or October. Trump said he had narrowed his choice to three or four people and called Powell terrible. The reported shortlist includes Kevin Warsh, Kevin Hassett, former World Bank President David Malpass and current Fed Governor Christopher Waller.

As markets reacted to the report that Trump was considering naming Powell's successor early, the Bloomberg dollar spot index fell 0.2% and the 10-year Treasury yield declined two basis points to 4.27%.

A commentator said announcing Powell's successor well before his term ends could undermine Powell's credibility and ability to lead, weaken the Fed's credibility and weigh on the US dollar, while describing Kevin Warsh and Kevin Hassett as credible, accomplished candidates whose appointments markets would welcome.

Finance editor Alex Francos warned that naming Powell's successor ten or eleven months before his term ends, rather than the usual three or four months, could create a backseat-driver effect: the successor could signal future policy reversals, reducing market predictability and raising the prospect of abrupt changes during an extended leadership overlap.

The story cites a Wall Street Journal report that Trump could announce Powell's successor in October or November. A commentator said installing a shadow chair favoring rapid rate cuts could create competing voices within the Fed and make Powell a lame duck. Markets were beginning to price more aggressive cuts under this scenario, with the US 10-year Treasury yield falling to about 4.26% and the dollar weakening sharply.

Amid speculation about an early successor announcement, traders raised the probability of a July quarter-point rate cut from 0% to 20% and expected total cuts through year-end from 0.50 to 0.62 percentage point in one week. The two-year Treasury yield fell nearly 0.20 percentage point to 3.75%, a seven-week low, while the Bloomberg dollar index fell 0.6% to its weakest level in more than three years. Goldman Sachs strategist Simon Dangoor cautioned that Trump has historically made conventional Fed appointments, including Powell.
Following the succession report, swap markets were pricing two rate cuts, with a third beginning to enter expectations.

FT editor Claire Jones said potential candidate Christopher Waller recently supported a rate cut as soon as July. She explained that an early nominee signaling more dovish policy could lower expected future rates and potentially US government borrowing costs, but conflicting signals from a shadow chair and the FOMC majority could sow confusion. She noted that regional Fed presidents are difficult for Trump to influence and current FOMC members would not necessarily follow the prospective chair.

A commentator said Trump explicitly intends to appoint a Fed chair in 2026 who will cut rates, rather than selecting on broader economic, price-stability, financial-stability or employment criteria. The commentator predicted that an early-announced shadow chair could accelerate rate cuts as Fed members increasingly listen to the prospective successor, further weakening the dollar.

A commentator predicted that identifying a prospective Fed chair in a few months, followed by that candidate's statements, would further intensify pressure for rate cuts and make near-term dollar appreciation difficult.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent outlined two options for choosing the next Fed chair: appointing a candidate to the governor position opening in January to await Powell's term ending, or selecting an existing governor closer to Trump's views. A commentator said the first option could make Powell a lame duck and accelerate rate cuts, and predicted that either approach would increase pressure on him.

The commentator said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent favored naming a new Fed chair in October or November, with a January 1 start, and urged against rushing. The commentator linked this timing to Bessent's expectation that inflation would decline during the first four months of next year.
At Tuesday's cabinet meeting, Trump asked whether someone who would lower interest rates should be appointed and answered yes.

WSJ reporter Brian Schwartz said Trump is already talking to potential replacements for Powell. Kevin Warsh and Kevin Hassett are in the top tier of candidates, though the selection has not necessarily narrowed to those two.

A White House spokesman said Fed monetary policy needs to complement Trump's pro-growth agenda. Hassett met Trump about the chair position at least twice in June and now says he would accept it. Warsh has discussed visiting Washington this month to meet Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent about the position. Reporting suggests Hassett's prospects are rising and Warsh's are fading, while Bessent could have first refusal. At Tuesday's cabinet meeting, Trump told Bessent he liked him better than Powell and floated having him hold both jobs, which the story says Fed law prohibits.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Bloomberg Television interview that the process to choose the next Federal Reserve chair is getting underway.
The story reports that Kevin Hassett is being described as the leading candidate to replace Powell.
A commentator argued that Kevin Hassett would follow Trump's instructions, including lowering interest rates to 1%, while noting that rate decisions are made by the Federal Open Market Committee.
Trump told reporters he was considering Kevin Hassett to succeed Powell as Fed chair.

Trump said he was only interested in candidates favoring low interest rates. Investors are betting that threats to Fed independence will raise long-term inflation, expecting Trump's next chair to bow to political pressure and lower rates too much to contain prices.

Mary Nicola warned that political capture of Fed policy under Powell's successor could unanchor inflation expectations and produce excessively low rates despite a healthy economy, worsening investor jitters and the sell-America trend.

A commentator said prospective chair candidates Christopher Waller and Kevin Warsh were increasingly making statements appealing to Trump, with candidates seeking to demonstrate ideological as well as monetary-policy alignment.
A commentator said prospective Fed chair candidates were voicing expectations for aggressive interest-rate cuts while the administration continued its campaign to discredit Powell.

Scott Bessent said the candidate list is long and could include regional Fed presidents as well as current governors. He said the selection process is beginning, the administration is not rushing, and Trump will make the final decision.
Spencer Jacob said bond yields had reacted in recent days to expectations that Powell's successor would be more aligned with Trump's views on interest rates.

Correspondent Lennart Samberge suggested that Christopher Waller's dissent in favor of a rate cut appeared aimed at winning Trump's favor as a contender to succeed Powell. Both dissenting governors were Trump appointees.

Adriana Kugler announced Friday that she would leave her governor position early, accelerating the White House's appointment plans ahead of her expected January departure. Trump said he had several people in mind and would announce her replacement within days. He claimed she left because she agreed with him on interest rates, contrary to her past public comments. The replacement is expected to favor lower rates and could succeed Powell as chair in May; Kevin Hassett and Kevin Warsh were cited as potential choices.

Commentators said appointing another Trump-aligned governor would give him three governors of his choosing but not a majority on the 12-member rate-setting committee. They described the effort as intended to isolate Powell, increase pressure on him and narrow his room to act, warning that internal divisions could damage market confidence in the Fed.
The White House indicated it would move to fill the newly opened Fed position. Investors are watching whether the appointee will be perceived as nonpartisan and mainstream or more loyal to Trump.

In a CNBC interview, Trump said Scott Bessent wants to remain Treasury secretary and would be removed from the Fed chair shortlist. Trump said he was considering four candidates, naming Kevin Warsh and Kevin Hassett, but did not plan to decide soon. He acknowledged that he could appoint his future chair choice to Adriana Kugler's vacant board seat, but also entertained appointing someone else for the term ending January 31. Nick Timiraos described this alternative as potentially installing a publicly confrontational critic of Powell to influence public opinion rather than persuade the Fed's policy committee.

A commentator suggested that Adriana Kugler's early departure to return to teaching at Georgetown University involved pressure or persuasion. Another argued that any incoming Fed chair would speak in Trump's voice, increasingly undermining Fed independence and causing markets to look first to the president rather than the central bank. Bessent was described as preferring his Treasury role because it gives him greater influence over economic decision-making.

Reports said advisers urged Trump to fill Adriana Kugler's vacant seat temporarily until January, and Trump made a similar statement the previous day. The proposed approach would select a government-aligned person who had already received congressional approval to avoid another approval process, then place the intended successor to Powell in the seat in January. The commentator described the plan as continuing to increase pressure on Powell.

Commentators described Kevin Hassett and Kevin Warsh as strongly Trump-aligned potential successors and questioned whether their leadership would change the Fed's public messaging. One argued that expecting the Fed's institutional identity to prevail over political demands was overly optimistic, warning that its independence could erode faster than expected.

Trump announced the appointment of Stephen Marin, also referred to in the story as Myron, to Adriana Kugler's vacant Fed board seat. The current Council of Economic Advisors chief is described as a close Trump confidant and would serve temporarily until the end of January 2026, when Trump plans to appoint another governor. Senate confirmation remains pending and is considered highly likely given the Republican majority.

Hours before his appointment was announced, Stephen Mirren praised Trump's tariffs as historic and said there was "zero macroeconomically significant evidence of price pressures from the tariffs," contrasting with the Fed's concerns about their inflationary impact.

Stephen Mirren, Trump's temporary Fed governor nominee, was described as a critic of the central bank who echoes Trump's calls for lower rates. Heath Moss said Christopher Waller and Michelle Bowman appeared to be auditioning to succeed Powell by being the only two officials to vote for a cut last month. He said markets expect Trump's eventual chair pick to share his economic principles and align with his policies.

A commentator cited Bloomberg as placing Christopher Waller potentially near the top of the shortlist for Fed chair next year. The commentator predicted that Trump's incoming economic adviser would join the two governors favoring rate cuts and argued that Trump would eventually have four of seven voting members on his side, giving him control of the central bank.

A commentator said Stephen Mirren's temporary appointment would give Trump more time to choose Powell's successor while signaling the kind of Fed he wants. Mirren was described as an intellectual architect of policies Trump has begun implementing, including tariffs and a weaker dollar. The commentator cited a paper Mirren wrote two years earlier criticizing Fed groupthink for suppressing differing views and causing risks to be overlooked, suggesting his appointment could change the institution's internal outlook.

A commentator characterized Trump's appointment of Miran as prioritizing loyalty over merit and seeking policy designed around Trump's wishes rather than Powell's adherence to established rules. The story reports that the dollar reversed earlier gains after news of Miran's appointment, with EUR/USD around 1.1645 the following morning.
