Commentators warned that continued Fed rate cuts despite rising inflation could undermine confidence in the dollar and US assets, reduce demand for Treasuries and harm global risk appetite.

A commentator described Stephen Mirren as highly dovish and an ideological supporter of Trump, suggesting that the forthcoming chair change and changes in Fed membership could make rate-cut decisions easier.

The story identifies Michelle Bowman, Philip Jefferson, Dallas Fed President Lori Logan, former St. Louis Fed President Bullard and Mark Sumerlin as additional potential Fed chair candidates. It reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is meeting candidates individually to prepare the selection, with Trump making the final decision. Commentators described the process as focused on who would follow Trump's wishes most closely and reduce interest rates to his preferred level fastest.

A commentator reported that Christopher Waller met with Scott Bessent's team the previous week and proposed shifting the Fed from data-driven responses toward a more proactive forecasting methodology. The team reportedly found his presentation impressive; the commentator characterized the approach as opportunistic in the context of the Fed chair succession contest.

Katie Martin described Trump's Fed appointee as having radical ideas for completely reforming the institution. She said markets remained remarkably calm despite the appointment and warned that benign market reactions could encourage Trump to put further pressure on key institutions.

A commentator said Trump had expanded the field by introducing ten additional candidates after narrowing it to a few. He predicted Trump would choose Kevin Hassett because he would follow Trump's instructions, warning that presidential control and excessively low short-term rates could weaken the dollar and complicate financing of the US deficit.

Commentators said Trump's team was trying to accelerate Stephen Miran's appointment process. They cited an earlier article in which Miran advocated replacing the Fed's reactive, data-driven approach with a more proactive approach emphasizing forecasts.
Trump's Fed board nominee Stephen Mirren supports deep interest-rate cuts and has floated reforms that could allow presidents to sack Fed chairs.

A commentator linked strong demand for gold and silver mining shares to uncertainty over monetary policy under Trump, predicting that his Fed chair would cut rates regardless and effectively put Trump in control of the central bank.

A commentator identified May 2026, when Powell's chairmanship ends, as a critical point for the risk of rapid rate cuts under his successor. They interpreted rising gold and cryptocurrency prices as reflecting this risk and warned that global selling pressure could intensify as the succession approaches.

FED.title: Renovation allegations prompt pressure for Powell's resignation
summaries: The Federal Housing Finance Agency director alleged that Powell gave misleading Senate testimony about luxury features in a $2.5 billion Fed building renovation project and said he could face an investigation. Following those allegations, Trump called for Powell's immediate resignation on July 2.

Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Poult requested a congressional investigation into whether Powell lied to lawmakers about the Fed renovation and demanded his resignation. Trump echoed the allegations on social media, saying Powell should resign immediately if they were true. At Tuesday's cabinet meeting, Trump called Powell terrible and said misleading Congress would justify a rapid departure. Powell had rejected reports of extravagant renovation features during Senate testimony weeks earlier, calling them misleading and inaccurate.

FED.title: Hassett accuses Powell of politically motivated rate decisions
summaries: In a recent Fox Business interview, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett accused Powell of cutting rates before the election to help Kamala Harris and raising rates before Trump's first inauguration. He said Powell's policy actions suggested he was doing what Elizabeth Warren wanted. Powell rejected the accusation that the Fed behaves politically.

FED.title: Warsh backs Trump's criticism of Fed policy
summaries: Prospective Fed chair candidate Kevin Warsh publicly expressed sympathy with Trump's frustrations, saying US economic growth was poised to boom but was being held down by bad central-bank policies.

FED.title: Bessent urges Powell to leave Fed board after chairmanship
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested that Jerome Powell should also step down from the Federal Reserve board when he is replaced as chair.

A commentator said Bessent is trying to persuade Trump that Powell's successor could take over Powell's remaining two-year board term, presenting this limited tenure as an arrangement Powell might accept.

A commentator characterized Bessent's effort to have Powell surrender his remaining two board years as an attempt to limit the tenure of a Trump-aligned successor who would lower rates, rather than giving that person a full 14-year term.

FED.title: Trump administration attacks Powell over Fed renovation spending
summaries: The Trump administration continues efforts to discredit Powell through allegations of corruption or irregularities in the $2.5 billion refurbishment of Fed buildings. Powell is also accused of glossing over details and attempting to mislead the Senate when explaining the spending.
A commentator said excessive spending on the Federal Reserve building project is being used as grounds for trying to remove Powell.
Trump suggested he could remove Powell for cause over possible fraud in the $2.5–$2.7 billion renovation of two historic Fed office buildings, alleging that Powell lacked proper clearance.
Trump said removing Powell was highly unlikely unless he had to leave for fraud.

Reports that Trump was again considering firing Powell drove longer-term Treasury yields higher. Alex Frankos said investors seek higher yields to compensate for the inflation risk of replacing Powell with a Trump-picked chair who would cut rates immediately.

The story says renewed reports of Powell's possible removal hurt markets, which partially recovered after Trump said he would accept Powell's resignation but would not remove him without grounds. Bank executives Brian Moynihan, David Solomon and Jamie Dimon warned against weakening the Fed and stressed its independence. Bankers also offered to mediate between Trump and Powell.
Trump asked Republican members of Congress during an Oval Office meeting whether they should remove Powell; they reportedly supported the idea.

Senate Republicans questioned Powell last month about renovation costs, budget overruns and expensive finishes; Powell disputed reports about the finishes. The White House sent Powell a letter last week questioning his truthfulness and whether the Fed properly updated plans with local building authorities. The Fed defended his testimony and attributed overruns partly to unexpected asbestos, soil contamination and a higher water table. Legal experts doubt there are grounds for court-sanctioned removal and suggest the campaign may seek to force Powell to resign or become more accommodating on rates. Nick Timiraos warned that a contested removal could produce an unprecedented institutional conflict.

Betting markets at one point this week assigned a 40% probability that Powell would leave before his term ended. Mark Cranfield said traders were taking the political pressure seriously, with concerns also reflected in the US dollar and yield curve, although they still viewed early removal as a somewhat remote risk.

A correspondent reported that the Norwegian krone moved by a full percentage point following Trump's press conference two nights earlier amid discussion of the Fed chair's potential early removal. Finance ministers at the G20 gathering expressed concerns about global financial stability arising from US trade policy and domestic politics surrounding the Fed chair.

A commentator said that if Trump's threats to remove Powell result in his replacement, the successor is expected to ease monetary policy more aggressively, risking higher inflation, negative real yields and a weaker US dollar.

Powell sent a letter Thursday to White House budget director Ross Vought responding to criticism of the $2.5 billion renovation, saying the Fed takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of public resources.

The story reports that uncertainty over Powell's future weighed on financial-sector stocks despite strong bank earnings. Trump raised the possibility of firing Powell in a closed-door meeting Tuesday before denying Wednesday that he planned to oust him.

A commentator said reports are now offering trading strategies to hedge changes in short- and long-term interest rates if Trump attempts to remove or neutralize Powell, and questioned whether political damage to institutions could undermine the dollar's long-term credibility.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Trump this week not to try to fire Powell, arguing that the economy was holding up better than expected and that historical coordination between central banks and treasuries to keep government borrowing costs low had produced substantial inflation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a detailed breakdown of spending on the Fed building's refurbishment. A commentator described the administration's continuing reputational campaign as an effort to raise suspicions of irregularities and potentially induce Powell to leave early after removing him appeared infeasible.
The US commerce secretary said the previous day that Powell should leave. A commentator said it appeared the administration would investigate both the Fed and Powell.

Trump visited the Fed on July 24, joining a previously arranged construction-site tour for White House advisers alongside Powell. Republican Senator Tim Scott, who also attended, had sent Powell a letter the previous day requesting more detail on management of the $2.5 billion headquarters renovation. Trump said he wanted the project finished and regretted that it had begun.
Trump said it was not necessary to fire Powell.

During his Fed visit, Trump claimed renovation costs had reached $3.1 billion and said he would fire the contractor. Powell disputed the figure in front of cameras, explaining that it included a third building completed five years earlier. Trump said he would not fire Powell over this issue.

A commentator said Trump's unexpected interventions concerning the Fed the previous week disrupted a decline in the euro-dollar exchange rate, linking his interference to further potential dollar depreciation.

Claire Jones said Trump-appointed officials during his previous administration had sought preservation of National Mall buildings using materials such as marble, contributing to the Fed renovation's costs. Adam Posen characterized the renovation attacks as a pretext for pressure rather than a valid legal case. He warned that ousting Powell could raise Treasury risk premiums and government borrowing costs. Jones said Powell understood the institutional stakes and would not be bullied into resigning.

A commentator said footage of Trump's renovation-site visit portrayed him as inspecting the construction while Powell defended himself with documents and Trump did not listen. The commentator argued that this public treatment damaged both Powell personally and the Fed's institutional standing.
Trump threatened a lawsuit over cost overruns in construction of the Fed headquarters, adding pressure on Powell.

FED.title: Johnson pressured Burns to cut interest rates
summaries: A commentator recounted that Lyndon B. Johnson summoned Fed chair Burns to his ranch and demanded interest-rate cuts, citing difficulties with the Vietnam War. The commentator said Burns yielded and inflation subsequently worsened dramatically.

FED.title: Warsh criticizes Fed diversity efforts and limits of independence
summaries: Former Fed governor Kevin Warsh called the Fed's efforts to recruit and employ underrepresented groups through diversity, equity and inclusion a major mistake. He said central bank independence is essential but does not mean independence in everything. A commentator interpreted these remarks as an effort to appeal to Trump.

FED.title: House passes legislation barring Fed digital currency work
summaries: The US House of Representatives approved legislation last week prohibiting the Federal Reserve from creating or even studying a central bank digital currency. Republicans cited privacy concerns and the risk of government surveillance. Paul Krugman argued that Trump and Republicans instead feared a digital currency would compete with private bank accounts and threaten the financial industry.

FED.title: Bessent urges review of Fed functions and budget
summaries: Scott Bessent urged Powell to conduct an internal review separating monetary policy from the Fed's other functions, arguing that its expanding remit threatens monetary-policy independence. He criticized the institution's size and growth in its central board budget since 2004, suggested a committee or outside experts could assist, and said an independent external review might follow if the internal review was not considered serious.

FED.title: Mohamed El-Erian calls for Powell's resignation
summaries: Investor Mohamed El-Erian recently called for Jerome Powell to resign, citing policy mistakes, including Powell's insistence after the pandemic that rising inflation was temporary.

FED.title: Hassett demands transparency on Powell's tariff-inflation analysis
summaries: White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett criticized Powell's tariff-inflation argument, calling for greater transparency and a model demonstrating how tariffs would cause inflation so that a substantive discussion could take place.
Hassett was cited as arguing that tariff-related price increases are a one-time effect rather than continuing inflation.

FED.title: Trump repeatedly calls for Powell's resignation over interest rates
summaries: Trump has repeatedly demanded Powell's resignation amid his refusal to lower interest rates and unprecedented public pressure from the White House on the Fed.

Nick Timuros described attacks portraying Powell as incompetent and untrustworthy as attempts to undermine the Fed's independence. Powell's associates said he remains focused on completing his job and handing over to his successor next spring with inflation under control and the economy in a good position.
The story reports that Trump has threatened to fire Powell over the Fed's decision to keep interest rates stable this year.
Trump has said he wants interest rates lowered by one percentage point and argued that high rates are a problem for housing.

FED.title: Trump demands Lisa Cook resign over mortgage-fraud allegations
summaries: FHFA head Bill Pulte accused Fed Governor Lisa Cook of declaring two properties her primary residence on mortgage applications 14 days apart. His social media post showed signatures but not the applications' full context. Trump demanded Cook resign immediately and, according to sources familiar with the matter, is discussing firing her for cause if she refuses. Whether Trump has authority to remove her remains disputed.

Bloomberg Opinion columnist Daniel Moss described Trump's demand for Cook's resignation as a new front in the campaign against the Fed, implying a willingness to scrutinize FOMC officials' personal financial affairs.
Lisa Cook strongly denies the mortgage-fraud allegations made by Trump's camp.

Cook said she would defend herself against the allegations. Commentators characterized the attack as targeting a governor who did not support a rate cut at the previous meeting and warned that scrutiny of officials' private lives could intimidate Fed members into following the president's wishes.

The story says Cook rented out one of the two homes she allegedly designated as primary residences to obtain more favorable mortgage terms. Cook said she would not resign. A commentator reported that the Fed had found 22,000 similar examples while examining the issue.
On Thursday, the US Department of Justice wrote to Fed chair Jay Powell urging him to remove Cook. Trump called on the DOJ to investigate the allegations against her.

The story reports that the Justice Department decided to open an investigation into allegations that Cook designated two purchased homes as primary residences to obtain lower mortgage rates. A commentator described the campaign as an effort to control the Fed, saying Cook's departure could enable Trump appointees to hold four seats on the Board of Governors.
According to Bloomberg, police removed a Trump supporter who physically confronted Lisa Cook at Jackson Hole over the weekend.
The story identifies James Fishback as the person removed from the Jackson Hole meeting after confronting Lisa Cook and shouting Trump's criticisms of her.

Trump said Monday night that he was firing Lisa Cook, citing sufficient reason to believe she made false statements on mortgage agreements as cause for removal. The Fed declined to comment. The story says Cook's refusal to step down could trigger a constitutional standoff between the White House and the Fed.

Cook responded to Trump's attempted firing by saying he has no authority to remove her and she will not quit. The story reports that no charges have been filed against her. Brookings Institution's Aaron Klein described the move as a "killshot" at Fed independence.
The standoff over Trump's attempted removal of Cook is expected to go to court and could reach the Supreme Court. Gold prices rose in response to the news as investors sought a safe haven.

The story says Trump issued an executive order directing Cook to leave her position. A commentator said the alleged mortgage fraud could qualify as misconduct permitting removal if substantiated, but that Cook could contest removal rather than leave immediately.

Trump said on Truth Social that it was inconceivable Cook did not know the mortgage rules and that this called her expertise and trustworthiness into question. His removal announcement specified immediate effect. The Bloomberg dollar index, two-year Treasury yields and S&P 500 futures fell following the announcement. Cook said she would continue carrying out her responsibilities.

The alleged false information on Cook's mortgage applications dates to 2021. Alex Frangos said replacing Cook would require Senate approval and would increase pressure for rate cuts, but would not necessarily give Trump enough votes to control monetary policy.

The story says Trump's attempted dismissal of Cook would be the first time a US president dismissed a senior central banker. Legal experts say removal is permissible only for serious misconduct and question whether Cook's case meets that standard.

Cook has hired an attorney and plans to pursue legal avenues to remain in office, noting that the mortgage application predates her joining the Fed. A Fed spokesperson said governors may be removed only for cause, that removal protections serve the American people's interests, and that the Fed will abide by any court decision.

Cook's lawyer said Tuesday they will sue the Trump administration, arguing that the attempted firing based solely on a referral letter lacks any factual or legal basis. The Congressional Black Caucus condemned the move as a racist, misogynistic and unlawful attack on Fed integrity and independence. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the central question was whether Cook committed mortgage fraud. The story notes uncertainty over whether Cook will remain in office and vote at the Fed's mid-September meeting while the legal dispute proceeds.

Correspondent Lennart Sandberger said the White House has made the same mortgage-fraud allegation against two other Trump opponents and characterized the campaign against Cook as political retaliation. He noted that the Supreme Court had previously signaled that the Fed is a unique institution whose officials cannot simply be dismissed by the president. Whether Cook may attend meetings while the dispute proceeds remains unclear.
Cook voted at every interest-rate decision this year to support Powell's position of keeping rates at their existing high level.
Cook's term was due to end in 2038. The story reports fears that Trump intends to replace her with a loyalist.

Long-term US Treasuries sold off and yields rose Tuesday following Trump's attempted firing of Cook. Claire Jones said investors viewed it as part of a multipronged attack on the Fed and feared weakened independence would impair inflation control and increase government borrowing costs. She noted that a potential Trump-appointed majority on the seven-member Board could influence the selection of regional Fed presidents who vote on interest rates. Cook said she would answer questions about the mortgage transactions in the future.

Federico Fubini argued that replacing Cook could give Trump control of the Fed's leadership for at least five years, ending its political independence and increasing his influence over the dollar, market interest rates and Wall Street.

Trump said he was prepared for a legal fight with Cook and stated that his appointees would hold a four-member majority on the seven-member Fed Board, with influence over regional Fed governors. Bloomberg strategist Mary Nicola warned that a prolonged legal battle could undermine Fed credibility and weigh on the dollar and US assets.

The disputed mortgage applications concerned properties in Michigan and Georgia. The dollar fell as much as 0.3% and gold rose 0.6% after Trump's announcement; both moves partly reversed after Cook said she would remain in office. S&P Global Ratings warned that the dispute could affect international confidence in the United States and put pressure on its credit rating. Senator Elizabeth Warren and other Democrats called the attempted dismissal illegal and authoritarian and said it should be overturned in court.

Trump told advisers he wants to announce a nominee to replace Cook quickly. He told reporters he is considering Stephen Myron, a close economic adviser already nominated for a different Fed Board seat, because Cook's seat has a longer term. Another potential candidate is former World Bank Group President David Malpass, a close Trump ally.

BlackRock Investment Institute characterized Trump's attempt to remove Cook as another example of structural, long-lasting uncertainty that investors should price through higher term premiums, citing this uncertainty as a reason to remain underweight long-term US Treasuries.

FED.title: Republican senator attacks Cook's qualifications during appointment
summaries: During Lisa Cook's appointment, a Republican senator accused her of lacking monetary-policy expertise and instead holding far-left views.

The story reports that Republican lawmakers and conservative media questioned parts of Cook's résumé during her 2022 confirmation. Cook denied the accusations and was confirmed in a divided Senate vote, with Vice President Kamala Harris breaking the tie.

FED.title: Liz Truss endorses Trump's pressure on the Fed
summaries: Former UK Prime Minister Liz Truss said she was very sympathetic to what Donald Trump was saying about the Fed, arguing that monetary policy is incredibly important and central banks should be accountable to politicians.

FED.title: Trump and Bessent demand zero interest on Fed bank deposits
summaries: Trump and Treasury Secretary Bessent want the Fed to pay zero interest on roughly $3 trillion in bank deposits held there, seeking to push banks to buy government bonds instead.

FED.title: David Malpass criticizes Fed for not cutting rates
summaries: Former World Bank Group President David Malpass, a close Trump ally and potential nominee to replace Lisa Cook, has criticized the Fed for not cutting interest rates.

FED.title: Trump challenges Powell over Fed construction costs
summaries: The story describes Trump confronting Powell over construction at the Fed, with the two disagreeing over the figures. A commentator characterized the encounter as an apparently staged confrontation.

FED.title: Trump moves to fire Cook from the Fed
summaries: The story describes Trump firing Cook despite lacking the authority to do so, criticizing the move as interference that weakens the Fed as an institution.
In discussing Lisa Cook and the Fed's upcoming September meeting, the story says Trump is trying to reshape the Fed's committee in his favor.

In a letter posted on social media Monday, Trump cited unproven mortgage-fraud allegations concerning conduct before Cook joined the Fed as cause for dismissal. Trump-appointed Federal Housing Finance Agency head Bill Pulte publicized the allegations and referred them to the Justice Department. Cook has not been charged with a civil or criminal violation and has vowed to challenge her removal; her lawyer said she would sue. The case could reach the Supreme Court and test presidential removal authority and the Federal Reserve Act's protections allowing governors to be removed only for cause.
The story says replacing Lisa Cook could increase Trump-supporting members of the seven-member Fed Board from three to four.

Cook filed a lawsuit in Washington, DC Federal District Court alleging that Trump attempted to remove her without a legally valid reason. The suit also names Jerome Powell and the Fed Board as defendants and seeks to block them from complying with Trump's removal order. The Fed previously said it would abide by any court decision on the matter.
Markets reacted only modestly to Trump's attempted removal of Cook.
Cook filed her lawsuit on Thursday, August 28, asking a federal judge in Washington to quickly issue an order blocking her removal while the case proceeds.

Cook's lawyers suggest that the alleged falsification of mortgage-application documents was an unintentional administrative error. The story characterizes Trump's move against Cook as a fallback after he failed to remove Fed Chair Jerome Powell.
Cook remains in her position while challenging Trump in court. The report links Trump's move against her to increased market volatility and safe-haven buying of gold.

The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into whether Cook submitted fraudulent mortgage application information and has issued subpoenas. The probe followed two criminal referrals from Bill Pulte and includes investigations in Michigan and Atlanta, where two of her properties are located. Cook denied committing mortgage fraud in a recent court filing.

The story specifies that Cook is accused of designating two mortgaged properties as her primary residence to obtain favorable treatment. It describes Trump's attempt as the first presidential effort to remove a Fed governor in the institution's 112-year history.
A US federal judge temporarily blocked Lisa Cook's dismissal, allowing her to remain in office while she challenges Trump's decision, including during the upcoming interest-rate decision.

The judge said Cook is likely to succeed on her claim that Trump violated the Federal Reserve Act because her removal did not satisfy its requirement that governors can be removed only for cause. The administration maintains that alleged inconsistent representations in Cook's mortgage application provide cause for removal.
The judge also found that the manner of Cook's dismissal likely violated her constitutional due-process rights.
In granting the temporary order blocking Cook's dismissal, the judge defended the Federal Reserve's independence as protecting the stability of the national banking system.

At least two documents reviewed by the Wall Street Journal show that Cook described her Atlanta condo as a vacation home, casting doubt on the administration's mortgage-fraud allegations. Cook will be among the voting policymakers at the Fed's upcoming two-day policy meeting.
An appeal has been filed against the court decision keeping Lisa Cook on the Fed Board, with a ruling expected on September 15 or 16.
A US appeals court ruled on September 15 that Lisa Cook can remain in her job for now, likely allowing her to participate in this week's FOMC interest-rate decision.
A commentator claims that the mortgage-fraud allegations against Cook are false and alleges that Pulte drew the idea for them from conduct by his own parents.
The story describes Cook's lawsuit against Trump as being over insults directed at her.

FED.title: Nixon pressures the Fed to cut interest rates
summaries: Citing a Bloomberg report, the story recounts that President Nixon repeatedly demanded interest-rate cuts in the 1970s and that the Fed chair complied.

FED.title: Trump pressures the Fed to lower interest rates
summaries: The story discusses Trump's pressure for interest-rate cuts, linking his position to high short-term real interest rates and the Treasury's interest costs.
Trump argues that the Fed should cut rates rather than make Americans pay more, contrasting the 4.25–4.5% policy rate with 2.7% inflation.
Trump has called for a three-percentage-point interest-rate cut.

The commentary says Trump wants lower interest rates to support the construction sector and US economic growth, and contrasts that pressure with his tax cuts, which it says will increase the budget deficit by $3 trillion and require additional debt issuance.

The commentary warns that if tariff increases generate inflationary pressure, Fed rate cuts under Trump's pressure in an environment where rates should not fall could create major economic risks in 2026.

Trump said there was no inflation in the US and prices were low, adding pressure on the Fed to cut rates. Analysts said concerns about Fed independence were driving investors toward safe-haven assets such as gold.

The story says Trump's social-media attacks on the Fed undermine confidence in the US Treasury market and trigger gold buying. Over the weekend, Trump claimed inflation was nonexistent and tariffs were bringing in trillions of dollars, following an August 29 report showing core personal consumption expenditure inflation at 2.9%, its highest since February.

The report links Trump's attacks on Federal Reserve independence to rising US long-term borrowing costs and a steepening government yield curve. The global bond sell-off spilled into equity markets on Tuesday, when US stocks opened lower.

The commentary says rising US borrowing costs linked to weakened confidence in Fed independence are also pushing up European borrowing costs. It argues that the accompanying weaker dollar strengthens the euro, potentially reducing euro-area inflation and giving the ECB more room to lower its policy rate.
Following weaker jobs data, Trump posted on Truth Social that Jerome Powell should have lowered rates long ago, calling him "too late."

The commentary says weak US payroll growth of 22,000 and unemployment rising to 4.3% intensified criticism that the Fed was late to cut rates amid Trump's pressure. It argues that incoming economic data now independently support cuts, potentially enabling the Fed to act more boldly rather than cutting solely because of Trump's pressure.

The commentary says Trump's team is demanding rate cuts despite some analysts viewing US financial conditions as loose, the economy as resilient and the benchmark rate as not particularly restrictive. Ahead of the September 16–17 Fed meeting, it argues that a cut risks being seen as capitulation to Trump, while no cut risks criticism for restraining the economy.
Trump predicted a "big cut" ahead of this week's Federal Reserve interest-rate decision, following his pressure on the Fed.

Trump wants lower rates on mortgages, car loans and longer-term business loans and claims a three-percentage-point Fed rate cut could save the government $1 trillion annually. Economists quoted in the story argue that such a cut would instead raise inflation, long-term borrowing rates and government debt-service costs. They warn that a cut made at the president's direction would also make investors perceive US government debt as riskier by undermining institutional independence.

The commentary links concerns about Trump's influence on the Federal Reserve to a higher risk premium for the US dollar and its broad weakening, helping the Australian dollar reach a ten-month high against it.

The discussion says Trump wants interest rates lowered to 1%, linking this demand to US government interest expenses now exceeding defense spending. It warns that highly expansionary Fed policy could generate inflation.

Trump posted on social media Monday morning that Powell must cut interest rates immediately and by more than he had planned, indicating he wants more than the quarter-percentage-point cut widely expected at this week's meeting.

FED.title: Trump seeks a supportive majority through Fed appointments
summaries: Trump says he will obtain a majority at the Fed. The story describes Stephen Miran, an architect of Trump's economic policies, as temporarily replacing Adriana Kugler and says a permanent appointment for Miran if Lisa Cook leaves is being discussed. Former World Bank president David Malpass is also mentioned as a potential candidate for open or prospective vacancies.

The interview says Trump is trying to install allies who favor much lower interest rates. It warns that a four-member majority on the seven-member Fed Board could potentially remove regional Fed presidents, giving Trump broader control over the central bank. Markets are described as beginning to price in some probability of this outcome through steeper yield curves, greater expectations of Fed easing next year and higher expected inflation.

The Senate Banking Committee will hold a confirmation hearing on September 4 for senior White House economic adviser Stephen Myron to join the Fed's Board of Governors. At a cabinet meeting last week, Trump highlighted his desire to influence interest-rate policy more directly, including through Myron's confirmation.

Stephen Myron's Senate confirmation hearing took place on September 4. Myron, who agrees with Trump's view that the Fed should cut rates, told lawmakers he would act independently based on his own analysis and judgment. He also said the president has a right to express views on monetary policy. The Republican-majority Senate is expected to confirm him, but the timing is unclear.

FED.title: Trump seeks to remove Fed Chair Powell
summaries: The story states that Trump has been unable to remove Fed Chair Jerome Powell and has instead targeted other Fed leaders to gain control over the institution.
Trump and his team have been looking for replacements for Powell even though his term as chair does not end until next year.
The story states that Trump has threatened to fire Fed Chair Jay Powell.

FED.title: Trump challenges Powell over Fed renovation costs
summaries: During a visit to the Federal Reserve construction site, Trump challenged Jerome Powell over alleged cost increases from $2.7 billion to $3.1 billion. Powell disputed the figures, saying Trump had included a third building whose renovation had been completed five years earlier.

FED.title: Bessent calls for Fed policy recalibration
summaries: Bessent said a recalibration was needed as the Fed approached its interest-rate decision. The discussion places his call in the context of possible rate cuts and downward revisions to US employment data.

FED.title: Trump demands modern data sources at the Fed
summaries: Trump said the previous day that the Fed's organization was broken and that it needed to use modern data sources.

FED.title: Trump replaces statistics commissioner amid push for lower rates
summaries: The commentary says Trump abruptly fired the Bureau of Labor Statistics commissioner last month and is installing EJ Antony. It portrays this as an alternative route to securing lower Fed rates, alleging that subsequent economic figures have favored Trump's demand for cuts.

FED.title: Trump threatens to remove Fed Chair Powell
summaries: The commentary says Trump has publicly discussed firing Jerome Powell, while noting that he lacks legal grounds to remove Fed officials absent serious misconduct.

FED.title: US administration seeks replacement for Fed Chair Powell
summaries: The story reports talks that the US administration is starting to find a replacement for Fed Chair Jerome Powell. It links this to concerns about Fed independence and increased demand for gold as a hedge against political interference.

The commentary says the Fed chair will change in May 2026 and predicts that the incoming chair will pay greater attention to Trump's statements. It links this expectation to Trump's preference against dollar appreciation and a potentially higher euro-dollar exchange rate in 2026.

FED.title: Trump seeks greater Fed influence through allied nominees
summaries: Trump is seeking greater influence over the Federal Reserve by proposing candidates aligned with him.

Stephen Miran, described as a Trump ideologue particularly on tariffs, is being appointed to the Fed. Senate confirmation is expected on September 15, which would allow him to participate in this week's interest-rate decision.

Trump's Fed nominee currently chairs the White House Council of Economic Advisers and plans to take leave rather than resign, an arrangement described as unprecedented for the modern Fed. The Fed term runs through year-end. The story identifies possible subsequent arrangements: returning to the White House, remaining at the Fed if Trump names no successor, or receiving a nomination to a longer-term Fed seat. The nominee has said he will be independent but has not disclosed his intended rate vote.
The Senate confirmed Trump's nominee on September 15, allowing him to participate in the FOMC meeting beginning September 16.
The Senate confirmed Stephen Miran by a narrow 48–47 vote.

The discussion links Stephen Miran's arrival and further changes to the Fed's composition to the possibility of more aggressive rate cuts. Commentators say a shift toward a more dovish membership could weaken the Fed's adherence to economic fundamentals.

Stephen Miran's confirmation took two weeks, among the fastest processes in the past 25 years, to ensure he could vote at this Fed meeting and influence policy discussions. Some Republicans who worked for other presidents criticized his continued White House employment as inappropriate and undermining the appearance of independence. Analysts raised concerns that this arrangement could facilitate disclosure of confidential Fed deliberations to the administration.

FED.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent urges a 50-basis-point Fed rate cut
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the federal funds rate should be much lower and advocated starting with a 50-basis-point reduction rather than a massive one-time cut. He also said the administration aims to lower the ten-year Treasury yield rather than focus on the federal funds rate.

FED.title: Trump attacks Powell over Fed headquarters renovation
summaries: A few weeks before the policy meeting, Trump made the expensive renovation of the Fed's headquarters an issue to argue that Chair Jerome Powell had not been doing his job well.

FED.title: Bessent meets Bullard about becoming Fed chair
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met former St. Louis Fed president James Bullard about the Fed chairmanship. Bullard said he would accept provided that preserving the dollar's reserve-currency status, maintaining low and stable inflation, and protecting the Fed's institutional independence remained priorities. Bessent described the meeting as good; whether Trump would accept Bullard's conditions remained unclear.

FED.title: Uncertainty over Lisa Cook's departure from the Fed
summaries: Lisa Cook's possible departure remains uncertain. Following the latest decision concerning her position, she is expected to remain and participate in this week's policy meeting.

Trump is trying to fire Cook over allegations that she submitted fraudulent information on a mortgage application. Her lawyers deny fraud, and she is challenging her firing in court. Late Monday night, an appeals court rejected Trump's request, hours before the Fed meeting began.
Lisa Cook is attending the September Fed meeting. The Trump administration said it would appeal the federal appeals court's rejection of its emergency request to remove her to the Supreme Court.
Trump ordered Cook's dismissal in August.

Cook voted in the September meeting. The story also cited press reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had previously designated two addresses as primary residences, similar to the allegation Trump used to justify removing Cook.

The Trump administration filed an emergency Supreme Court request to remove Cook while litigation over her firing proceeds, arguing that the president has legal authority to dismiss her. The Justice Department has opened an investigation into the mortgage allegations, but Cook has not been charged. Solicitor General John Sauer argued that someone who appears to have lied to secure favorable mortgage rates should not set interest rates for Americans. Cook's lawsuit alleges that Trump manufactured grounds for dismissal to fill her seat and undermine Fed independence.
The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times and other media outlets reviewed mortgage documents containing details that contradict the White House's allegations against Cook.
The story attributes the allegations that Cook provided false information for a private loan to a Trump confidant.
The commentary says Cook's removal, combined with Powell's anticipated departure, could allow Trump to gain a Fed majority, a prospect causing market concern.

The Supreme Court deferred a decision on Cook's removal, meaning she will not immediately be terminated. Analysts described the decision as thwarting Trump's attempt to seize control of the Fed by removing her.
Cook is expected to continue voting on the Federal Open Market Committee until January.

The discussion identifies January's Supreme Court proceedings over Cook as pivotal for Fed independence. It warns that replacing her with a Trump-friendly governor before a February meeting concerning regional Fed officials' reappointments could enable Trump to gain control of the institution.

Cook's lawyer provided the first detailed defense of her mortgage applications, arguing that apparent discrepancies were either accurate at the time or an inadvertent notation that could not constitute fraud given other disclosures to her lenders.

FED.title: Trump demands lower Fed rates to reduce government borrowing costs
summaries: Trump wants the Fed to lower interest rates, arguing that inflation will not be a significant problem and seeking lower federal government borrowing costs amid a budget deficit.
Trump has pressured the Fed for months to lower rates significantly, including verbal attacks on Chair Jerome Powell.
Trump has called for 300 basis points in interest-rate cuts.
Trump wanted a half-percentage-point rate cut at the September meeting, rather than the quarter-point cut adopted by the Fed.
The day before the Fed's decision, Trump said the Fed should cut rates and listen to smart people like him.
Trump has threatened to remove Fed Chair Jerome Powell and other central bank governors in his push for interest-rate cuts.
Trump is demanding a policy rate of around 1–2%. The story also reports that he publicly called Fed Chair Jerome Powell 'terrible.'
Erik Strand said Trump is politicizing the Fed and linked this to weakening confidence in the dollar.

Trump explicitly said his side would become the majority at the Fed. The commentary describes his administration's pressure to loosen monetary policy as contributing to dollar weakness and supporting stocks and other assets.

The commentary links September's sharp rise in gold prices partly to fears that Trump's continuing attacks on the Fed could threaten its independence and lead to politically motivated interest-rate policy.

The commentary argues that Trump's pressure is backfiring: 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields are above their levels before the latest Fed rate cut. It also attributes officials' relatively restrained projected cuts partly to tensions created by Trump's rhetoric.

The commentator attributed some of the Fed's internal uncertainty to Trump's pressure and argued that, after Powell's departure in May 2026, his replacement could reshape rate projections toward larger or more frequent cuts if Trump maintains his current stance.
A commentator warned that political pressure on the Fed could lead to short-term monetary policymaking, citing this as a concern when assessing exposure to US assets.

Commentators said Trump tries to steer Powell toward his preferred policy and blame him for negative economic developments. One argued that Trump's desire for lower rates also reflects his own interests as a property developer. They warned that forced rate cuts could trigger selling of long-term bonds over inflation and Fed-independence concerns, raising global borrowing costs and potentially contributing to a debt crisis in 2026 around Powell's replacement.

The discussion describes Trump as wanting the Fed's policy rate cut to zero. A commentator cites a survey in which 78 of 83 economists believed the Fed was already being influenced by political pressure, and warns that confidence in the central bank has suffered while inflation is rising.

A commentator describes Trump's firing of the BLS chief as indirect pressure in his pursuit of lower rates. A Citi rates strategist reportedly said 10–15% of surveyed American clients feared future CPI figures might be unreliable, contributing to weaker demand for inflation-protected Treasury securities.

The discussion says Trump wants rates lowered to 1% very quickly. A commentator argues that he will likely choose a new Fed chair who shares his preference for lower rates, and that advocating a low neutral-rate estimate provides a way to justify cuts within the Fed's framework.

The discussion describes Trump's pressure on the Fed and Powell as unprecedented. It says economists, investors and Fed observers see the selection of Powell's successor as a risk to Fed independence, depending on whether the nominee follows Trump or makes independent, data-based decisions.
On October 28, Trump called Powell an 'Antiperson' and said he was late in everything, continuing his pressure for lower interest rates.

Mark Cudmore said the administration continues to pressure the Fed to cut rates despite Powell's warning against assuming a December cut. He suggested Trump might renew his pressure if markets do not restore December rate-cut pricing.

A commentator saw no clear Trump influence on the latest Fed decision, but said his belligerent stance was reflected in interest-rate futures expectations for additional cuts after Powell's term ends in May 2026.

At an investment forum on November 19, Trump said interest rates were too high and that he wanted to fire Fed Chair Jerome Powell, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had advised against it. Trump also threatened to fire Bessent unless he got the Fed's high rates fixed quickly.
Scott Bessent said Trump is not allowed to fire Jerome Powell.
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump reiterated that he would remove Powell if he could, but said others were preventing him from doing so.

A commentator predicted that Powell would deliver a third rate cut partly because of Trump's pressure, contrasting it with two cuts justified by economic conditions, and cited Trump's humiliating criticism of Powell over Fed building renovations.

A commentator argued that many Americans may view Trump's pressure for rate cuts despite still-high inflation as sensible rather than bad policy, because they regard interest payments as part of their cost of living and believe lower rates would reduce inflation.
Trump considers the quarter-point rate cut expected at the Fed's December meeting insufficient.

The discussion says the Trump administration, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, has become more vocal about perceived shortcomings in Fed decision-making. It anticipates more contentious policymaking even before Powell's replacement takes office.
At a White House event after the Fed's December 10 quarter-point rate cut, Trump said the Fed had not cut rates enough.
Trump wanted a rate cut twice as large as the 25-basis-point reduction announced on December 10.
Trump insulted the Fed chair and argued that the Fed's fear of inflation was stifling growth. He said growth need not cause inflation and that policy could be tightened later if inflation emerged.
A commentator said Stephen Miran had voted for a 50-basis-point cut for the third consecutive meeting, describing this as doing what Trump had asked him to do.

Trump said Powell did not understand his demand for continually falling interest rates and called him thick-headed and rigid. A commentator attributed the latest Fed cut partly to political pressure and said markets would likely have reacted much more sharply without a cut.
Trump had described the December rate decision as another test for Fed Chair Jerome Powell while pressing for faster rate cuts.
Trump called the central bank a "deadhead Fed" while criticizing its December rate cut.

A commentator describes Trump's pressure on the Fed to lower interest rates as an attempt to mask inflation and affordability problems, noting that lower rates reduce consumer borrowing costs but also raise asset prices, benefiting asset owners while making homeownership less affordable for others.

A commentator argued that Trump's demands for lower rates are aimed at long-term rather than short-term rates, and that the Fed's three cuts this year have not lowered long-term rates because of concerns about Trump's economic program.
Trump said that, as president, he should have the right to comment on what US interest rates should be.

Stephen Miran, described as Trump's Fed representative, advocated large rate cuts to avert what he called a catastrophe, even as Trump celebrated unexpectedly strong GDP figures. The commentator argued that Miran would favor cuts regardless.
Trump said interest rates should still be cut despite stronger-than-expected US GDP growth of 4.3%.

The discussion said international investors are divided over whether Trump-appointed Fed official Stephen Miran advocates lower rates because of his economic beliefs or because he sees that as his assigned political role.

A commentator said some Fed policymakers likely advocate lower rates partly to please Trump, and that political considerations now clearly operate alongside economic analysis. The commentator said lower rates would benefit Trump politically by improving households' finances.

A commentator described Trump as pressuring the Fed to lower rates, increase liquidity and expand the economy, arguing that a global liquidity contraction was therefore a black-swan risk in the current environment.
A commentator said lower oil prices following US action in Venezuela could help keep inflation low and support the lower interest rates Trump wants the Federal Reserve to deliver.

Stephen Miran, described as Trump's appointee within the Fed, advocated 150 basis points of rate cuts in 2026, after previously calling for 100 basis points, despite including relatively high inflation in his forecast range.
The story reports that Trump considered dismissing Powell during his first term and again last spring, but backed off after advisers warned of a negative market impact.
During a visit to the Fed renovation site, Trump told Powell jokingly that he was more concerned about lowering interest rates than the project's cost overruns.
Commentators said the latest labor-market data did not suggest Powell would yield to Trump by cutting rates at the January 28 meeting.

Fubini linked Trump's demand for 1% interest rates to weak growth outside the technology sector, low job creation, poor polling and the approaching November midterm elections. He warned that 1% rates with inflation at 3% would accelerate inflation and disproportionately hurt low-income and fixed-income Americans.

FED.title: Trump adviser Stephen Myron joins Fed board
summaries: Stephen Myron, a close economic adviser to Trump who supports his interest-rate and tariff policies, is participating in the Fed board's policy meeting for the first time.
The rate-cut vote was 11 to 1; Spencer Jacob said the dissenter very likely was Stephen Myron, who had been on the board for less than 48 hours and simultaneously worked for the president.
Stephen Myron preferred a half-percentage-point rate cut rather than the quarter-point cut adopted by the Fed.
Myron remains chair of the White House Council of Economic Advisers while on leave, raising questions about his independence at the Fed.

Myron argued that a 1977 Fed document establishes a third mandate: keeping long-term interest rates under control. Asked whether Myron influenced the additional projected 2025 rate cut, Powell said each member has one vote and the revised projections reflected the committee's own decisions.

The discussion attributed a projection of five rate cuts bringing rates below 2.8% this year to Stephen Miran. Former Dallas Fed president Richard Fisher criticized Miran's position as unserious because it would produce negative real interest rates amid rising inflation, and said Miran needed to argue his case rather than simply act as Trump's man.

Stephen Miran favored cuts totaling 125 basis points this year. The two other Trump-appointed members supported the quarter-point cut rather than a half-point cut, which commentators described as reassuring markets that political influence remained limited.

Myron was confirmed on Monday before the Fed meeting began Tuesday. His unpaid leave from the Council of Economic Advisers without fully resigning was described as unprecedented. The two other Trump-appointed officials who supported the quarter-point cut had dissented at the previous meeting in favor of a rate cut.
Miran is scheduled to give his first speech as a Fed member on September 19.

In his first public speech after his appointment, delivered the previous day, Stephen Miran advocated aggressive rate cuts this year and smaller cuts in 2026–2027. He argued that Trump's tariff, immigration and tax policies lower the neutral interest rate toward zero, and cited a rapidly cooling labor market and elevated employment risks. Miran said he dissented at the September meeting because he could not pretend there was consensus and indicated he would continue dissenting at future meetings.
Stephen Miran warned that failing to cut interest rates would leave the economy in a crater.

Miran argued that the policy rate should already be two percentage points lower. He said reduced immigration would lower rental demand and inflation, tariff revenues would reduce government borrowing and the neutral rate, income-tax cuts would boost supply, and a more negative output gap would permit further easing. The commentary criticized these arguments as one-sided and reported that Summers dismissed them as lacking an economic foundation.
The commentator said Trump appointed Miran to defend Trump's argument for larger interest-rate cuts, describing Miran's unusually low dot-plot projection as evidence of that role.
A commentator described Trump's appointment of Miran to the Fed as placing a 'Trojan horse' inside the institution.
The discussion describes Stephen Miran as wanting the Fed's policy rate cut to zero and identifies him as a source of pressure on the Fed.

In a recent speech, Stephen Myron put the neutral real interest rate at around 0.5%, about half a percentage point below the Fed's official estimate. Commentators challenged his immigration argument, noting that reduced labor supply could increase wage pressure and lower saving, pushing rates in the opposite direction.
A commentator expects Miran to advocate a larger rate cut than the quarter-point reduction widely anticipated at the Fed's October meeting.

Myron has conceded in recent weeks that conversations with other Fed board members indicate his push for a larger cut is highly unlikely to succeed. He now expects cuts totaling 50 basis points by year-end, with 25-basis-point reductions at each of the next two meetings.
Stephen Miran continued to call for a 50-basis-point rate cut at the latest Fed meeting.

In remarks the previous day, Stephen Miran called for a 50-basis-point rate cut, saying the Fed should at least cut by 25 basis points if the larger reduction was not possible. A commentator linked his appointment to weakening Fed independence and the dollar.

A commentator described Stephen Miran as conducting Fed debates in an openly partisan manner. He argued that the faction favoring model-based rate cuts without waiting for more data was motivated by helping or pleasing the Trump administration, and warned that the Fed's politicization could further undermine the dollar's reserve-currency status.
A commentator argues that Miran's appointment was intended to acclimate markets to the coming leadership change and learn the Fed's internal workings so he could brief the incoming chair.

FED.title: Elizabeth Warren attacks Myron's Fed appointment as Trump intervention
summaries: Before the confirmation vote, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren accused Stephen Myron of entering the Fed as Trump's puppet and a Trojan horse, there to do whatever Trump instructed.

FED.title: Dan Katz advocates structural reforms to Fed governance
summaries: Dan Katz, identified as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's chief of staff and a possible nominee for IMF deputy managing director, advocates reducing Fed governors' terms from 14 to eight years and curtailing powers he believes the Fed has accumulated. Katz, who has coauthored work with Stephen Miran, also supports state governors appointing or nominating regional Fed presidents and giving those presidents permanent voting rights.
Katz advocates requiring government approval for Fed balance-sheet expansion and bond purchases or their discontinuation.

FED.title: Trump's Fed renovation intervention targeting Powell
summaries: Daniel Moss described Trump's tour of the Fed renovation site with Jerome Powell a couple of months earlier as an unsuccessful attempt to undermine the Fed, preceding the administration's move against Lisa Cook.

FED.title: Scott Bessent criticizes quantitative easing and balance-sheet expansion
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has expressed concern in recent articles about the extent of central bank balance-sheet expansion, describing it as mission creep and comparing quantitative easing to a lab experiment. His interventions have brought scrutiny of QE back onto the US policy agenda.

FED.title: Trump's Fed chair selection tied to loyalty and 1% interest rates
summaries: Scott Bessent has presented five candidates for Fed chair: Christopher Waller, Michelle Bowman, former governor Warsh, Kevin Hassett and BlackRock's Rick Rieder. They are to undergo final interviews with Trump. Commentators predict Trump will ask whether they would cut rates to 1% if he considers that appropriate, and that Hassett will get the job because he would follow Trump's wishes.

A commentator expects Powell's successor to be dovish rather than hawkish, consistent with Trump's preference, and to maintain better relations with the Treasury. The commentator said expectations of a more dovish Fed leadership are already partly reflected in equity-market pricing.

Commentator Uwe Jean Häuser expects any of the five candidates to succeed Powell in May 2026 to follow Trump's wishes much more readily than Powell. He warned that drastic early rate cuts under the successor could trigger a spiral of rising inflation, interest rates and government debt.

Markets expect Trump to appoint a successor who will deliver more rate cuts. A commentator cautioned that the new chair would need to persuade the other policymakers with data and consistent arguments, and could face unusually numerous dissents if unable to do so.
The discussion expects Trump to install four or five preferred officials and produce a dovish Fed after Powell leaves in May 2026, but notes that members opposed to rate cuts will remain.

A commentator expects the new Fed chair to be named before Christmas and predicts Kevin Hassett will be chosen. The commentator cited Hassett's recent warning that US GDP could contract in the fourth quarter and expects him to signal rate cuts toward 1% in loyalty to Trump.
A commentator suggested that Trump could ease near-term market concerns about the Fed chair appointment by choosing a market-friendly figure such as Scott Bessent.
Asked on Brett Baier's Fox News show whether he was a candidate to lead the Fed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent firmly said he would not become Fed chair.

Trump said he believes he knows whom he will choose as Fed chair but declined to identify his favorite or confirm whether that person is on Bessent's shortlist. He said he would like Bessent to take the role, but suggested Bessent would not because he enjoys serving as Treasury secretary too much.

Commentators said aspiring Fed chairs are proposing 50-basis-point cuts, describing a competition to advocate the largest cuts to secure the appointment. They argued that Hassett's appeal to Trump includes his television performance and willingness to follow Trump's instructions, potentially pushing rates toward zero in real terms rather than levels justified by economic conditions.

Bloomberg reports that Kevin Hassett has emerged as the favorite to become Fed chair, with prediction-market odds rising to 54%. A commentator said Hassett had used statistics unavailable to others at the time to argue for a December rate cut and predicted aggressive rate-setting if he becomes chair, citing his close relationship with Trump.

Bloomberg reports that Trump's advisers and allies favor Kevin Hassett, who shares Trump's approach to interest-rate cuts. Scott Bessent is under pressure to balance candidates' support for rate cuts with financial-market confidence. White House spokeswoman Carolyn Leavitt said nobody really knows what Trump will do until he does it.

Kevin Hassett said in a Fox News interview that he would accept the Fed chair position if asked, saying he wanted to serve his country and president. A commentator predicted that Trump's chosen successor would begin with a rate cut, possibly of 50 basis points, to please Trump.

The discussion cites foreign press reports that the intended chair could first be appointed as a governor when Stephen Miran's term expires on February 1, then become chair from within the Fed. A commentator expects the successor to serve Trump's MAGA agenda and begin pursuing a policy rate of 3%.

Trump said his chosen Fed chair would, like him, be more inclined toward interest-rate cuts. Betting-market expectations that Kevin Hassett would become the next chair rose to roughly 75–80%; the discussion noted that Hassett had not denied the reports.

A commentator predicts Trump will appoint Kevin Hassett as Fed chair on the same day as a possible Supreme Court ruling against his tariffs, potentially in December, and use the appointment to announce a push for interest rates to fall to 1%. The commentator calls that target unrealistic but expects a one-percentage-point decline following the tariff ruling.

Trump hinted at Kevin Hassett as a possible next Fed chair and said he would not announce the appointment until next year. A commentator predicted that, following a possible adverse tariff ruling and resulting lower inflation, Hassett could press Powell to begin cutting rates, creating a path toward lower rates ahead of the autumn elections.

The White House abruptly cancelled finalist interviews scheduled for this week on the same day Trump said he had narrowed the candidates to one. The reason for cancellation was unknown. Nick Timiraos said Hassett appeals to Trump because he is trusted and a credible conservative economist unlikely to spook bond markets, while Trump believes Powell failed to reward him with loyalty.

PGIM Fixed Income co-chief investment officer Gregory Peters said Hassett's ties to the administration raise Fed-independence questions and doubted he has the credibility within the policy committee to build consensus for Trump's desired rapid easing. Trump allies are reportedly considering making Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent the White House's top economic adviser if Hassett becomes Fed chair.

Bloomberg Economics' Stuart Paul said incoming hawkish FOMC voters, including Dallas Fed president Lori Logan and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, would make it difficult for any new chair to build consensus for Trump's desired rapid rate cuts. He said reports identifying Kevin Hassett as the finalist had prompted equities to rally and two- and ten-year yields to fall, suggesting markets accepted his credibility despite concerns about his commitment to the Fed's 2% inflation target.

A commentator predicts Trump and Kevin Hassett will push down real interest rates ahead of the election, with cuts at every meeting if tariff removal lowers inflation. The commentator argues that a one-percentage-point decline in mortgage rates would stimulate homebuilding and refinancing.
Kevin Hassett, described as the strongest candidate for Fed chair, said late last week that he would cut interest rates if he were chair.

A commentator expects Trump's appointees to favor more economy-supportive policy but doubts they would cut rates uncontrollably or disregard economic data, predicting leadership that is somewhat more commercially minded and less academic.

At the WSJ CEO Council summit, Kevin Hassett said there was currently room to cut rates by more than 25 basis points if supported by the data. He said that as Fed chair he would rely on his own judgment rather than political pressure, commit to nonpartisanship, and expressed concern that the Fed had been partisan.
In an interview with Politico, Trump said yes when asked whether cutting interest rates immediately was his litmus test for the next Fed chair.

A commentator expects three Fed rate cuts in 2026 regardless of whether Hassett or Bessent becomes chair, describing both as members of the MAGA camp. The commentator predicts the Fed and Trump's appointed chair will do everything possible to prevent a financial-market confidence crisis from materializing ahead of the November midterm elections.

A commentator expects the incoming MAGA-aligned Fed chair to deliver 75 basis points of cuts, potentially starting with a 50-basis-point cut, bringing rates to 2.75–3% and meeting Bessent's stated 3% target. The commentator warns that aggressive cuts in a still-strong economy could instead drive market borrowing rates higher.
Mark Cranfield said the White House is methodically seeking to alter the Fed's balance of power through personnel replacements beyond the chair, with additional vacancies expected next year.
The story reports that Trump interviewed Warsh the previous day and reiterated that interest rates were a non-negotiable issue in selecting the next Fed chair, demanding substantially lower rates.

A commentator described Trump's chair selection process as a behind-the-scenes bidding contest over how many rate cuts candidates would deliver if appointed, and warned that choosing a more politically responsive chair could strengthen dollar weakness and demand for dollar alternatives. Another commentator argued that the candidates' views were not as radical as Stephen Miran's.
Trump said he was meeting with finalists for Fed chair and was not asking candidates to commit to cutting rates, but reiterated that rates should be much lower.

Commentators warned that additional Trump-aligned appointments could shift the Fed toward tolerating inflation well above its 2% target to support the economy, potentially prompting market concerns about future inflation.

Trump praised Kevin Hassett and former Fed governor Kevin Warsh as both 'great,' indicating they were the leading candidates. In a weekend CBS interview, Hassett said the president's views on the interest-rate path were important and should be considered, while emphasizing that the Fed makes decisions independently. Jamie Dimon said Warsh could be closer to Trump's preference for monetary easing, while Hassett appeared likely to maintain an appropriate stance.
Trump said the next Fed chair, whom he is expected to appoint soon, will be someone who believes in lowering interest rates by "a lot."

A commentator warned that a strongly Trump-aligned chair such as Kevin Hassett could clash with a committee majority opposing rate cuts, potentially damaging the Fed's institutional credibility and predictability. The commentator viewed Christopher Waller favorably as a known internal candidate and Kevin Warsh as less concerning because of his Fed experience and market relationships during the Lehman crisis, while criticizing Hassett's lack of central-banking experience and close political ties.

Commentators warned that a Trump-aligned successor unwilling to counter renewed inflation could unsettle long-term inflation expectations, depress stocks and bonds, and cause a sharp dollar decline. Another commentator predicted that Hassett or another leading candidate would resist presidential pressure once appointed, citing reputational concerns and market pressure.

A commentator said Hassett's repeated advocacy of rate cuts could produce an amplified version of the 'Greenspan put,' with the Fed quickly cutting rates when conditions deteriorate. The commentator warned that diminished confidence in monetary policy could increase Treasury risk premiums, steepen the yield curve and encourage international investors to shift away from US markets.
Just before Christmas, Trump wrote on Truth Social that anyone who disagrees with him will never be Fed chairman.

Scott Bessent said the announcement of the next Fed chair would probably come around Davos. Trump said he had made his choice. The discussion identified Kevin Hassett and Kevin Warsh as the contenders and said Warsh had gained prominence in recent days.
Trump is expected to announce Powell's replacement in the coming days.

Commentators said Fed leadership unanimously decided the previous week to retain the regional Fed presidents, describing this as a stabilizing factor that would slow efforts to change the Fed's policy approach and noting that hawks still held a relatively clear majority.

FED.title: Kevin Hassett says Fed has lost control of inflation
summaries: White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett said on November 19 that the Fed had lost control of inflation.

FED.title: Bessent seeks a simpler Fed with a reduced public role
summaries: The discussion describes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent as wanting the Fed to simplify its activities and complex balance sheet, move into the background, and selecting a chair with that objective. Commentators suggest simplification could mean holding only Treasury securities rather than Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac securities, while warning that a larger Treasury role could create competing centers of authority.

FED.title: Kevin Hassett attacks Fed as partisan
summaries: Nick Timiraos said Kevin Hassett has adopted a more menacing tone toward Fed independence this year, attacking the Fed as partisan. Hassett says he supports an independent Fed but suggests the institution itself has become more partisan, contrasting with his earlier opposition to firing the Fed chair and support for letting the Fed do its job.

FED.title: Trump seeks to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook
summaries: The story reports a hearing scheduled for today concerning Trump's attempt to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook. It says Supreme Court approval of the removal would renew concerns over Fed independence, and notes that the Fed's special legal status may mean rulings allowing removals at other agencies do not apply to it.

The story links the attempted removal to mortgage-related allegations and says Cook's term normally ends in 2038. A commentator warns that allowing her removal could enable the president to find grounds to remove other Fed officials, while another suggests the attempt could serve as a warning to those remaining.
A commentator warned that, if Lisa Cook were removed, appointing a replacement resembling Stephen Miran could raise concerns about changes to the Fed's institutional structure.

The commentator said the latest court decision kept Cook in office, with her case due before the Supreme Court in January. People consulted in the US viewed her removal and replacement by a Trump ally as potentially decisive for a February meeting concerning regional Fed leaders' reappointments, warning that this could enable Trump to gain control of the Fed.

FED.title: Bessent and Hassett propose changes to regional Fed leadership
summaries: The discussion attributes to Scott Bessent and Kevin Hassett the view that regional Fed presidents speak too frequently and should be required to have lived in their regions for three years, describing these ideas as efforts to change the Fed's structure.

FED.title: Hassett presses Fed to provide six-month policy guidance
summaries: Kevin Hassett, described as the expected next Fed chair, said ahead of the Fed's announcement that failing to provide public guidance on its interest-rate or economic outlook for the next six months would be irresponsible.

FED.title: Republican senators oppose Fed interest payments on bank reserves
summaries: Several Republican senators have criticized the Federal Reserve's interest payments on bank reserves as a waste of public money and argued that the Fed should stop paying banks to leave their money there.

FED.title: Federal prosecutors launch criminal investigation into Powell over Fed renovations
summaries: Federal prosecutors opened a criminal investigation into Fed Chair Jerome Powell over renovations of the central bank's Washington headquarters. Powell confirmed the investigation on Sunday evening. The story describes it as a major escalation in the conflict between Trump and the Fed.

The investigation concerns the Fed's $2.5 billion headquarters renovation and Powell's testimony to the Senate Banking Committee last summer. Powell called the administration's action a pretext to curtail Fed independence and intimidate monetary policymaking, and pledged to continue his job.

Powell said he had received a subpoena and feared criminal charges. In a telephone call with NBC, Trump denied involvement in the investigation but criticized Powell's job performance and knowledge of building construction.
Powell said the Fed received grand jury subpoenas on Friday; his response video was released Sunday evening. The dollar weakened and gold prices rose following the news.

US futures fell following the news. Analyst Kyle Rudder said markets viewed the action as not undertaken in good faith by the Department of Justice or White House and were initially surprised by Powell's pointed response. He warned that escalating tensions could undermine Fed independence, worsen policy outcomes and reduce confidence in US assets.
The story reports that gold prices rose 2% over the weekend following news of the Justice Department's action against Powell.

Powell said the Fed had made every effort through testimony and public disclosures to keep Congress informed about the renovation project. He said the threat of criminal charges resulted from the Fed setting interest rates based on economic evidence rather than the president's preferences.

The investigation is being run by Washington's U.S. Attorney's office, overseen by Trump ally Janine Pirro, and concerns Fed spending records. Trump threatened a lawsuit last month alleging Powell's incompetence over renovation cost overruns. Powell denied wrongdoing and said potential prosecution would not affect his ability to serve through May 15. Long-term bond yields rose following the news. A commentator warned that the investigation could intimidate Powell's successor.
The story reports that Trump said in August he was considering allowing a criminal case against Powell over the renovation project.

A commentator said the investigation could create uncertainty over when Powell's successor takes office and suggested the administration opposed Powell remaining as a governor after relinquishing the chairmanship. The commentator said the testimony underlying the investigation had been prepared and shared in advance. Following Powell's statement, gold reached a record, the Swiss franc attracted buying, short-term US Treasury yields rose and long-term yields fell.

The story reports that the Fed's renovation budget rose from $1.9 billion in 2023 to $2.5 billion in 2025, with unforeseen costs cited to the relevant authorities. Following the subpoena news, gold and silver rose nearly 5%, while US futures losses reached 0.85%, led by Nasdaq. A Financial Times commentary said the action also raised questions about Justice Department independence and damaged its credibility.

A commentator expects Powell and the Fed to continue making data-based monetary policy decisions despite the legal action, noting that Powell cannot decide rates alone. The commentator expects Trump not to escalate the dispute substantially, but warns that a prolonged escalation could create global uncertainty and warrant investors reducing risk.

A commentator warned that continued pressure stemming from the Fed renovation dispute could weaken monetary-policy decision-making and call the institution's governance into question, threatening the US credit rating over the medium to long term and increasing doubts about confidence in the United States and the dollar.

Commentators interpreted increases in two-year and ten-year Treasury yields as partly reflecting higher inflation premiums, arguing that the action against Powell was seen as a move to accelerate rate cuts and could leave inflation higher.
The investigation includes whether Powell lied to Congress about the scope of the headquarters renovation project.

Former Fed chairs Alan Greenspan, Ben Bernanke and Janet Yellen, alongside other former officials from Democratic and Republican administrations, defended Powell and called the investigation an attempt to undermine Fed independence. White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett characterized it as promoting accountability. Trump said he did not know about the Justice Department subpoena and denied that the investigation was related to disagreements over interest rates.

Federico Fubini recalled that during Trump's July 2025 visit to the Fed renovation site, Powell publicly disputed Trump's $3.1 billion cost allegation, saying it included another building renovated five years earlier. Fubini interpreted the investigation as a warning to all FOMC members that they could face similar action, aimed at intimidating the committee rather than merely installing a loyal chair.
Trump denied that the investigation was an act of personal or political retaliation against Powell.

A commentator warned that the legal pressure could backfire by encouraging Powell to remain a Fed governor until January 2028 to defend the institution, rather than leave when his chairmanship ends.
