The discussion suggested Trump wants Powell's governor seat vacated so he can appoint a Trump-aligned replacement.

The renovation involves two historic Fed buildings. Janine Pirro, who oversees the investigation, was appointed by Trump as U.S. attorney for Washington, D.C., in May and confirmed by the Senate in August.

Former Fed chairs Janet Yellen, Ben Bernanke and Alan Greenspan compared the Justice Department's action to conduct in emerging markets with weak institutions. FT commentator Rob Armstrong argued that the investigation undermines the credibility of Powell's eventual successor, saying accepting a nomination under this cloud would signal disregard for Fed independence. He described the market reaction as mild and warned that renewed inflation could expose the risks of weakened Fed independence.
Federico Fubini interprets the attack on Powell primarily as Trump's search for a scapegoat for an economy performing worse than it appears, ahead of midterm elections and amid weak polling.

Other Republicans expressed discomfort with the DOJ subpoenas to the Fed. The New York Post editorialized that the action would backfire. Alistair Bull said the administration's effort to lower borrowing costs ahead of elections was being undermined by reduced confidence in monetary policy; ten-year Treasury yields were hovering around 4.2%, raising concerns about mortgage affordability.

The story reports that Trump ally Bill Pulte suggested allegations that Powell lied under oath could provide legal grounds for his removal, and Representative Anna Paulina Luna formally requested a Justice Department investigation. Powell disputed allegations that the renovation included extravagant features such as VIP rooms and rooftop gardens, saying many such elements were no longer in the plans. The Fed attributed increased costs partly to materials, labor and unexpected toxic contamination.

Kai Chen interpreted the investigation as pressure on the Fed to cut rates and as an effort to give the government greater control over monetary policy. US stocks reached records and Australian, Japanese and German markets rose despite the investigation.

A commentator argued that unexpectedly low inflation could make Trump more likely to dismiss Powell, saying Powell's position was less secure than commonly assumed and that the Fed should have lowered rates if inflation was falling.

According to an Axios report cited in the discussion, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the market reaction could be very damaging. Commentators described the legal pressure as a structural threat to institutional credibility, warning that continued escalation could cause sharper dollar depreciation and broader economic harm, while arguing that markets had not yet fully priced the risks.

The story says the renovation was approved in 2017 and estimated at $1.9 billion in 2021. It clarifies that the disputed garden is at ground level above underground parking, new water features were removed from the plans, and the marble work restores original marble. The commentators argue that the Fed's website supports Powell's testimony and question whether any alleged discrepancies would have materially affected congressional decisions.

The story reports that no indictment has yet been issued against Powell and that the precise allegations remain unclear. The correspondent expects any legal dispute over his removal to be lengthy and unlikely to conclude before his chairmanship ends in May 2026.

After Powell's June testimony, White House budget director Russell Vogt sent a letter alleging that it contradicted public renovation plans, implying either false testimony or failure to notify building authorities; Powell defended his testimony. Janine Pirro said Monday night that her office had repeatedly contacted the Fed about renovations but was ignored. House Speaker Mike Johnson supported the investigation. Scott Bessent warned Trump that it could complicate confirmation of the next Fed chair. Trump called Powell either incompetent or crooked. The story also recalls Trump dismissing renovation overruns as grounds for firing Powell at the end of his July site visit.

FED.title: Senator Tillis vows to block Fed appointments during Powell investigation
summaries: Republican Senator Tom Tillis said he would not confirm any Fed appointee while the investigation involving Powell remains ongoing.
The story quotes the Republican senator as saying the legal system was being used for other purposes in explaining his refusal to support a new Fed chair until the case concludes.

Tillis's opposition could prevent nominations from advancing out of the Senate Banking Committee, which has 13 Republicans and 11 Democrats, if he votes with Democrats. This could block Trump's appointment of a replacement for Powell when his chairmanship expires in May.
Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska expressed support for Tillis's refusal to approve Trump’s Fed nominees while the Powell investigation continues.

Tillis called the investigation a vindictive prosecution and urged those responsible to give the president better advice. Murkowski described it as an attempt at coercion. The story notes that a handful of Republican opponents could also block confirmation on the Senate floor.

FED.title: Trump seeks reform of Fed governing structure
summaries: The story describes Trump as seeking to reform the Fed's internal governing council by drawing members from individual states, characterizing the proposed structure as more democratic but less independent of politics.

FED.title: Senator Tim Scott challenges Powell over Fed renovation features
summaries: At Powell's Senate Banking Committee update in mid-2025, Republican Senator Tim Scott challenged renovation plans describing rooftop garden terraces, ornate water features, elevators serving a VIP dining suite and white marble. Powell called some descriptions misleading, saying the elevator already existed and some features were no longer planned.

FED.title: Trump pressures Powell to lower interest rates and considers firing him
summaries: Trump repeatedly demanded lower interest rates over the past year, publicly insulted Powell and considered firing him. The story links his campaign to stimulating the economy ahead of November's midterm elections and installing loyal Fed officials who would deliver lower rates. It also describes his preference for a weaker dollar to reduce the US trade deficit.
Trump linked his criticism of Powell's high interest rates to people being unable to buy homes and repeatedly called for replacing him before his term expires in May.

Trump continues to demand further rate cuts despite three reductions in the second half of last year. He wants US interest rates to be among the world's lowest and wants a say in monetary-policy decisions.

Trump said he wanted markets to rise on good news, complained that markets instead react negatively because of expectations about the Fed's interest-rate decisions, and called Powell a 'jerk,' saying things would normalize after he leaves. Interviews with candidates to succeed Powell are continuing, despite Trump's earlier statement that he would announce his choice by the end of last year.
Trump said he would not choose a new Fed chair unless the candidate committed to lowering interest rates.
A senior Wall Street trader at a large firm warned that Trump's pressure on the Fed would weaken its credibility and hurt its ability to fight crises.
Trump wants lower interest rates as part of his focus on affordability in America.
Trump now says he has no plans to remove Powell, backing away from the idea after taking a strong stance on it the previous week.

Trump said he may keep Kevin Hassett as National Economic Council director, putting Kevin Warsh in the apparent lead to succeed Powell, though no decision has been announced. The selection timetable has shifted to the next few weeks. Analysts expect either candidate would seek a couple more rate cuts in 2026 in line with Trump's demands.

Trump said in a speech this week, 'When the market is doing great, interest rates can go down,' calling this the old-fashioned way of economics. He argued that inflation was gone and rates could fall, although the story reports inflation at about 2.7%.
Trump faces resistance from Republican colleagues on the Senate Banking Committee, who have warned that approval of whoever he nominates to lead the Fed is not assured.
An economist interviewed in the story said Trump's attacks were increasing resistance among Fed officials, with more officials publicly reaffirming that they conduct monetary policy independently.

The story says Trump's pressure for lower rates to boost growth, particularly under a new chair, could influence the Fed toward cuts in the second half of 2026, despite strong economic data suggesting cuts are not needed.

In a CNBC interview, Trump discussed BlackRock executive Rick Rieder as a possible Fed chair candidate and described the three candidates under discussion as impressive. The story says Rieder repeatedly advocates lower interest rates, aligning with Trump's preference.
Trump signaled in his Davos speech that his choice to replace Powell would be a man. Bessent's remarks suggested the nominee could be announced as early as the following week.

Trump says he has decided whom he wants to succeed Powell, with an announcement possible this week. Rick Rieder became the betting-market favorite on Friday following an interview that impressed Trump. Kevin Warsh and Christopher Waller remain contenders, but their willingness to deliver the sharp rate cuts Trump wants is in question.

The story says potential Fed chair candidate Rick Rieder has advocated lowering interest rates to 3%, equivalent to three rate cuts. Commentators note that he would need support from the Fed's voting committee to deliver those cuts.

An economist forecasts one additional rate cut, potentially in June when a new Fed chair is expected to be in place, despite seeing no substantial current need for further easing. The discussion links lower rates under the next chair to Trump's efforts to win the midterm elections.

The discussion identifies Rieder's expectations of falling inflation and AI-driven productivity gains, along with his support for increased homebuilding to reduce inflation, as views that could appeal to Trump when choosing the next Fed chair.

In his Davos speech, Trump portrayed a Fed chair who does not follow his wishes as disloyal and accused Powell of being late to lower rates while acting favorably toward the other political side before the election. The story recalls Trump's 2019 argument that an overly strong dollar hurts manufacturers and growth, and says he argues that central banks exaggerate the inflation risks of lowering rates.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel called Trump's attacks on Powell deeply concerning in an interview with the FAZ, warned against undermining Fed independence, and praised Powell as an excellent central banker and a fundamentally decent person.

GSFM strategist Steven Miller said the prospect of a politically pliant Fed delivering Trump's desired rate cuts is supporting precious metals, as markets expect lower rates to weaken the dollar and reduce its appeal as a safe asset.

A commentator predicts Trump will do everything he can to secure rate cuts under the next Fed chair and expects a cut at the new chair's first meeting. He says Trump wants additional cuts to support housing investment and consumption ahead of the elections.
Trump said yesterday that he welcomed the dollar's decline and that the dollar was doing very well, as it fell to its lowest level in four years.

Stephen Lyron and Christopher Waller, both Trump appointees, dissented from the decision to hold rates steady and each sought a quarter-point cut. WSJ columnist Spencer Jacob linked Waller's dissent to his candidacy for Fed chair and Trump's explicit demands for rate cuts.

Powell emphasized that central bank independence prevents politicians from manipulating interest rates to boost economic growth around elections, and warned that public trust in the central bank is difficult to restore once lost.
Trump said he would announce his choice for Fed chair later. Bloomberg reported that the administration was preparing to nominate former Fed governor Kevin Warsh to replace Powell.

Trump says US interest rates should be 1%. Market-implied odds of Kevin Warsh's appointment as Fed chair exceeded 90% after he visited the White House the previous day, with an announcement expected today. Commentators described Warsh as less dovish than other candidates and questioned how far he could steer the Fed toward Trump's desired rate cuts.

The Financial Times reports that Kevin Warsh will be Trump's choice for Fed chair. A commentator argues that Warsh would follow Trump's wishes despite his previously hawkish views and would face pressure to cut rates from Trump and his father-in-law, Ronald Lauder, a longtime Trump associate. The discussion notes that Warsh would still need to persuade other policy committee members to support cuts.

Trump is expected to nominate Kevin Warsh today. Warsh has advocated rate cuts during the selection process and has recently aligned with Trump on tariffs. The story says Trump's major reservation was that Warsh might act independently and go against him once installed.

Trump has selected Kevin Warsh to succeed Jerome Powell, ahead of Kevin Hassett and BlackRock executive Rick Rieder. On Truth Social, Trump said he had known Warsh for a long time and predicted he could become the best Fed leader in history.

The story reports that Trump had considered nominating Powell's successor much earlier to put a rival at his shoulder. Powell has said he will not resign voluntarily and intends to stay until May. The correspondent suggests Warsh's nomination could sideline Powell if markets begin following the designated successor's statements instead.

The story reports that Trump passed over Warsh in 2017 partly because he wanted a chair who favored low interest rates and doubted Warsh's record supported that preference. Warsh has recently dismissed concerns about Trump's attacks on Fed independence, contrasting with his 2010 defense of independence. He has called for 'regime change' in monetary policy, communications, and bank supervision and regulation.

The story reports concerns that the chosen successor's family ties to Trump could compromise his independence: his father-in-law, Lauder, was Trump's schoolmate and made large donations to Trump's campaign for his second term.

Analysts viewed Trump's selection of Kevin Warsh as reassuring despite Warsh's recent support for Trump's rate-cut demands. The announcement calmed markets: gold fell 10%, silver dropped nearly 30% in one session, the US dollar appreciated, and Bitcoin fell to about $77,000.

The story reports that Trump preferred Kevin Hassett but encountered opposition when Wall Street was consulted, whereas Wall Street supported Warsh. The commentator says Powell could remain on the Fed board after his chairmanship ends in May to protect central bank independence.

Commentators said Trump expects Warsh to deliver rate cuts regardless of economic conditions. Warsh argues that an AI-driven productivity boom could allow strong growth without inflation, supporting further cuts. The story recalls Trump's warnings in Davos that appointees may promise one thing before selection and act differently once in office.
Greg says Trump's efforts to weaken Fed independence may make investors more reluctant to hold dollars, potentially contributing to dollar weakness, though he cannot establish a direct link.

The commentary says Warsh's active support for rate cuts in recent months was why Trump selected him. It notes doubts about his ability to persuade the policy committee to follow his preferences and expects the appointment not to change rate-setting dramatically.

Trump said he did not think his Fed chair nominee would raise interest rates and that he would not have nominated him if he expected rate increases. The commentary describes a shift in Trump's rhetoric from demanding rate cuts to opposing rate increases.

In a Monday Fox interview, Trump said the next Fed chair should be able to raise US economic growth to 15%. Nathan, who worked with Warsh at the Fed, said Warsh would face challenges keeping the White House satisfied amid its pressure for easier monetary policy, while maintaining focus on the Fed's dual mandate.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon advocated Kevin Warsh's selection as Fed chair. At a Wall Street Journal conference, hedge fund executive Ken Griffin praised Trump's choice as calming tensions in the short term.

The latest Fed meeting minutes show that some FOMC members floated raising interest rates if inflation remains sticky. The discussion says this division would make it extremely challenging for Trump's chair nominee, Kevin Warsh, if approved, to steer the committee toward further rate cuts this year.

Trump formally submitted Kevin Warsh's nomination to the Senate for a four-year term as Fed chair and a 14-year term on the Board of Governors, the latter beginning February 1, 2026. The story says the Middle East war's impact on oil prices could increase Fed officials' caution about further rate cuts despite Trump's demands.
Ahead of the Fed's upcoming decision, Trump continued criticizing its policy as mistaken and called for officials to meet immediately and cut interest rates.

Stephen Myron dissented from Wednesday's decision to keep rates at 3.50–3.75%, seeking a quarter-point cut despite inflation concerns. The story says Trump appointed him specifically to pursue rate cuts and that Kevin Warsh has the same mandate, warning that Warsh would face Trump's anger if he did not follow Myron's lead.

The commentary argues that macroeconomic data do not justify the urgent rate cut Trump has called for, citing Atlanta Fed growth estimates of about 2.7% and a New York Fed estimate of an 18% probability of recession over the next 12 months.
The commentary argues that rising inflation from the Iran war limits a new Fed chair's ability to deliver Trump's desired rate cuts, reducing the immediate value to Trump of installing a successor.

A commentator predicted no US rate cuts this year and argued that Kevin Warsh's incentives would change upon entering the Fed: he would need support from other committee members and might resist cuts to avoid being remembered as a chair who lost control of inflation. The discussion noted that Powell left open the possibility of remaining on the rate-setting committee until January 2028.
In a Fox Business interview, Trump renewed his threat to fire Powell if he does not leave on time, saying he had held back despite wanting to fire him.

Bloomberg economist Stuart Paul said Trump has little statutory scope to fire Powell and that Senate resistance to a successor would further constrain that effort. He assessed that Warsh probably would lack the committee votes to deliver Trump's desired cuts, with officials focused on resisting rising inflation expectations.

Ahead of Warsh's Senate Banking Committee appearance today, Bloomberg reported excerpts of his prepared remarks emphasizing preservation of Fed independence while reviewing its communications and economic models. Commentators said he would likely avoid pursuing Trump's desired rate cuts against opposition from other committee members, using current conditions to justify holding rates.

At his Senate Banking Committee hearing, Kevin Warsh said he had made no promises to Trump about lowering interest rates and that Trump had never pressured him to make such a commitment. Asked about Trump's continued threats to fire Powell, Warsh said he was not a legal expert and wanted the issues to play out in court.

At his Senate Banking Committee appearance, Warsh questioned the suitability of the Fed's current economic models and advocated a broader data foundation to capture actual price changes, while emphasizing that the Fed should operate independently of the US government.

Elizabeth Warren and John Kennedy repeatedly questioned Warsh about whether Trump had instructed him on interest rates or received promises from him. Warsh reiterated that he would make independent decisions, while listening to advice from the president and senators.

Commentators discussed the possibility of Trump installing Steven Miran as acting Fed chair if Warsh is not confirmed. They said Miran has sought a full percentage-point rate cut since joining the Fed, but doubted he could persuade other Fed members, particularly as an acting chair. They predicted intensified Trump attacks on Powell if Powell remains chair.

Trump suggested that, if confirmed, Warsh would follow his agenda of lower interest rates. At the confirmation hearing, Senator Elizabeth Warren warned that a presidential 'sock puppet' leading the Fed could enable Trump to enrich himself, his family and his Wall Street associates. Warsh denied that he would be the president's sock puppet.

Trump said he would be very disappointed if Warsh did not lower interest rates. At the confirmation hearing, Elizabeth Warren challenged Warsh to demonstrate independence by acknowledging that Trump lost the 2020 election; Warsh replied that Congress had certified the election. Warsh defended Trump's public rate demands by saying every president wants lower rates.

Asked whether Trump would still consider firing Powell if he remained a governor after his chairmanship ended, a White House spokesperson said she had not discussed that specifically with Trump but believed he would be satisfied once Kevin Warsh was confirmed as Fed chair.
The commentary says Trump's camp wants Powell to retire rather than remain a Fed governor after leaving the chairmanship, allowing Trump to nominate another board member.

The discussion cites Bloomberg's assessment that Powell's departure could be seen as yielding to political pressure and undermining Fed independence, while his remaining on the Board could complicate Kevin Warsh's ability to unite the policy committee. A commentator predicts Powell will leave because continuing the struggle would be difficult.
Trump criticized Powell's decision to remain a Fed governor, saying he was staying only because he could not find another job and nobody wanted him.
The Fed left interest rates on hold despite White House pressure to cut, in its most divided decision since 1992.

Trump-appointed governor Stephen Miran was the only member to favor a quarter-point rate cut at the latest meeting. All other members supported unchanged rates, although some disagreed with the statement's wording.

The story reports that Powell's remaining on the Board denies Trump a vacancy he had counted on to intervene in the institution. It also reports that Kevin Warsh has hinted that his monetary-policy decisions will satisfy Trump.

Former Fed official Bill Dudley said Warsh's argument that AI-driven productivity gains justify rate cuts was weak: AI investment has instead increased demand and demand for capital, pushing rates upward. He predicted Warsh would struggle to persuade the policy committee to ease without supporting economic data.

The commentary says the Trump administration's desire for rapid rate cuts increasingly risks going unfulfilled before the midterm elections. Bank of America has pushed its rate-cut expectations into next year, while Goldman Sachs sees a possible December cut but little prospect of one before then.

April inflation rose to 3.8% year over year, the largest increase in three years, driven by energy costs linked to the Iran war. The report says this effectively removes investors' expectations of Fed rate cuts and makes it difficult for Kevin Warsh to deliver the cuts Trump expects.

The Senate confirmed Kevin Warsh as Fed chair by 54–45, the closest approval margin since Senate confirmation became required in 1977. Democrat John Fetterman joined Republicans in supporting him. On the Senate floor, Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen questioned whether Warsh's shift toward lower rates reflected genuine economic judgment or Trump's preferences. Powell's last day as chair is Friday.
The story traces Trump's conflict with Powell to 2018, when the Fed raised rates four times and Trump discussed firing Powell amid a December market selloff.
The story reports that Kevin Walsh takes office as Fed chair today, succeeding Powell, who remains on the Board of Governors.

A commentator predicts Trump will soon pressure incoming Fed chair Kevin Warsh to cut interest rates ahead of the autumn elections, despite rising inflation. The discussion cites producer-price inflation of 6% and consumer-price inflation approaching 4% as obstacles to delivering those cuts.

During his confirmation hearing, senators asked Warsh whether he disagreed with Trump to assess his independence. He cited only a lighthearted disagreement over Trump's description of him as a stereotypical Fed chair, rather than a policy disagreement.
The story recalls that after the Fed raised rates early in Powell's tenure, Trump questioned whether Powell or China's Xi Jinping was a bigger enemy to America.

The story quotes Trump calling Powell a 'moron' for not cutting interest rates. A commentator says Trump believes annual inflation is 1.7%, while actual inflation is approaching 4%, and predicts pressure on Kevin Warsh to cut rates in the autumn if the Iran conflict remains unresolved.

Incoming Fed chair Kevin Walsh is due to be sworn in tomorrow night and is expected to face Trump's demand for rate cuts, while money markets price in an 80% chance of a Fed rate increase this year amid inflation concerns linked to the Middle East war.

A commentator suggests that alternative assessments of employment and productivity could allow the Fed under Warsh to cut rates despite war-driven inflation, pleasing Trump, though not necessarily acting for that purpose.

Kevin Warsh was sworn in as Fed chair at the White House. Trump said he wanted Warsh to be totally independent, but moments later urged the view that a booming economy need not be reined in and that strong growth does not cause inflation, saying, 'We want to stop inflation, but we don't want to stop greatness.'

A commentator said the current US administration is trying to control monetary policy much more than previous administrations, encouraging markets to expect pressure for low rates and weaker inflation fighting. The discussion suggested that concerns about the incoming Fed chair's commitment to fighting inflation may be contributing to higher inflation expectations, as the US 10-year Treasury yield reached 4.66%, up half a percentage point since the start of the year.

A commentator argues that Warsh could please Trump through institutional changes at the Fed, including reducing its staff and reliance on economic models, while high oil prices prevent rate cuts. The commentator expects Trump's pressure for cuts to intensify in the autumn ahead of the elections if oil prices fall.

Mark Cudmore said a segment of the market believes Kevin Warsh is Trump's lackey and therefore will not deliver interest-rate increases that orthodox monetary policy might suggest. He noted that rising bond yields are already tightening financial conditions even without Fed hikes.

Kevin Warsh appointed two advisers described as conservatives, including Paul Winfrey, who previously served in the Trump administration. The commentary says Winfrey's writings advocate reducing the central bank's role in the economy and questions whether Warsh, whose statements have aligned with Trump's rate-cut agenda, would raise rates if needed to fight inflation amid strong US economic data.

A commentator said new Fed chair Kevin Warsh had indicated that a rate increase would be unpopular and unsupported by President Trump, while a 25-basis-point hike was being priced in for the remainder of the year.

The story says May's addition of 172,000 jobs and upward revisions totaling 93,000 jobs for March and April further weaken the case for Trump's demanded rate cuts. With hiring strengthening and inflation at 3.8%, it argues that cuts would add to inflation and that some economists might instead see grounds for a rate increase.

Trump renewed his call for lower interest rates in a message directed at the Fed chair, arguing that he needs room to increase defense spending and cannot afford that spending at current borrowing costs.

A commentator predicts that Kevin Warsh's June 17 speech will propose a new inflation measure, argue that inflation is mismeasured, and signal rate cuts once oil prices normalize. The commentator links these expected signals to Trump's electoral needs, arguing that Warsh was installed to deliver them and cannot wait until November.
The story says US inflation rose to 4.2% in May, driven primarily by energy prices linked to the Iran war, complicating Kevin Warsh's ability to deliver the rate cuts Trump installed him to pursue.

Ahead of Kevin Warsh's first policy decision as Fed chair, the commentary says Trump appears willing to give him the benefit of the doubt on rate cuts because war-driven inflation has flared up. Warsh is expected to face scrutiny over whether his remarks demonstrate independence and commitment to controlling inflation.

Ahead of Kevin Warsh's first Fed policy meeting, a commentator said Trump would be unlikely to accept an interest-rate increase. Market expectations of a hike by year-end had fallen below 30% amid hopes that the war would end; the commentator expected the Fed to hold rates, judging an immediate cut too aggressive.

Ahead of Warsh's first policy decision on June 17, investors are selling US Treasury bonds and increasing bets on a December rate hike, contrary to Trump's demand for lower rates. The story frames the decision as the first test of Warsh's promise to protect Fed independence, with markets looking to his press conference and the updated rate projections for a credible commitment to fighting inflation.
Ahead of today's Fed policy decision, Kevin Warsh clarified that he would not lower interest rates solely because Trump demands it.

Senator Elizabeth Warren said Warsh must prove his independence, arguing that he abandoned his longstanding inflation-hawk stance after Trump demanded a Fed chair who agreed with lowering rates. She said Warsh could not identify a single Trump economic statement he disagreed with during his Senate hearing.

Ahead of Kevin Warsh's first Fed policy decision, a commentator warned that signaling rate cuts despite elevated inflation could constitute a policy error and push longer-term Treasury yields higher. The commentator argued that the Fed should wait, with falling oil prices potentially creating scope for cuts in the final months of the year.

At Kevin Warsh's first policy decision as chair, the Fed held rates at 3.5–3.75%, disappointing Trump's demand for cuts, and removed its forward guidance. Nine of the 18 officials submitting projections considered at least one rate increase possible this year; Warsh unusually submitted no projection. The Fed raised its 2026 inflation forecast from 2.7% to 3.6%, while Warsh emphasized that the committee would deliver price stability.

A commentator argued that Warsh's five task forces buy him time against immediate pressure from Trump and predicted a quarter-point rate cut at the September 15–16 meeting, linking it to Trump's electoral needs. Another commentator suggested Warsh could tighten policy by shrinking the Fed's balance sheet without provoking Trump's anger over interest rates, and said his first appearance as chair did not suggest he was Trump's puppet.

Asked at the G7 meeting in France about the Fed's decision to hold rates, Trump said it was fine and did not matter, adding that the Fed now had a very good leader and that he would go along with what Warsh wanted.
The story reports that six voting Fed members said rates might need to rise later this year because of inflation.

Commentators interpret Warsh's five external, independent task forces as a way to accommodate Trump's continuing demands for rate cuts while holding rates for now. They say reviews of AI-driven productivity and alternative inflation measures could support eventual easing; a proposed trimmed-mean inflation measure has historically produced lower readings. They also discuss potentially raising the inflation target to 3%, but only after first achieving 2%.

The story reports that only one Fed official now predicts a rate cut this year, down from twelve, despite Trump's push for lower rates. The two-year Treasury yield rose roughly ten basis points this week to its highest level in more than a year as traders adjusted to the prospect of rates remaining higher for longer.

A commentator said Trump's criticism of the previous Fed chair and his interest-rate rhetoric made a July rate increase by his newly appointed chair unlikely, and considered two increases before the midterm elections overly ambitious. Markets were pricing a 58.5% probability of an increase by September and 42.8% by July. The commentator expected the Fed to hold rates while using its new communications and review initiatives to buy time, then prefer cutting rates when conditions permit.
The Trump administration has argued that the Fed should not worry about inflation, citing Greenspan's refusal to raise interest rates in 1996 and 1997 as a precedent.

A commentator said Kevin Warsh has initially reassured markets about his inflation-fighting credentials, weakening the outlook for gold. The commentator saw no current evidence of renewed Trump administration interference with Fed operations, while noting that it remains a risk.

A commentator said Trump is pressing retailers and gasoline-station chains to lower prices, seeking to bring inflation down over the summer so he can obtain his desired September interest-rate cut. Trump said he had called Walmart about reductions in meat, soda, chips and seasonal grilling-product prices.

The story says Trump's chosen Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, is now discussing raising interest rates despite Trump's repeated public demands for lower rates. Bloomberg Economics' projections show virtually no US rate cuts through 2027, compared with a full percentage point expected at the start of the year, as inflation from Trump's Iran war constrains easing.

At his July 14 appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Kevin Warsh said the Fed would not tolerate elevated inflation. Asked directly whether he worked for Trump, he said the central bank was independent and that its independence came from Congress. Representative Nydia Velázquez asked how he would respond if the administration disagreed with Fed interest-rate decisions; Warsh said he would continue doing his job and cited the Supreme Court's recognition of monetary-policy independence.

Ahead of Kevin Warsh's second Fed policy decision on Wednesday, the story frames a possible rate increase as a test of his defense of central bank independence despite his closeness to Trump and Trump's push for lower rates. Bloomberg Economics expects a restrictive stance, with Warsh likely to emphasize elevated inflation and keep a September rate increase on the table, while recent inflation data allow the Fed to avoid an increase this week.

A commentator predicted that a rate increase at Kevin Warsh's second policy meeting would provoke a strong reaction from Trump, given Trump's demands for lower rates. He expected the Fed to hold rates, while judging political pressure on its decisions to be limited.

At Warsh's second policy decision, the Fed again held rates at 3.5–3.75%, resisting Trump's demand for lower rates while also refraining from an increase. Warsh reiterated that he would not accept persistently elevated inflation. After his press conference, 30-year Treasury yields rose to as much as 5.23%, their highest level since 2007, amid concerns that the Fed would fail to contain war-related inflation.

The Fed voted 9–3 to hold rates, with the Dallas, Cleveland and Minneapolis Fed presidents dissenting in favor of an increase of at least 25 basis points. Warsh rejected any suggestion of a flexible inflation target during his tenure, reaffirming the 2% target, but did not endorse raising rates. The story frames such an endorsement as a significant assertion of his leadership after his nomination by Trump, who continues to seek lower rates.

The commentary interpreted Warsh's post-decision press conference as suggesting that markets would do the work of raising borrowing costs, and said the lack of forward guidance left investors questioning whether the Fed would eventually raise rates.

A commentator said Trump is pressuring the Fed against high interest rates because the large US budget deficit and rising debt make him want to prevent debt from growing even faster. The commentator described this fiscal dominance as constraining monetary-policy responses and contributing to investor caution and market volatility.

Bloomberg strategist Edward Harrison said September could be a more practical time for a Fed rate increase than October, immediately before an election, given Trump's vocal criticism of the Fed. He noted that weaker jobs data had reduced market expectations of a hike and said it was unclear how the Fed viewed the timing.

A commentator argued that White House opposition to a rate-hike strategy leaves Kevin Warsh likely to hold or cut rates despite his tough rhetoric. The commentator said weak employment data further constrain hikes, potentially leaving the Fed on hold even if renewed oil-price increases push inflation higher.

Trump said last week that he speaks with Fed chair Kevin Warsh every week and respects him, but that raising interest rates is not a decision Warsh can make alone. The commentator argued that doubts about the Fed's willingness to raise rates under political pressure are increasing market concerns that long-term inflation could escape control.
In a television appearance this morning, Trump renewed his demand for lower interest rates, saying, 'We've got a strong economy and then of course we need to have a lower interest rate.'

The discussion describes Trump, and possibly Bessent, criticizing the Fed for not cutting rates. A commentator rejects the suggestion that Warsh promised to lower rates regardless of conditions and argues that he cannot secure committee support for cuts unless the economy clearly needs stimulus. The discussion notes that lower short-term rates would benefit the administration as it increasingly finances its debt through short-term borrowing.

Ahead of Jackson Hole, a commentator argued that Warsh's five task forces buy him time to avoid raising rates before the election. The commentator claimed Warsh received a $100 million family gift for taking the job and speculated that a pre-election rate increase could jeopardize his standing with his father-in-law and family.

A commentator predicted the Fed would seek to hold rates unchanged at its September 15–16 meeting rather than raise them before the elections, potentially citing pending productivity reviews and expected disinflation. He warned that renewed Middle East fighting and higher oil prices could instead require a December rate increase.

At Jackson Hole last week, Kevin Warsh signaled that the Fed might need to raise rates again to control persistent inflation, despite Trump's expectation that he would lower rates. Investors remain uncertain whether Warsh will appease Trump; traders now price roughly equal chances of a rate increase or unchanged rates at the Fed's next meeting.

Trump reiterated this week that US interest rates should be the lowest in the world, criticized discussion of rate increases following strong economic figures, and argued that GDP growth could reach 14–20% without requiring higher rates.
The story links Trump's repeated instructions on interest-rate policy and challenges to Fed independence to unease about foreign central banks storing gold at the Fed in New York.

Trump said US interest rates should be 0.5%. The commentary argues that this demand makes raising rates more difficult for the new Fed chair ahead of next week's meeting, as renewed oil-price increases fuel inflation concerns and markets price roughly a 70% chance of a September rate increase.

Bloomberg Economics expects a quarter-point rate increase at the upcoming Fed meeting, putting Kevin Warsh in conflict with Trump's explicit demand for cuts two months before the midterm elections. The commentator said markets have almost fully priced in an increase, although the decision remains a close call within the FOMC.

Ahead of this week's Fed meeting, futures traders assign an 80–90% probability to a rate increase despite Trump's continued pressure on Kevin Warsh to lower rates. The story warns that failing to raise rates could trigger a major selloff in 10- to 30-year government bonds and spill over into other markets.

Trump said Warsh would lower interest rates because the United States is the world's most efficient economy and a leader in AI. A commentator argued that political pressure makes a rate increase difficult despite rising diesel and other prices, with August annual inflation at approximately 3.4%.

Speaking from Ireland on Sunday, Trump reiterated that the United States should have the world's lowest interest rates, an indirect demand aimed at Fed chair Kevin Warsh ahead of Wednesday's policy decision.

As the Fed meeting begins today, the commentary describes Kevin Warsh as caught between markets pricing in and demanding a rate increase and Trump's demand for the world's lowest interest rates, between 0.5% and 1%. US 10-year Treasury yields are around 5.02%, while 30-year yields are approaching 5.38%.
Trump demanded lower interest rates and said that if rates do not fall, he will stop trade with all countries that have trade surpluses with the United States.

A commentator said Trump's intervention in Fed policymaking is undermining investor confidence and raising concerns about Fed independence, warning that a rate increase could provoke a reaction from the president or Treasury.

Markets price a greater than 90% chance of a quarter-point Fed rate increase today, the first since 2023, despite Trump's push for lower borrowing costs, with another increase priced in by year-end. Carlyle CEO Harvey Schwartz said near-zero rates would generally be inconsistent with the economy's current strength.

A commentator predicted that Warsh would leave rates unchanged despite markets assigning a 94% probability to an increase, partly because a hike shortly before the November 3 elections would anger Trump, who continues demanding cuts. He argued that holding rates would raise questions about Fed independence.

Trump has suggested that Kevin Warsh does not want to raise interest rates and that a hostile Fed committee is dragging him toward an increase. The story says dissent against a rate hike could therefore create awkwardness for Warsh.

The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point, its first increase since 2023, despite Trump's demand for lower rates. The decision was unanimous. A White House spokesman called it unfortunate; Trump had not yet responded. Most officials projected at least one more rate increase this year. The story describes the decision as reassuring investors about Warsh's independence from Trump.
The story reports that Trump was greatly frustrated by the Fed's interest-rate increase under Kevin Warsh yesterday.

Asked what his message was to Trump after raising rates despite the president's repeated calls for cuts, Warsh declined to discuss the president, saying, "I have nothing for you on a discussion with the president."
Trump called current interest rates 'ridiculous.' The Fed's quarter-point increase brought rates to 3.75–4%.
After the Fed's rate increase, Trump demanded on Truth Social, in capital letters, that US interest rates be lowered quickly, saying the policy rate should be one percentage point lower.
After the Fed raised interest rates, Trump accused its Board of Governors of making a political decision intended to harm him.
Responding to the Fed's rate increase, Trump demanded interest rates of 1% or lower but said he still had confidence in Fed chair Kevin Walsh.
After the rate increase, Trump described the Fed board as 'very hostile' in comments to reporters, while stopping short of criticizing his appointed chair, Kevin Walsh.

In last night's message calling for rates of 1% or lower and rapid cuts, Trump and the White House argued that the United States has the world's best credit standing and that its economy is booming with new investment.

The White House posted a message demanding that US interest rates be lowered quickly, sharply and brutally. A commentator interpreted the Fed's unanimous 12–0 rate increase and Warsh's tightly controlled press conference, which allowed no follow-up questions, as a clear message to the White House resisting Trump's demands.

Trump said he spoke with Warsh before the rate increase. Despite reiterating his demand for 1% rates, he accepted that the board wanted to raise rates and did not threaten to fire Warsh. The commentary said this response gave investors some relief about Fed independence.
Trump said he had spoken with Warsh but had not tried to persuade him, telling him to do what he wanted. Warsh also declined to answer questions about his relationship and communications with Trump.
Trump reacted to the Fed's interest-rate increase during a campaign event in North Carolina ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump said he told Warsh to vote with the rest of the board, describing it as a bad board that would raise rates anyway. Analysts interpreted the unanimous rate increase as evidence of Fed independence; bond yields fell as markets welcomed its willingness to fight inflation.

The Fed has not confirmed Trump's account of his conversation with Warsh before the rate decision, and its timing remains unknown. WSJ Washington bureau chief Damian Paletta warned that routine consultations with the White House could give Trump the impression that he has a say in rate policy and erode the Fed's credibility among other board members.

A commentator warned that the uneasy peace between the Fed and White House could deteriorate if further rate increases exceed expectations or the Fed needs to slow the stock market to control inflation.

The commentary says the Fed's rate increase against Trump's wishes reassured equity markets that it was tackling inflation. Stocks recovered, the dollar strengthened, short-term yields rose and long-term yields fell, with the 10-year Treasury yield declining to 4.92% from above 5.02% earlier in the week.

In his Truth Social post demanding rates of 1% or less and rapid cuts, Trump claimed that stopping trade with every country running a surplus with the United States would generate at least $1.5 trillion a year.

A strategist said political pressure for rate cuts had led investors to believe the incoming Fed chair would be unable to raise rates. Following September's increase and the chair's commitment to fighting inflation, investors now expect further increases, contributing to higher Treasury yields.

Megan Swiber said uncertainty about whether Warsh would raise rates after Trump demanded a rate-cutting chair contributed to falling short-term yields and rising long-term yields following July’s Fed meeting. That pattern reversed immediately after Jackson Hole and September’s meeting as markets gained confidence in the Fed’s willingness to fight inflation.
The story reports continuing pressure from President Trump on former Fed chair Jerome Powell to resign.

FED.title: Trump seeks to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook amid mortgage-fraud investigation
summaries: Trump said in August that he was firing Fed Governor Lisa Cook, after which the Justice Department opened a criminal investigation citing alleged mortgage fraud. Cook denied wrongdoing and challenged her removal in federal court; courts have allowed her to remain in office. Her case is scheduled to go before the Supreme Court the following week, and her advocates argue that the grounds for dismissal are a pretext.

The Supreme Court hearing is scheduled for Wednesday. The story identifies Federal Housing Finance Authority chairman Bill Pulte as being behind the attack on Cook and reports a congressional investigation announced in December into his alleged misuse of federal resources and authority against Trump's political opponents.
The Supreme Court has given no deadline or exact date for its decision following Wednesday's oral arguments.
The story reports that Powell plans to attend the Supreme Court hearing on Cook's removal.
The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments today. Cook named Powell and the Fed as defendants in her initial lawsuit contesting her removal.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on January 21. Justices questioned whether Trump's dismissal letter, posted on Truth Social, satisfied the legal requirement for removal for cause and whether Cook should have received a hearing or an opportunity to defend herself. Legal analysts said the justices appeared inclined to let Cook remain in office while her broader challenge proceeds. Justice Brett Kavanaugh questioned the implications for Fed independence and whether future Democratic presidents could make similar removals.

Solicitor General John Sauer conceded that the president cannot fire a Fed governor for disagreeing with his policy choices. Justice Samuel Alito questioned the hurried handling of the case by the executive branch and lower courts. Powell attended the hearing.
Powell was asked about Cook's Supreme Court case at the post-decision press conference but declined to be drawn into the issue, maintaining his focus on the economy.
Powell defended attending the court hearing on Cook's removal, describing the case as exceptionally important in the Fed's history and emphasizing that the process should be conducted properly.
Senator Tom Tillis characterized the Cook case, alongside the Powell investigation, as an attempt to undermine the credibility of Fed independence.

FED.title: Justice Department investigates Powell over Fed renovation and congressional testimony
summaries: The Justice Department served Powell with subpoenas and opened a criminal investigation concerning the costly renovation of Fed headquarters and alleged false statements to Congress. In a video released Sunday evening, Powell said the threatened criminal charges resulted from the Fed setting rates according to economic evidence rather than Trump's preferences, and characterized the administration's action as a direct threat to US economic security. Leading central bank governors issued a joint statement supporting Powell and central bank independence.

Three former Fed leaders and four former Treasury secretaries defended US monetary and economic stability following the investigation. A Republican senator said he would reject any Trump nomination to succeed Powell until the criminal legal matter is resolved.
Following threats to Powell and Fed independence, precious metals continued rising: silver exceeded $90 an ounce, while gold approached its record high above $4,620.
JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warned that the pressure on Powell would backfire and urged against it.
Federal prosecutors sent grand jury subpoenas to the Federal Reserve on Friday related to Powell's testimony last summer about the central bank's building renovation project.
Jamie Dimon said the Justice Department's attacks on the Fed could undermine central bank independence and potentially increase borrowing costs.
Speaking before departing the White House for Detroit, Trump called Powell incompetent and corrupt, citing the budget for renovating Fed buildings and alleging that he was doing a poor job.
Trump-appointed Fed governor Steven Myron told the twelve central bankers who supported Powell to mind their own business.

The story reports that Powell retained an assertive Washington, D.C., law firm. In his Sunday evening message, he said he had served under four presidents and would continue doing his job in the same way.

The story recalls a July 2025 visit to the Fed construction site during which Trump publicly claimed renovation costs exceeded $3 billion and handed Powell a document. Powell disputed the figure, saying it included a separate building completed five years earlier that was not part of the current project. The current renovation is estimated at roughly $2.5 billion, compared with an original budget below $2 billion.
The Fed board appears to be unifying behind Powell amid the criminal investigation.

Backlash on Capitol Hill to the Justice Department probe has intensified Senate scrutiny of the next Fed chair's independence. Analysts suggest this could disadvantage Hassett because of his closeness to Trump and make a candidate with greater distance from Trump easier to confirm.

Trump denied being behind the investigation. The story identifies Federal Housing Finance Authority chairman Bill Pulte as being behind the attacks on Powell and reports that a congressional investigative body announced an investigation into Pulte in December over alleged misuse of federal resources and authority against Trump's political opponents. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly privately told Trump that the situation was becoming a mess.

The Norwegian, Swedish and New Zealand central bank governors signed the statement supporting Powell and central bank independence. New Zealand's foreign ministry criticized its central bank governor, Anna Breman, for signing without consulting politicians.

Bessent criticized Powell for not meeting with federal prosecutors last month before they issued grand jury subpoenas concerning the Fed's building project. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Dick Durbin demanded administration records about the criminal probe, calling it a serious misuse of power.

The upcoming policy meeting will be Powell's first since announcing the Justice Department investigation. Bloomberg correspondent Michael McKee characterized the investigation as presidential vengeance and said he did not expect it to affect the rate decision, as other committee members would ignore it.

Senate backlash against the Powell probe is seen as potentially improving Rieder's confirmation prospects. Hassett is now viewed as largely ruled out, partly because Trump's close ally would likely struggle to win confirmation amid that backlash.

Investors' concerns about Federal Reserve independence following the DOJ investigation into Powell are contributing to demand for safe havens. Gold surpassed $5,000 for the first time and is up 17% in 2026; silver rose 8% this morning and is up 55% this year.

The commentary links the confrontation between Trump and Powell, including Powell's Sunday video response, to increased doubts about the dollar and US institutional governance, encouraging investors to seek alternatives such as precious metals.

The story identifies Attorney General Pam Bondi and prosecutor Jeanine Pirro as coordinating the legal action against Powell. In a quoted statement, Trump said Powell should be fired and arrested for spending $4 billion on a small building.
Asked about the Justice Department investigation at the post-decision press conference, Powell declined to be drawn into the issue and kept his remarks focused on the economy.

Republican Senator Tom Tillis of North Carolina said he would block approvals in the Senate Banking Committee unless the Justice Department dropped its case against the Federal Reserve and Powell, creating an obstacle to Warsh's confirmation.

After Trump's announcement on Friday, Senator Tom Tillis reiterated that he would not advance any Fed nominees until the Powell probe was resolved, while describing Warsh as qualified. Tillis characterized both the Powell and Cook cases as attempts to undermine Fed independence.
On Monday, Trump told reporters at the White House that the investigation should continue to its conclusion.

A federal judge ruled that two Justice Department subpoenas issued to the Federal Reserve were improper, finding that their purpose was to harass and pressure Powell either to yield to the president or resign. U.S. Attorney Janine Piro said she would appeal.

Powell said he has no intention of leaving the Fed Board until the investigation is fully over, reiterating a position stated in a legal filing last week. He can remain a governor after his term as chair ends in May.
The commentary says Powell could continue as Fed chair if senators block Kevin Warsh's confirmation until the investigation is resolved.

Trump defended continuing the criminal investigation in his Fox Business interview. Two prosecutors visited the Fed construction project yesterday. Powell said that even if the investigation is resolved, his decision about remaining on the board would depend on what he considers best for Fed independence. Warsh's Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing is scheduled for next week.
DOJ prosecutors appeared unannounced at the Fed renovation project and were turned away for safety reasons.

Bloomberg economist Stuart Paul characterized the DOJ probe as an attempt to establish grounds to remove Powell for cause, but said that route appeared unlikely to succeed. He expected Tillis's opposition to stall Warsh's nomination in committee for weeks or months.

Following Warsh's confirmation hearing, the White House had shown no readiness to drop the Powell investigation, leaving no clear resolution to Senator Tom Tillis's refusal to support confirmation until the probe is dropped.

At Warsh's Senate Banking Committee hearing, Tom Tillis reiterated that he would withhold approval until the Trump administration dropped all investigations into Powell, Lisa Cook and other Fed officials.

The Justice Department announced it was closing the criminal investigation into Powell, days after Trump insisted in a CNBC interview that it continue and Jeanine Pirro publicly said she intended to press on. Pirro said an already ongoing review by the Fed's inspector general would take its place, but she would restart a criminal investigation if the facts warranted it. That qualification left uncertainty over whether the closure would satisfy Tom Tillis and remove the obstacle to Kevin Warsh's confirmation.

Tillis criticized the timing of the investigation shortly before the Fed chair vacancy and argued that renovation cost overruns were commonplace. The story explains that without his support, the Senate Banking Committee would split 12–12, preventing Warsh's nomination from advancing.

Tom Tillis said Sunday that he would no longer block Kevin Warsh's nomination after prosecutors dropped the Powell probe. Tillis indicated that the DOJ had assured him the investigation would reopen only if the Fed's inspector general recommended it. The Senate Banking Committee is scheduled to vote Wednesday on advancing Warsh's nomination.
The story reports that the investigation found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing.

Tillis said he had worked over the weekend to obtain DOJ assurances that it was not being used to undermine Fed independence. He said that without the now-closed investigation, Warsh would have been confirmed by May 5.

The White House said the Fed inspector general's review was sufficient to investigate the renovations and argued that the inspector general had substantial resources, potentially greater than a grand jury's. It said investigating financial misconduct and renovation cost overruns remained a presidential priority.

The story says a noncriminal inquiry remains ongoing after the criminal investigation was withdrawn. Tillis expects that inquiry also to be withdrawn but remains concerned that the case could resurface.

Powell confirmed he will remain a Fed governor for an unspecified period, insisting that the investigation end with transparency and finality before he leaves. He warned that the series of legal attacks threatens the Fed's ability to conduct monetary policy without considering political factors. The Senate Banking Committee advanced Kevin Warsh's nomination today. Powell said he expects a normal transition and will keep a low profile, leaving Warsh to lead the Fed.

Powell said the Justice Department had assured him it would not reopen the investigation without a criminal referral from the Fed's inspector general and would not use its appeal to restart the investigation or issue new subpoenas absent such a referral.

Powell said he had intended to retire but was remaining on the Fed Board solely because of the legal persecution. He described the offensive against Fed independence as unprecedented in its 113-year history.
The story reports that Powell believes remaining on the Fed Board offers him better protection against the threatened renovation investigation than leaving would.

FED.title: Nixon pressures Fed to lower rates ahead of elections
summaries: In the early 1970s, President Nixon exerted substantial pressure on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates ahead of elections, when Arthur Burns was Fed chairman. The story describes this as a contributing starting point for the inflation that subsequently escalated during the decade.
The story describes Nixon's pressure on Arthur Burns to lower interest rates as discreet and exerted behind the scenes at the White House, contrasting it with Trump's public attacks.

FED.title: Bessent pressures Powell not to attend Cook removal hearing
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Powell's attendance at the Supreme Court hearing on Lisa Cook's removal inappropriate, saying it would politicize the Fed and put his thumb on the scale.
Speaking from Davos, Bessent questioned why Powell would attend to support Cook when the Fed had not examined whether she committed mortgage fraud.

Powell defended attending the Supreme Court oral arguments, calling Cook's case perhaps the most important legal case in the Fed's 113-year history and saying it might have been hard to explain his absence. He noted that past Fed chairs had attended Supreme Court cases.

FED.title: Bessent and Warsh advocate shrinking the Fed's role
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Fed chair nominee Kevin Warsh argue that the Fed has become too powerful and advocate a smaller role for it. Warsh wants to shrink its balance sheet and rethink the Fed-Treasury Accord to give the Treasury a larger role. Fed officials disagree with their criticism of quantitative easing and oppose rapid balance-sheet reductions because of potential money-market turmoil.

Warsh advocated Fed reform in a letter courting Trump last autumn, including ending quantitative easing and reducing the balance sheet. The story describes his opposition to the Fed indirectly financing government spending through large holdings of government securities.

The commentary says Warsh wants the Fed to sell bonds to reduce its holdings, but warns that selling $500 billion to $1 trillion in securities could push up long-term interest rates, contrary to Trump's wishes.

The commentary says Stephen Miran has expressed views similar to those of Kevin Warsh and Scott Bessent about Fed balance-sheet actions encroaching on Treasury authority. It raises the possibility that revising the 1951 Fed-Treasury Accord could require the Fed to consult the Treasury and obtain its approval before expanding its balance sheet, renewing concerns about Fed independence.

The discussion says the Trump administration opposes rapid Fed balance-sheet reductions because the resulting tightening could hurt the economy. It raises the possibility that Treasury approval could be required for balance-sheet contraction as well as expansion, and suggests any intervention may focus on mortgage-backed securities because of their direct effects on households and voters.

Commentators discuss possible Treasury influence over yield-curve control, the securities the Fed purchases or reinvests in, and balance-sheet decisions. They warn that Treasury approval requirements could complicate emergency Fed action, increase volatility in short- and long-term interest rates, and undermine inflation targeting if debt-management priorities override it. They emphasize that such Treasury control is not currently in place.

FED.title: Ongoing investigation into Fed Governor Lisa Cook
summaries: The story reports an ongoing investigation into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook as part of the backdrop to Kevin Warsh's Senate confirmation hearing.
Tom Tillis said he would withhold approval of Warsh until the Trump administration dropped its investigations, explicitly including the investigation into Lisa Cook.

FED.title: Trump attempts to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook
summaries: Democratic senators questioned Kevin Warsh about Trump's attempt to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook. Warsh took a neutral position, saying he was not a legal expert and wanted the issues to play out in court.
The story says Trump's attempt to fire Lisa Cook concerned allegations of mortgage fraud, which she denies. Cook remains at the Fed.

The story says Cook was not given a meaningful opportunity to respond to the mortgage-fraud allegation before Trump attempted to fire her within days. She sued, arguing that Trump lacked the authority or cause to remove her. The case has reached the Supreme Court, and she remains in her position.

FED.title: Elizabeth Warren urges the Fed to lower interest rates
summaries: The story reports that Senator Elizabeth Warren sent numerous letters to the Fed over recent years demanding lower interest rates.

FED.title: Elizabeth Warren challenges Warsh over undisclosed investments
summaries: At Warsh's confirmation hearing, Senator Elizabeth Warren demanded disclosure of his investment holdings and plans to sell them, questioning potential conflicts involving his employer Stanley Druckenmiller and investments in Trump businesses. Warsh said he had agreed with the Office of Government Ethics to sell assets, while maintaining that details of certain fund holdings were confidential.

FED.title: Nixon pressures Arthur Burns and the Fed to lower rates before reelection
summaries: While running for reelection, President Richard Nixon pressured Fed Chair Arthur Burns and the Federal Open Market Committee to lower interest rates to stimulate borrowing, spending and economic activity. Burns yielded and lowered rates despite economic conditions not warranting it. The story identifies this policy as one contributor to the subsequent high inflation and stagflation.

FED.title: Republicans accuse Fed of politically timed rate cuts before 2024 election
summaries: Republicans criticized the Fed's fall 2024 interest-rate cuts, accusing it of making the Biden administration look good just before the presidential election.

FED.title: Trump sidelines Fed digital currency plans in favor of stablecoins
summaries: Trump set aside the Federal Reserve's plans for a digital currency in favor of privately issued stablecoins designed to maintain a stable dollar value.

FED.title: Elected officials urge Greenspan to ease interest rates
summaries: In a 2018 interview, former Fed chair Alan Greenspan said he received numerous requests from elected officials to change interest rates during his tenure, none of which sought higher rates. He described elected officials as consistently favoring more stimulus and looser financial conditions.

FED.title: Trump administration's Lisa Cook affair raises Fed independence concerns
summaries: The commentator recalled that the Lisa Cook affair last year raised concerns about Trump administration interference with Fed independence and its ability to tackle inflation, contributing to demand for gold.

The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that Lisa Cook may remain a Fed governor while contesting Trump's attempt to fire her. Chief Justice Roberts emphasized that Cook had not been given a chance to explain the allegations and that the Fed's for-cause removal standard cannot be circumvented to make governors serve at the president's will. Trump moved to fire Cook last August after housing official Bill Polte alleged she misrepresented her primary residence on mortgage paperwork; she had not been charged with a crime. Critics viewed the allegations as a pretext to remove a governor amid Trump's frustration over interest rates. Cook called the ruling a vindication of Fed independence, but her underlying case remains unresolved.
The story describes Trump's attempt to dismiss Lisa Cook as the first attempt by a US president to remove a member of the Fed's Board of Governors.

Cook denied Trump's mortgage-fraud allegations. The Supreme Court distinguished the Fed from independent agencies exercising executive power, citing the Fed's history of independence from the White House as grounds for protecting its officials from removal at the president's whim.

The Chief Justice stated that monetary policy should not be subject to political interference. The Court contrasted its protection of Cook with a ruling accepting the president's arguments for removing a commissioner of the consumer protection agency.
Chief Justice Roberts stated that evidence supporting any dismissal of Lisa Cook must be presented in an understandable manner.

FED.title: Trump administration launches new effort to influence Fed
summaries: The story refers to reporting the previous day on a new Trump administration effort to influence the Federal Reserve, without specifying its demands or methods.

FED.title: J.D. Vance calls on the Fed to cut interest rates
summaries: Vice President J.D. Vance called on the Fed to cut interest rates at a White House press briefing on September 3.

FED.title: Bessent intervenes to lower Treasury yields despite possible Fed tightening
summaries: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on August 19 that Treasury bond-buyback budgets would double from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation starting September 9. In a CNBC interview this week, he argued that markets had misunderstood economic fundamentals and that yields were moving in the wrong direction. The story describes his intervention as potentially counteracting Fed monetary policy while Kevin Warsh considers raising rates. Bessent said he and Warsh were on the same page.

Bessent also supported intervention to prop up the Japanese yen earlier this summer, partly hoping to calm the US bond market. The story reports that neither this intervention nor the expanded Treasury bond-buyback program has had a lasting effect.

A commentator characterized Treasury purchases of long-term bonds as political intervention aimed at capping yields despite market signals that monetary policy needs tightening. He said investors reject the intervention because it does not address inflation or concerns about fiscal debt and discipline.

A commentator argued that Warsh's support for Bessent's long-term Treasury purchases and close coordination with him undermined Fed independence. He said the purchases were too small to control the yield curve.

Bank of America’s Megan Swiber said Treasury is funding buybacks of older long-term bonds by issuing more Treasury bills. She argued that the program has not lowered yields partly because the Fed is raising rates rather than signaling steady or lower rates. Treasury remained price-sensitive in its first enlarged buyback operation, purchasing only bonds it considered cheap.

FED.title: Indictment of former Fed chair raises concerns about independence
summaries: The story reports an indictment against the former Fed chair, citing it as a source of uncertainty in its discussion of Trump's challenges to Fed independence and the security of foreign gold reserves stored in New York.

The Fed's inspector general found no evidence of administrative misconduct in the headquarters renovation and no grounds for criminal referrals, removing the last formal threat to former chair Jerome Powell. The report nevertheless criticized the Fed's management of the renovation. The project had become a vehicle for the Trump administration's potential legal campaign against Powell, which Powell described as part of Trump's pressure to lower interest rates.

Trump renewed his attacks on former Fed chair Jerome Powell despite his clearance by the Fed's inspector general. The story describes Trump as seeking a scapegoat for current Fed monetary policy, which he considers too restrictive.

FED.title: Hassett warns Fed against raising rates before elections
summaries: National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Trump would not be happy about a Fed rate increase ahead of November's midterm elections. He argued that an independent Fed should stay out of the way of elections.

MNB.title: Intento de aumentar la vigilancia del banco central húngaro
summaries: En Hungría se ha intentado aumentar la vigilancia de las actividades en torno al banco central. La noticia no identifica a los responsables ni detalla las medidas propuestas.

NB.title: Norges Bank supervisory council summons governor over Tangen appointment
summaries: Julie Brodtkorb, chair of Norges Bank’s supervisory council, has summoned the central bank governor amid controversy over Nikolai Tangen’s appointment as head of the oil fund, including scrutiny of his tax-haven holdings and hospitality.

NBB.title: Political criticism of NBB advice on savings rates
summaries: Politicians criticized the National Bank of Belgium as siding too much with banks after Finance Minister Vincent van Petegem requested its advice on low savings rates. The NBB recommended avoiding abrupt intervention and following a path of increases. Vooruit, Groen and PS advocated government measures compelling banks to raise savings rates; the NBB examined several proposed variants.

NBP.title: Proposed investigation of NBP governor over alleged political involvement
summaries: In Poland, an investigation is being sought into the central bank governor's alleged political involvement before last year's general elections.

NBP.title: Polish president pushes NBP gold plan to fund defence
summaries: The Polish president proposes selling and repurchasing NBP gold to realise accounting profits that could be transferred to the state budget for defence spending instead of using EU loans. The story reports that the NBP governor, appointed by PiS, feels pressure to support the president's plan despite wanting to retain the gold reserves.

NBP.title: Tusk opposes NBP gold-based defence financing
summaries: Prime Minister Donald Tusk opposes the president and NBP governor's plan to finance defence spending through transactions involving the central bank's gold reserves. He instead favours an EU lending programme that would provide Poland with around 43 billion.

NORGES BANK.title: Politicians pressure Tangen to relinquish ownership interests before leading oil fund
summaries: Politicians pressured incoming oil fund chief Nikolai Tangen to relinquish ownership interests that could create conflicts of interest, despite Norges Bank's statutory authority to appoint the fund's chief. At a press conference on August 24, Tangen announced he would transfer his stake in Ako Capital's management company to Ako Foundation, reversing his earlier insistence on retaining it as a condition of accepting the job.

NORGES BANK.title: LO challenges Norges Bank’s rate increases and seeks mandate clarification
summaries: LO criticizes Norges Bank for raising interest rates too quickly and sharply in response to imported inflation, arguing that this unnecessarily harms households and the domestic economy. It demands greater weight on domestic conditions and employment in rate decisions and calls for the government or Parliament to clarify the bank’s mandate if the bank does not change its interpretation. LO also urges a review of the mandate’s weighting of domestic versus foreign conditions. The discussion cites the LO leader’s call for Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre to take action on interest rates.

An LO adviser criticizes the use of employment and unemployment as instruments to reduce inflation rather than treating full employment as the goal. The adviser argues that Norges Bank effectively dictates fiscal policy because policymakers avoid creating additional economic pressure for fear of further rate increases, and says Norway’s coordinated wage-setting system should instead be the instrument against inflation.

NORGES BANK.title: Selvaag executive criticizes prolonged high interest rates
summaries: A Selvaag executive questioned the effectiveness of Norges Bank’s high interest rates, noting that the Norwegian krone remained weak while Sweden’s currency had strengthened despite rate cuts. Following Norges Bank’s decision to leave rates unchanged, he said prolonged high rates hurt the housing market and warned that delayed cuts would weaken buyers’ purchasing capacity and willingness to buy.

NORGES BANK.title: Property and housing sector voices urge Norges Bank to hold rates steady
summaries: Property and housing sector voices have criticized making the housing market bear the burden of imported inflation and argued that housing's large weight in the consumer price index impedes reaching the inflation target. The story describes substantial pressure in favor of keeping interest rates unchanged.

NORGES BANK.title: Unnamed interviewee urges caution on Norges Bank rate increases
summaries: An unnamed interviewee urged Norges Bank to be very cautious about raising interest rates, arguing that the economy is not overheated and further tightening could harm households with depleted savings buffers and a construction sector facing rising bankruptcies. The interviewee framed this as advice under the existing mandate, which they considered sound and sufficiently flexible, rather than a demand to change it.

NORGES_BANK.title: Jan criticizes Norges Bank’s interest-rate increases
summaries: In an interview, Jan criticized Norges Bank’s rate increases as unnecessarily aggressive, citing weak consumption, low credit growth and a moderate wage settlement. He argued that higher rates cannot resolve war-related supply disruptions and urged more gradual monetary tightening.

NORGES_BANK.title: Jan advocates relocating Norges Bank out of Oslo
summaries: Jan said he would move Norges Bank to Tingvoll or a similar location if he became governor. He argued that relocating central government institutions out of Oslo was necessary to address housing-price pressures and the concentration of population growth.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO criticizes Norges Bank’s rate hikes as unnecessary interference in wage formation
summaries: LO continues criticism of Norges Bank’s interest-rate policy that began last year. Its leader called the latest double rate increase incomprehensible and irresponsible. An LO representative argues that inflation is entirely imported, that higher rates cannot address its causes, and that aggressive tightening unnecessarily raises unemployment, suppresses wage growth and interferes with income distribution and collective wage bargaining.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO representative suggests a higher inflation target
summaries: An LO representative suggests that raising the inflation target could be useful during the green transition, arguing that a low target can obstruct the relative price changes needed to shift demand away from fossil energy.
