The representative stresses that changing the target would not resolve the current supply-driven inflation problem.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO urges mandate clarification over Norges Bank’s rapid rate increases
summaries: LO criticizes Norges Bank for raising interest rates too quickly and sharply in response to imported inflation, arguing that this unnecessarily harms households and the domestic economy. It calls for greater weight on domestic conditions and employment, and asks the government or parliament to clarify the bank’s mandate if the bank does not change its interpretation. LO also advocates a review of the mandate’s weighting of domestic versus foreign conditions, saying five years have passed since the new central bank law. The discussion cites the LO leader’s call for Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre to take action on interest rates.

An LO adviser argues that Norges Bank’s use of employment and unemployment to reduce inflation reverses Norway’s economic-policy goals and constrains fiscal policy because policymakers fear triggering further rate increases. The adviser says Støre should not set interest rates, but the government and parliament should determine the mandate and guide its interpretation, and cites the Gjedrem committee’s recommendation for an evaluation after five years as grounds for a review now.

LO argues that Norges Bank must restrain further rate increases because Norway’s wage-setting model will prevent imported inflation from becoming entrenched regardless of rate hikes. It calls the reliance on heavily indebted households to transmit monetary tightening, largely justified by the krone exchange rate, untenable. LO says rate increases have depressed domestic demand and harmed housing, and rejects using that policy-driven downturn to moderate industrial wage demands in the spring settlement. It expects worsening economic conditions to force Norges Bank to reverse its rate increases and eventually cut rates.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO criticizes Norges Bank’s rate hikes and demands greater attention to employment
summaries: LO, chiefly through its chief economist Bjørnstad, has argued that Norges Bank should stop raising interest rates because inflation is imported and the hikes unnecessarily damage construction and other struggling industries. The story discusses the bank’s updated monetary-policy strategy, which emphasizes employment even when inflation deviates from target, as a possible response to LO’s criticism. The governor also countered the argument about imported inflation by stating that the bank can influence import prices in kroner through the exchange rate.

NORGES_BANK.title: Politicians propose commission on the krone
summaries: Several prominent politicians have raised the possibility of a commission on the krone. Asked whether Norges Bank could undertake such work internally, Governor Ida Wallenbakke said the bank already devotes substantial resources to understanding the foreign-exchange market, the drivers of the krone exchange rate and its effects on Norway’s economy.

Erna Solberg expressed openness to a krone commission proposed by Venstre. Governor Ida Wallenbakke welcomed bringing more knowledge to light but stressed that any commission would need a clear, narrowly defined mandate. She also said the threshold for intervening in the krone exchange rate should be high.

In discussing the proposed commission, Governor Ida Wallenbakke stressed the need to communicate existing knowledge, including research from Norges Bank, more effectively. A participant interpreted her insistence on a narrowly defined mandate as a warning against a commission being seen as opening debate on tying the krone to the euro, which could send damaging signals to currency markets.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO demands new Norges Bank mandate to secure rate cuts
summaries: LO is criticizing Norges Bank after it did not deliver an anticipated March interest-rate cut and is demanding a change to the bank’s mandate to secure lower rates for its members. LO attributes the decision to keep rates unchanged to attention to chocolate prices. It seeks a mandate change rather than replacing the people running the bank.

NORGES_BANK.title: Government repeatedly promises interest-rate cuts
summaries: The Norwegian government has repeatedly said an interest-rate cut would come, alongside promises to restore order to the economy and end high living and electricity costs. Norges Bank nevertheless kept its policy rate unchanged on May 8.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO demands Norges Bank accept negotiated wage growth without raising rates
summaries: LO leader Kine Asper Visnes told NRK that Norges Bank must accept wage growth negotiated with internationally exposed industries without blaming the settlement for inflation or counteracting it with interest-rate increases. The story describes this as a continuing LO demand, also voiced by her predecessor and supported by LO economist Roger Bjørnstad. The current wage settlement has a 4.4% framework.
LO leader Kine Asper Visnes said Norges Bank risks ruining the wage settlement if it raises interest rates, calling such a move interference in the wage negotiations.

NORGES_BANK.title: Magne Mogstad calls for earlier and larger Norges Bank rate cuts
summaries: Economist Magne Mogstad said the central bank should have cut interest rates much more and much earlier, and signalled that approach. He argued that inflation concerns were misplaced in debates about oil-revenue spending and wage bargaining, and that monetary policy should address aggregate prices.

NORGES_BANK.title: LO challenges Norges Bank’s mandate and interest-rate increases
summaries: LO has called for changes to Norges Bank’s mandate and criticized its interest-rate increases, questioning whether monetary policy achieves its intended goals. The criticism is part of a debate over wage formation under the frontfag model and the central bank’s responsibility for controlling inflation.

OPEC.title: Biden criticizes Saudi Arabia and Russia over oil production
summaries: Joe Biden chided Saudi Arabia and Russia for not producing more oil ahead of Thursday's OPEC+ meeting.

PBOC.title: US demands yuan stability in trade negotiations
summaries: The US is asking China to keep the yuan stable to prevent Beijing from devaluing its currency to counter American tariffs. The request calls for the PBOC to intervene more proactively to maintain currency stability.

PBOC.title: Trump accuses China of currency manipulation
summaries: President Trump tweeted that China and the EU were manipulating their currencies and pumping money into their systems, adding that the US should match them. His accusations came as US and Chinese officials prepared to resume trade talks.
The US formally named China a currency manipulator. The PBOC subsequently set a stronger yuan fixing at 6.9, acting to limit the currency's plunge.
Trump and the US Treasury labeled China a currency manipulator on Monday after the PBOC allowed the yuan to weaken below a key level, accusing China of seeking an unfair trade advantage.
Trump tweeted on August 8 that he was not pleased with the very strong dollar, as US-China trade talks increasingly centered on the Chinese currency.

PBOC.title: Schumer urges Treasury to label China a currency manipulator
summaries: Chuck Schumer urged the US Treasury to label China a currency manipulator shortly before the designation was made.

PBOC.title: State Council calls for timely reserve requirement cuts
summaries: China's State Council called for timely use of tools including broad and targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. Analysts expected the PBOC to follow with a cut, potentially as early as this week.

PBOC.title: Chinese national security officials urge PBOC monetary easing
summaries: Chinese national security officials are suggesting that the PBOC become more accommodative, particularly toward small and medium-sized financial entities, amid concerns that economic growth could slow in the second half of the year. This contrasts with the central bank's recent signals that it was satisfied with monetary policy and did not plan to change course.

PBOC.title: Beijing’s cryptocurrency ban
summaries: Beijing imposed its latest cryptocurrency ban, with the PBOC declaring late last week that all crypto-related transactions are illicit financial activities. Two major Bitcoin exchanges stopped accepting new registrations from Chinese users to comply.

PBOC.title: Beijing presses McDonald's to expand digital renminbi payments
summaries: Beijing is pressuring Olympic sponsor McDonald's to expand its Shanghai digital renminbi payments pilot to restaurants across China before the February Beijing Winter Olympics, supporting the PBOC's digital currency rollout. McDonald's declined to say whether it was under pressure.

PBOC.title: Beijing pushes monetary easing to support slowing growth
summaries: Beijing is described as dissatisfied with growth falling below five percent and moving into easing mode. The PBOC's loan prime rate cut follows a reserve requirement cut the previous week, passing lower bank funding costs to borrowers to support investment and financially strained property companies.

PBOC.title: Former PBOC governor urges stronger support for domestic demand and housing
summaries: Former People's Bank of China governor Yi Geng urged the central bank to do more to support China's economy, suggesting appropriately increasing macroeconomic policies to bolster domestic demand and providing more help to the struggling housing sector. He said China had experienced only six months of recovery from COVID lockdowns, compared with about a year for the rest of the world.

PBOC.title: Xi and Politburo call for forceful rate cuts
summaries: President Xi Jinping and China's top leaders called for forceful rate cuts, sufficient fiscal spending and measures to stabilize the property sector. The 24-member Politburo pledged to meet the annual economic goals, including 5% growth, and push for the real estate market to stop declining.

PBOC.title: López Obrador sought an advance on Banxico’s expected operating surplus
summaries: In 2020, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, advised by an unnamed external adviser, sought an advance from Banco de México on an expected operating surplus after the peso depreciated to 25 per dollar early in the pandemic. Former deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel recalled that the governing board adhered to the law and refused the advance. No operating surplus ultimately materialized for fiscal year 2020.

RBA.title: Frydenberg urges RBA to monitor housing market overheating
summaries: Federal Treasurer Josh Frydenberg said he had spoken to the Reserve Bank about rising house prices and urged the RBA and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority to keep a close watch on whether the housing market was overheating.

RBA.title: OECD calls for independent review of RBA
summaries: The OECD called for an independent review of the RBA over its repeated failure to meet economic forecasts, citing pandemic-related institutional and structural changes and the bank's use of unconventional policy instruments.

RBA.title: Treasurer expresses openness to independent RBA review
summaries: Federal Treasurer Josh Freidenberg expressed openness to an independent RBA review following the OECD's recommendation. He said the bank and federal government had worked well together but there was always a need to examine lessons learned.

RBA.title: Federal election campaigning expected to restrain RBA rate increases
summaries: Centennial Asset Management principal Matthew Kidman said campaigning for Australia's federal election, expected in May, had virtually begun, with politicians returning to Queensland, a key swing state. He predicted the election would keep the RBA timid on interest rates, prolonging lower rates in Australia.

RBA.title: Peter Costello urges RBA to prepare for interest rate rises
summaries: Before the RBA's rate decision, former federal treasurer Peter Costello urged the bank to prepare markets for interest rate rises and criticised its previous guidance that rates would not rise until 2024. He said rates should begin rising later in 2022 or early in 2023.
On Tuesday, former federal treasurer Peter Costello called on the Reserve Bank to lift interest rates.

RBA.title: Josh Frydenberg nudges RBA to wait for wage data before raising rates
summaries: Ahead of the RBA's May board meeting, Treasurer Josh Frydenberg reminded the bank that it was also waiting for wages growth to reach between 2 and 3 percent, with wage data not due for roughly three weeks. While acknowledging the RBA's independence, his remarks were described as a gentle nudge amid election campaigning and stronger-than-expected inflation figures.

RBA.title: Dutton criticizes RBA decision to omit King Charles III from five-dollar note
summaries: Opposition leader Peter Dutton criticized the RBA's decision to replace Queen Elizabeth II's portrait on the five-dollar note with a design honoring First Australians rather than King Charles III, calling it another attack on Australia's systems, society and institutions.

RBA.title: ACTU urges RBA to pause interest rate increases
summaries: The Australian Council of Trade Unions warned that the RBA's rate rises risk pushing the economy off a cliff and called for a pause in further increases after the ninth successive rise lifted the cash rate to 3.35 percent.

RBA.title: Calls to deny RBA Governor Lowe another term
summaries: Amid pressure over interest-rate decisions, political calls have been made not to give RBA Governor Philip Lowe another term when his current tenure expires in September. The story does not identify who made the calls.

RBA.title: Greens urge government to override further RBA rate rises
summaries: Greens leader Adam Bant called on the Labor government to go beyond jawboning and override the RBA if it raises interest rates again.

RBA.title: Daniel Andrews criticizes RBA rate rise as harming families
summaries: Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews criticized the RBA's latest 25-basis-point interest rate increase, saying it was 'smashing the place' and 'smashing families.' He questioned whether the increase would effectively reduce inflation.

RBA.title: Albanese criticizes RBA's incorrect interest rate prediction
summaries: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese criticized the RBA's prediction that interest rates would not increase until 2024. Asked about the budget's forecast that the cash rate would remain at 3.85 percent, after the RBA raised it to 4.1 percent, he referred questions to Treasury Secretary Stephen Kennedy and said the budget forecast was not as incorrect as the RBA's earlier prediction. He also affirmed that the RBA makes decisions independently of government.

RBA.title: Chalmers signals possible replacement of RBA governor Lowe
summaries: Treasurer Jim Chalmers hinted that Philip Lowe would not be reappointed as RBA governor, saying the next leader needs to take the bank into the future. He said he would announce next month who would serve as governor from September, when Lowe's term expires.

The Australian government decided not to reappoint Philip Lowe following criticism of the RBA's performance and an independent review recommending major institutional changes. Deputy governor Michelle Bullock will replace him in September for a seven-year term, becoming the first woman to lead the RBA.
Chalmers said the decision not to renew Lowe's contract was not about one person and emphasized incoming governor Michelle Bullock's fierce independence and the respect she commands.

RBA.title: Calls for RBA governor Phil Lowe to resign
summaries: Before his departure, Phil Lowe faced calls to resign and public condemnation over accusations that he had misled Australians about future interest rate increases.

RBA.title: Government review prompts RBA governance overhaul
summaries: A government review resulted in reforms that new governor Michelle Bullock must implement, including a monetary policy committee with external experts, reducing annual policy meetings from 11 to eight, and press conferences after every meeting. External committee appointees are also expected to communicate publicly about monetary policy.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers will bring overhaul legislation to Parliament this week. It would create a separate governance board, focus the bank's mandate on inflation and unemployment with an inflation target at the midpoint of the 2–3 percent band, expand authority over payment services such as Apple Pay and Google Pay, and repeal the treasurer's power to override monetary policy decisions. The government is also formalising a statement on the conduct of monetary policy with Michelle Bullock, expected before year-end.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers released a new statement on the conduct of monetary policy implementing non-legislative recommendations of the independent RBA review. He dropped a proposal requiring equal consideration of full employment and inflation in favour of a less specific dual mandate allowing significant central-bank discretion. The statement says the timeframe for achieving 2.5 percent inflation depends on economic circumstances and should balance price stability and full employment where necessary. Despite RBA resistance, the bank agreed to publish unattributed board votes on interest-rate decisions after each meeting and require board members to give at least one speech or public engagement annually.

RBA.title: Chalmers suggests RBA need not raise rates
summaries: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has suggested over the past couple of weeks that interest rates do not need to rise, putting pressure on new RBA governor Michelle Bullock ahead of a board meeting widely expected to increase the cash rate to 4.35 percent.

The RBA raised the cash rate from 4.1 percent to 4.35 percent despite Chalmers' stated desire that rates not increase. Chalmers said the decision was in the interest of fighting inflation, which he noted extended beyond headline price pressures or higher oil prices.

RBA.title: Taylor seeks safeguards against partisan RBA board appointments
summaries: Shadow Treasurer Angus Taylor has indicated support for most proposed RBA reforms but raised concerns about ensuring appointment processes are followed to avoid partisan board selections.

RBA.title: Chalmers challenges RBA assessment of government spending and inflation
summaries: Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers publicly disputed the RBA's assessment that government spending was prolonging inflation following its decision to hold interest rates. He rejected Governor Michelle Bullock's assessment of excess demand, arguing that economic data and public feedback did not support claims the economy was running too hot. He said government policies were lowering living costs and budget spending was not the primary determinant of prices.

RBA.title: Prime Minister rejects RBA criticism of government spending
summaries: The Prime Minister rejected Governor Michelle Bullock's suggestion that government spending was contributing to Australia's ongoing inflation challenge.

RBA.title: Government offers RBA reform concessions to secure coalition support
summaries: Treasurer Jim Chalmers offered concessions to secure coalition support for splitting the RBA board into monetary policy and governance boards. He agreed to retain the treasurer's power to override interest rate decisions in special circumstances and accepted the coalition's demand to transfer all six external members of the existing board to the new monetary policy board.

Shadow Treasurer Angus Taylor said the coalition would oppose splitting the RBA board unless all six current external members joined the proposed nine-member interest-rate-setting board, warning that the plans left open the possibility of a politicized board 'stitch up'. Chalmers called the coalition's decision irresponsible and disappointing and said he would consider negotiating with the Greens.

RBA.title: Chalmers blames high interest rates for economic weakness, then walks back remarks
summaries: In a Sunday pre-GDP statement warning of a soft result, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said interest rates were "smashing the economy," prompting coverage that he was blaming the RBA. On Tuesday, he walked back his remarks, saying he and the RBA were working well together to address high inflation.

Following the June-quarter GDP release, Jim Chalmers issued a statement blaming weak growth on global economic uncertainty, higher interest rates and persistently high, though slowing, inflation. He said the figures vindicated the government's budget approach, arguing that without government spending there would have been no economic growth over the quarter.

In her first speech since Chalmers's remarks, Governor Michelle Bullock attributed economic pressures to inflation and declined to comment on the treasurer's statement. She warned that failure to return inflation to target in a timely manner would likely increase the share of borrowers whose incomes do not cover expenses, particularly among lower-income households.

Bullock said financially stressed borrowers had cut spending to essentials, traded down to lower-quality goods and services, dipped into savings or worked extra hours, and some might ultimately sell their homes. She said this was not an overall financial stability risk and reiterated that reducing inflation remained the RBA's primary focus despite its dual mandate to achieve full employment.

Chalmers ruled out changes to the RBA's inflation target, saying he absolutely endorsed it, while emphasizing the bank's dual mandate of targeting full employment. He also said he and Governor Michelle Bullock were aligned in fighting inflation.

RBA.title: Wayne Swan accuses RBA of prioritizing economic dogma
summaries: Former Labor treasurer Wayne Swan accused the RBA of punching itself in the face and putting economic dogma ahead of rational economic decision-making.

RBA.title: Greens demand retention of Treasurer's RBA veto power
summaries: The Greens said any new RBA reform legislation must retain the Treasurer's existing veto power over the Reserve Bank, which has never been used in the bank's 64-year history.

RBA.title: Greens demand interest rate cut in exchange for RBA reform support
summaries: The Greens demanded an interest rate cut in exchange for supporting legislation to create a specialist RBA monetary policy board. The government said it would not work with the Greens on that basis, leaving the reform plans apparently stalled and the six current external board members continuing to set rates alongside senior management.

RBA.title: Government RBA board changes seen as push for rate cuts
summaries: The story reports a market perception that the government wants to change the RBA board to increase the probability of an interest rate cut. The market is waiting to see the RBA's actions before judging the changes.

RBA.title: Chalmers calls for ending debit card surcharges
summaries: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has said he wants debit card surcharges abolished from next year, subject to the Reserve Bank agreeing. The RBA is reviewing surcharges and the broader payments system and has called for submissions.

RBA.title: Dutton pushes for RBA rate cut
summaries: Opposition leader Peter Dutton is pushing for an RBA rate cut ahead of the federal election. The story also reports calls for a cut from unnamed politicians on both sides of the aisle.

RBA.title: Australian government pressures RBA to cut interest rates
summaries: The story reports Australian government pressure on the RBA to lower interest rates. The RBA unexpectedly kept rates unchanged, postponing a cut that economists and markets had anticipated.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers expressed disappointment in a considered statement, saying the unchanged rate was not the result millions of Australians had hoped for or markets had expected. He stressed substantial and sustained progress on inflation, noting that interest rates had already been cut twice in five months.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the latest inflation data showed how well Australia was performing in the fight against inflation. Annual headline inflation fell to 2.1%, while underlying inflation was 2.6%, within the RBA's 2–3% target range.

RBA.title: Albanese denies targeting RBA Governor with inflation remarks
summaries: At an economic reform roundtable in Canberra, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese criticised economists who believed inflation could not fall without unemployment rising, saying that was not his government's approach. RBA Governor Michelle Bullock was seated three seats away. The Prime Minister's office rejected claims that the remarks were directed at her.

RBA.title: Hogan urges aggressive RBA rate hikes and warns of political consequences
summaries: Warren Hogan, managing director of EQ Economics and economic adviser at Judo Bank, urged the RBA to reverse its 2025 rate cuts, raise rates by 40 basis points at its next meeting and reach 4.5% by May, with rates potentially needing to reach 5%. He said the board and senior management must prove themselves, warning that failure to act would make the next change of government disastrous for them.

RBA.title: Government backing of RBA narrow-path strategy
summaries: Hogan said the federal government had endorsed and probably driven the RBA’s narrow-path strategy, which he criticised for putting insufficient emphasis on inflation. He also accused the government of encouraging the RBA’s use of global events and soft economic data as excuses not to tighten policy sufficiently.

RBA.title: Challenge to Treasury secretary’s RBA board membership
summaries: At Senate estimates, Governor Michelle Bullock pushed back against suggestions that Treasury Secretary Jenny Wilkinson’s membership on the RBA Monetary Policy Board threatened central bank independence because of her government role.

RBA.title: Canavan accuses RBA of gaslighting the public
summaries: National Senator Matt Canavan suggested the RBA was gaslighting Australians by saying the economy was doing well when people did not feel it was. Governor Michelle Bullock rejected the criticism and explained the bank’s assessment.

RBA.title: Chalmers attacks former RBA governor Lowe over spending criticism
summaries: Treasurer Jim Chalmers suggested former RBA governor Phil Lowe’s criticism of government spending reflected resentment that Chalmers had not extended his tenure. Lowe had argued that spending and handouts such as energy rebates prop up demand, complicate the central bank’s job and keep interest rates higher for longer.

RBA.title: Chalmers challenges Bullock on unemployment needed to curb inflation
summaries: Treasurer Jim Chalmers rejected RBA governor Michelle Bullock's suggestion that unemployment may need to reach five percent, arguing that inflation can fall without unemployment rising. Ahead of the RBA's interest rate decision, he cited periods of low unemployment alongside moderating inflation in the past couple of years.

RBI.title: Arun Jaitley and finance ministry blame RBI supervision for PNB fraud
summaries: Following disclosure of the PNB fraud, the finance ministry accused RBI of failing to regulate banks properly. Finance Minister Arun Jaitley said regulators should act as the 'third eye' but that politicians, rather than regulators, were held accountable. RBI Governor Urjit Patel responded by calling for RBI to have the same powers to regulate public-sector banks as private banks.

RBI.title: Tech founders urge RBI to reconsider Paytm Payments Bank decision
summaries: Earlier this week, founders of various tech companies wrote to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and RBI Governor Shaktikanta Das, urging review and reconsideration of RBI's decision on Paytm Payments Bank.

RBI.title: Chief economic adviser and senior ministers push exclusion of food inflation
summaries: The chief economic adviser proposed excluding food inflation from headline inflation in a news article, describing it as his personal view. Senior ministers subsequently highlighted the proposal, adding pressure for a change to the inflation framework that incoming RBI governor Malhotra may have to address.

RBI.title: India's finance minister criticizes RBI's high borrowing costs
summaries: About a month before the governor's appointment a year ago, India's finance minister openly expressed frustration that the RBI had kept borrowing costs high despite slowing growth, while inflation was at the upper end of its 6 percent target.

RBNZ.title: Government directs RBNZ to curb overheated housing market
summaries: The New Zealand government told RBNZ to keep a lid on the overheated housing market. The story reports that this could require an increase in the official interest rate and that New Zealand bond yields surged following the directive.

RBNZ.title: New Zealand foreign ministry rebukes RBNZ governor for signing Powell support statement
summaries: New Zealand’s foreign ministry rebuked RBNZ Governor Anna Breman for signing a statement supporting Jerome Powell and central bank independence without consulting politicians.

RBZ.title: Zimbabwe government directs RBZ to print money to finance deficits
summaries: The Zimbabwean government has dealt with funding shortfalls for more than a decade and a half by telling the RBZ to print more money, including to cover spending on roads. The central bank governor has now committed to ending the bank's longstanding practice of printing money to finance budget deficits.

SARB.title: Presión política para ampliar el mandato del SARB al empleo
summaries: Desde el poder político en Sudáfrica se pide ampliar el mandato del SARB para promover el empleo. El banco central está rechazando esa demanda.

SNB.title: Swiss authorities coordinate Credit Suisse rescue
summaries: Swiss authorities brokered UBS's $3.25 billion takeover of Credit Suisse after a $54 billion credit line from the Swiss National Bank proved insufficient to stem outflows. UBS was instructed to begin takeover preparations amid fears that Credit Suisse would otherwise go bankrupt.

The Swiss federal government brokered the merger without a shareholder vote and imposed its terms on the banks. The SNB guaranteed approximately $100 billion in liquidity, while the government guaranteed coverage of approximately 9 billion francs in Credit Suisse-related losses for UBS. Approximately $17 billion in Credit Suisse AT1 bonds were written down to zero while shareholders received consideration.

TCMB.title: Erdogan removes TCMB governor
summaries: President Erdogan removed the central bank governor a week before the report, raising concerns about central bank independence and Turkey's financial stability.

TCMB.title: Erdogan promises significantly lower interest rates
summaries: President Erdogan promised significantly lower interest rates by the end of 2019. The report said the new central bank governor was expected to cut rates significantly, raising concerns about a repeat of the previous year's lira crisis.

On July 25, newly appointed governor Uysal delivered a larger-than-expected 425-basis-point benchmark rate cut to 19.75%, the biggest reduction in at least 17 years. A commentator said the cut signaled that Uysal would closely follow President Erdogan's instructions to cut interest rates as fast as possible.

TCMB.title: Erdogan pushes interest rates toward single digits in 2020
summaries: Ahead of TCMB's rate decision, President Erdogan said interest rates would move to single digits in 2020, reinforcing his position that lower borrowing costs reduce inflation.

TCMB.title: Erdogan dismisses TCMB governor following rate hike
summaries: President Erdogan fired TCMB governor Naci Agbal after a 200-basis-point interest rate hike, surprising analysts who had assumed Erdogan supported the increase. The dismissal triggered sharp selloffs in the lira and Turkish stocks and speculation that the central bank would resume cutting rates.

TCMB.title: Erdogan calls for TCMB interest rate cuts
summaries: President Erdogan has been calling for an interest rate cut for some time. With inflation still a major constraint, all 20 economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect TCMB to hold rates at 19% at its August 12 decision.

TCMB.title: Erdogan replaces finance minister amid dispute over rate cuts
summaries: President Erdogan replaced Finance Minister Lutfi Ervan following a rift over TCMB's aggressive interest-rate cuts despite high inflation. His replacement, former Deputy Finance Minister Nureddin Nebati, has recently voiced support for Erdogan's campaign against high interest rates.

The newly appointed finance minister is from Erdogan's own party. The story describes concern that the consolidation of officials who publicly agree with Erdogan leaves no one in authority to push for a reversal of his interest-rate policy.

TCMB.title: Erdogan orders TCMB interest-rate cuts despite high inflation
summaries: President Erdogan ordered TCMB to lower interest rates despite inflation around 20%; the bank cut rates by four percentage points from September. Last week, Erdogan defended low rates as supporting production and exports.
Erdogan advocates lower rates based on his belief that higher interest rates cause inflation.

In recent weeks, Erdogan has repeatedly invoked Islam's prohibition of interest to justify low rates. He continues to defend his economic model despite inflation reaching 36%, and advisers are developing policy documents to provide a theoretical justification for it.

TCMB.title: Erdogan dismisses three governors over opposition to rate cuts
summaries: Erdogan has dismissed three TCMB governors who argued against further interest-rate cuts, warning that they would cause serious economic imbalances.

The story specifies that Erdogan dismissed the last somewhat independent TCMB governor in March because he had raised interest rates too quickly for Erdogan's liking. He was the third governor removed in two years; his successor is described as carrying out Erdogan's wishes.

TCMB.title: Turkish president opposes higher TCMB interest rates
summaries: Turkey's president opposes higher interest rates and wants growth at the cost of inflation ahead of elections next year. The story describes TCMB as beholden to his wishes, with its key rate at 14% despite inflation of 70%.

TCMB.title: Erdoğan says interest rates will continue to fall
summaries: President Erdoğan's recent statements that interest rates would continue to fall reinforced pressure on TCMB to maintain rate cuts, amid discussion of whether monetary policy would change after the election.

The story reports that under Erdoğan's pressure, TCMB cut interest rates from 24 percent to below 9 percent. Erdoğan opposed higher rates because he believed they increased inflation and that lower rates would boost investment and exports.

Following TCMB’s 6.5-percentage-point rate increase, commentators questioned whether President Erdoğan would permit substantially larger increases, casting doubt on the bank’s freedom to tighten policy sufficiently.

A commentator said TCMB’s new management operates under political constraints and suggested that an interest-rate ceiling of around 20 percent had been imposed. He said these constraints were pushing the bank toward alternative instruments rather than straightforward rate increases and also prevented aggressive sterilization of liquidity from exchange-protected deposit payments.

TCMB.title: Erdoğan asserts control over TCMB and fires its governor
summaries: The story recounts that Erdoğan began intervening in economic policy in 2018, declared that the central bank would have to answer to him, and subsequently fired its governor because interest rates were too high for his liking.

TCMB.title: Erdoğan fires a second TCMB governor
summaries: The story reports that Erdoğan fired a second central bank governor after dismissing the first, in the context of his opposition to high interest rates. It does not identify the governor or give a dismissal date.

TCMB.title: Erdoğan fires a third TCMB governor
summaries: The story reports that Erdoğan also fired a third central bank governor in the context of his opposition to high interest rates. It does not identify the governor or give a dismissal date.

TCMB.title: Government directs TCMB to support the lira instead of raising rates
summaries: Because Erdoğan opposed higher interest rates, the government had TCMB buy lira in foreign-exchange markets to support the currency. An economist estimated that TCMB spent over $170 billion on this effort since the end of 2021, depleting its foreign-currency reserves. The story reports that TCMB has now stepped back from supporting the lira.

TCMB.title: Erdoğan appoints Erkan as TCMB governor
summaries: After winning a third presidential term, Erdoğan appointed former Goldman Sachs executive Hafisa Gaya Erkan as central bank governor. She is expected to return Turkey to more orthodox monetary policy and raised the benchmark interest rate from 8.5 percent to 15 percent in her first major move.

TCMB.title: Government shifts exchange-protected deposit costs to TCMB
summaries: The story reports that responsibility for exchange-protected deposit costs previously borne by the Treasury has been transferred entirely to TCMB. A commentator criticized shifting a government burden onto the bank, saying it undermines the credibility of renewed institutional independence and obscures the budget deficit.

The commentator said the Treasury transferred all exchange-protected deposit costs to TCMB because it could no longer cover them. The discussion warned that continuing payments inject substantial lira liquidity, that further currency depreciation could cause costs to snowball, and that higher reserve requirements alone cannot provide lasting sterilization.

TCMB.title: Turkish politicians publicly urge interest-rate cuts
summaries: The discussion describes Turkish politicians making public statements urging lower interest rates and criticizing the central bank through the media. A participant cites newly accepted research finding that market interest rates rise after such statements, contrary to the politicians' stated aim.

TCMB.title: Concerns over political power to dismiss TCMB officials
summaries: The discussion highlights regulations allowing TCMB officials to be dismissed easily and cites a professor's proposal to change them to improve credibility. Selva Demiralp argues that setting wage increases according to a 36% inflation forecast requires granting TCMB full independence to achieve that target and prevent workers from being disadvantaged.

TCMB.title: Erdogan pushes TCMB to cut interest rates despite inflation
summaries: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan overcame bureaucratic resistance and got the central bank to cut interest rates in 2021 despite rising inflation, reflecting his conviction that high interest rates are bad. Rates fell to 8.5% in February 2023.

TCMB.title: Erdogan appoints new economic leaders in interest-rate policy reversal
summaries: In June 2023, Erdogan reversed his approach to interest rates and hired new economic leaders who began raising rates. By March 2024, the central bank had raised rates nine times since June, bringing them to 50%.

TCMB.title: Turkish president signals year-end interest-rate action
summaries: The Turkish president said the previous week that steps on interest rates toward year-end would bring falling inflation. The commentator interpreted the statement as potentially signaling a demand for rates to fall in line with inflation, which could put TCMB in a difficult position.

TCMB.title: Turkish minister signals reopening of swap channels after local elections
summaries: A participant reported that, at a meeting they attended, a Turkish minister signaled that restricted swap channels would reopen but that authorities were waiting until after local elections. The participant said the elections had since passed and argued that reopening was overdue given improved central-bank reserves and financial conditions.

TCMB.title: President argues that high interest rates fuel inflation
summaries: The discussion cites the Turkish president’s argument that interest rates cause inflation and that insufficient production is inflationary. A commentator invokes that presidential position while advocating an immediate TCMB rate cut, but distinguishes his own criticism of prolonged positive real interest rates from the president’s emphasis on nominal rates.

TCMB.title: Turkish political leadership reportedly pressures TCMB to cut interest rates
summaries: A commentator said Turkey’s political leadership had pressured TCMB to lower interest rates ahead of its latest meeting, at which the policy rate was held at 46%. The commentator suggested the bank had persuaded senior political authorities to wait another month because of heightened uncertainty.

TCMB.title: Election-related political constraints on TCMB rate increases
summaries: Commentators argued that approaching elections and the political leadership’s emphasis on preserving growth and employment could prevent TCMB from raising interest rates, despite its statement that all policy options remain available. One commentator linked this constraint to the president’s electoral priorities and expected political demands for wage increases ahead of 2027. These were presented as assessments of political constraints, not as reported direct instructions to TCMB.

TURKEY CENTRAL BANK.title: Erdogan pressures central bank to lower interest rates
summaries: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan opposes high interest rates, arguing that they cause inflation and calling them the mother and father of all evil. The central bank cut rates by two percentage points despite inflation around 20 percent; the story describes its repeated cuts as reflecting Erdogan's control.

TURKEY CENTRAL BANK.title: Erdogan dismisses three rate-setting committee members
summaries: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan recently fired three members of the central bank's rate-setting committee amid his opposition to high interest rates.

TURKEY CENTRAL BANK.title: Erdogan dismisses central bank governors
summaries: The story reports that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has fired several central bank governors over the past few years, in the context of his longstanding opposition to high interest rates.
